# Overview


This page is the entry point to the **mdSAM** repository: a companion codebase for the manuscript *Discovery of self-assembly motifs regulating membrane-protein organization and function* (Elazar, Trivedi, et al., Babu lab, St. Jude Children's Research Hospital). It contains 23 numbered analysis notebooks and the shared data tables they consume — everything needed to reproduce the computational analyses behind the paper's figures. Here you will learn what an mdSAM is, how the discovery pipeline works, how the repository is organised, and where to go next in the documentation.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L3)

## What is an mdSAM?

An **mdSAM** (membrane-disordered Self-Assembly Motif) is a short peptide motif — usually 7–9 residues long, with a median of 8 — located in an intrinsically disordered, solvent-exposed region of a transmembrane protein, predicted to self-assemble through beta-strand-mediated, amyloid-like interactions. The biological motivation is that cell-surface clustering of membrane proteins is central to many cellular processes, yet its molecular determinants remain elusive; the authors postulated that peptide motifs within disordered regions of transmembrane proteins may drive self-association and clustering.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L5-L12)

## How mdSAMs are discovered: the pipeline at a glance

The discovery workflow runs in three steps, each anchored to a specific data source and filter. First, a random-forest classifier is trained on WALTZ-DB 2.0 (1,402 hexapeptides: 510 amyloid-forming, 892 non-forming) using one-hot-encoded sequence plus summed beta-strand free energy, reaching F1 = 0.77 under stratified 5-fold cross-validation. Second, every hexapeptide window in human membrane proteins is scored; positive windows are called Self-Assembly Motifs (SAMs). Third, a SAM is promoted to an **mdSAM** only if it lies in a disordered region — AlphaFold pLDDT < 70, non-helical and solvent exposed, excluding transmembrane segments and signal peptides — with a ROC-derived threshold on consecutive positive windows defining the high-confidence set. The diagram below summarises this flow from training data to the final motif set.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["WALTZ-DB 2.0<br/>1,402 hexapeptides<br/>(510 amyloid / 892 non-forming)"] --> B["Random-forest classifier<br/>one-hot sequence + beta-strand energy<br/>F1 = 0.77"]
    B --> C["Score every hexapeptide window<br/>in human membrane proteins<br/>positive windows = SAM"]
    C --> D{"Disorder filter<br/>pLDDT < 70, non-helical,<br/>solvent exposed,<br/>no TM segments / signal peptides"}
    D -- passes --> E["Consecutive-window threshold<br/>(ROC-derived)"]
    D -- fails --> F["Discarded"]
    E --> G["High-confidence mdSAM set"]
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L13-L18)

The scale of the result explains why this repository spans so many notebooks: **1,425 high-confidence mdSAMs** were found in **945 membrane proteins** (about 20% of the 4,886 human membrane proteins analysed), with 91% of motifs sitting in N- or C-terminal tails and 72% of mdSAM-containing proteins carrying just a single motif. Crucially, the predictions were validated experimentally — of 44 synthesised mdSAM peptides, 36 (81%) gave a Thioflavin-T signal.

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Classifier training data | 1,402 WALTZ-DB 2.0 hexapeptides (510 amyloid-forming / 892 non-forming) |
| Classifier performance | F1 = 0.77, stratified 5-fold cross-validation |
| High-confidence mdSAMs | 1,425 |
| Proteins with mdSAMs | 945 (~20% of 4,886 human membrane proteins) |
| Motif length | 7–9 residues (median 8) |
| Motif location | 91% in N- or C-terminal tails |
| Single-motif proteins | 72% of mdSAM-containing proteins |
| Peptide validation | 36 / 44 synthesised peptides (81%) Thioflavin-T positive |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L11-L19)

## Repository layout

The repository is deliberately minimal: documentation, one folder of notebooks, and one folder of shared data. Notebooks are numbered **01–23 in pipeline order**, which doubles as a reading order for the analysis.

```
mdSAM/
├── README.md          # notebook map + figure-to-cell index
├── files/             # shared pickled pandas tables read by notebooks
│   ├── README.md
│   ├── dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl
│   └── hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl
└── notebooks/         # 23 analysis notebooks, outputs cleared
    ├── 01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb
    ├── ...
    └── 23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L23-L29)

Three shared tables in `files/` act as the backbone of the analysis — they are pickled pandas DataFrames loaded with `pd.read_pickle`, and the README also documents a `FIGURE_MAP.csv` as the machine-readable map from paper panel → notebook → cell. The mdSAM table is the primary input for most notebooks (motif sequences live in its `AAseq` column), while the other two provide protein-level context.

| File | Contents | Created by | Read by notebooks |
|---|---|---|---|
| `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl` | The mdSAM table (motif sequence in the `AAseq` column) | mdSAM identification pipeline (STAR Methods) | 05, 06, 07, 08, 09, 15, 18, 20, 21, 23 |
| `hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl` | Human transmembrane proteins with UniProt topology annotation | `03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb` | 03, 05, 06, 07, 08, 09, 15, 18, 20, 21, 23 |
| `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` | AlphaFold-derived per-protein annotations with ENSG gene IDs | `02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb` | 02, 03, 05, 06, 07, 08, 11, 15, 18, 19, 20, 21, 23 |

The following diagram shows how these pieces interact: notebooks read the shared tables from `files/`, and the README indexes which notebook and cell produced each paper panel.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph REPO["mdSAM repository"]
        R["README.md<br/>notebook map +<br/>panel-to-cell index"]
        subgraph NB["notebooks/ (01–23, pipeline order)"]
            N1["01–03: classifier<br/>& data preparation"]
            N2["04–09: discovery<br/>& diversity"]
            N3["10–12: in vitro<br/>self-assembly"]
            N4["13–16: cell-based<br/>clustering"]
            N5["17–19: HTR7 signalling<br/>& transcription"]
            N6["20–23: evolution"]
        end
        subgraph FL["files/ (shared tables)"]
            F1["dSAM_MPs_v_paper_...pkl"]
            F2["hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl"]
            F3["AF2_with_ENSG.pkl"]
        end
    end
    NB -- "pd.read_pickle('../files/...')" --> FL
    R -.->|"maps paper panels<br/>to notebook cells"| NB
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L23-L29), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L3-L9)

> [!TIP]
> Notebooks reference the shared tables as `../files/<name>`, so you must run every notebook with `notebooks/` as the working directory — launching it from the repository root will break the data paths.

## What the 23 notebooks do

Each notebook maps to a phase of the study, from building the classifier through computational characterisation to wet-lab assay analysis and evolutionary validation. The table below is the condensed map; the README carries the full per-notebook detail, including which paper panels each one draws.

| Group | Notebooks | Focus | Paper figures |
|---|---|---|---|
| Data preparation & classifier | 01–03 | Train/evaluate the WALTZ-DB random forest; build the shared AlphaFold residue table; sequence logos | Fig 1D; S1E–H |
| Discovery & diversity | 04–09 | PASTA comparison, UniProt keyword enrichment, sequence-space embedding, hyperLOPIT organelles, topology & membrane distance | Figs 1–2; S1–S2 |
| In vitro self-assembly | 10–12 | Thioflavin-T 96-well screens, GPCR proline mutants, Amytracker fluorescence | Fig 3; S3 |
| Cell-based clustering | 13–16 | TIRF puncta Poisson GLM, flow cytometry, BioGRID interactions, dSTORM cluster analysis | Figs 4–5; S5–S6 |
| HTR7 signalling & transcription | 17–19 | cAMP Emax/EC50, RNA-seq PCA/volcano, DESeq2 + GSEA | Fig 6 |
| Evolution | 20–23 | Alignment-based and ESM-embedding conservation, ortholog peptide ThT, overlap with LARKS/WIRS/FINCHES | Fig 7; S7 |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L35-L86)

## From notebook cell to paper figure

The repository is built for **figure-level reproducibility**: nearly every panel of the paper's main and supplementary figures is indexed to the exact notebook and 0-based cell index that draws it — for example, Figure 1D (classifier test-set performance) comes from `01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb`, cell 26. Notebooks are distributed with their **outputs cleared**, so you run a notebook to regenerate its plots; panels that are schematics, microscopy/EM images, NMR or mass-photometry data produced outside these notebooks are intentionally not listed. The full mapping lives in the [Figure-to-Notebook Reproducibility Map](9-figure-to-notebook-reproducibility-map) page.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L88-L96), [README.md](README.md#L242-L246)

## Conventions and safety notes

Two conventions matter before you dive in. First, **naming**: older notebooks call these motifs **dSAM** (disordered SAM), and the structured-region counterpart appears as **mSAM/sSAM/msSAM** — whenever you see `dSAM` in a file name or variable, it means mdSAM. Second, **data safety**: the `files/` tables are pickle files, which can execute code when loaded and depend on the pandas version used to write them — load them only from this repository with a compatible pandas version. The notebooks also rely on a broad set of Python packages (e.g. `Bio`, `Levenshtein`, `gseapy`, `logomaker`, `fcsparser`, `localcider`), listed in the README's "Running the notebooks" section.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L21), [README.md](README.md#L244-L250), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L13)

> [!TIP]
> The `dSAM` prefix persists in data files (`dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl`) and notebook names alike — searching the codebase for "dSAM" rather than "mdSAM" will find far more relevant code.

For a beginner, the natural progression follows the documentation's own pipeline logic: set up and run first, then understand the concept, then explore the machinery. Start with [Quick Start](2-quick-start) for environment setup and running your first notebook, then use [Repository Layout and Notebook Map](3-repository-layout-and-notebook-map) for a deeper tour of the file tree. From there, [mdSAM Concept and Discovery Rationale](4-mdsam-concept-and-discovery-rationale) explains the biology behind the filter chain, [Notebook Pipeline Architecture](5-notebook-pipeline-architecture) dissects how the 23 notebooks depend on each other, and [WALTZ-DB Random-Forest Classifier](6-waltz-db-random-forest-classifier) opens the technical deep dive at notebook 01.

| Step | Page | Why read it |

| 2 | [Repository Layout and Notebook Map](3-repository-layout-and-notebook-map) | Expanded tour of `notebooks/` and `files/` |

# Quick Start



This page gets you from a fresh clone to a verified, running environment in one session. The repository is a **notebook-only research codebase**: there is nothing to `pip install` from it and no package to import. Instead, you will (1) prepare a Python environment, (2) launch Jupyter from the correct directory, and (3) run a three-cell smoke-test notebook that touches every critical component — the shipped data tables, the plotting stack, and the output path. Everything you need ships in the repo except two optional dependency tiers explained below.

mdSAM stands for *membrane-disordered Self-Assembly Motif* — a short (7–9 residue) peptide inside a disordered, solvent-exposed region of a transmembrane protein, predicted to self-assemble via beta-strand, amyloid-like interactions. The notebooks reproduce the discovery, validation, and downstream analyses of that motif set.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L15), [README.md](README.md#L31-L37)

## Repository at a Glance

The project has a deliberately flat layout — two directories and two README files carry everything:

```
mdSAM/
├── README.md                  # paper context, notebook map, figure→cell index
├── files/
│   ├── README.md              # data dictionary for the shared pickle tables
│   ├── dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl   # mdSAM motif table (shipped)
│   ├── hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl                # human TM protein topology table (shipped)
│   └── placeholder
└── notebooks/
    ├── 01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb  # trains & saves the RF classifier
    ├── 02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb  # builds AF2_with_ENSG.pkl
    ├── 03…23_*.ipynb                      # analysis notebooks, numbered in pipeline order
    └── placeholder
```

The two-digit prefixes define execution order: `01`–`03` **build** models and tables, `04` onward **consume** them. All notebooks ship with their outputs cleared — you run them to regenerate the plots.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L31-L37), [README.md](README.md#L244-L246), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L3-L9)

## Prerequisites

| Requirement | Version / Notes | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Python | **3.9** (author kernel: 3.9.13) | Pinned by the notebook kernel metadata |
| Jupyter | any recent Notebook/JupyterLab | Notebooks were written for interactive sessions |
| Core scientific stack | pandas, numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, matplotlib, seaborn | Used by essentially every notebook |
| Smoke-test extras | tqdm, Levenshtein | Imported by the first notebook you will run |
| Full analysis stack | ~20 more packages (see table below) | Only needed for specific deep-dive notebooks |

The author kernel metadata pins Python **3.9.13**, so a 3.9 environment is the safest starting point. The README also warns that **pip package names can differ from import names** — for example, you `pip install biopython` but `import Bio`, and `pip install umap-learn` but `import umap`.

Sources: [notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb](notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb#L70-L86), [README.md](README.md#L250), [notebooks/05_uniprot_keyword_enrichment.ipynb](notebooks/05_uniprot_keyword_enrichment.ipynb#L18-L20)

The complete author-maintained import list lives in the README's *Running the notebooks* section — install lazily, per notebook, rather than up front.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L250), [notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb](notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb#L10-L25), [notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L9-L25)

## Environment Setup in Four Steps

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["1. Clone the repository"] --> B["2. Create a Python 3.9 environment"]
    B --> C["3. Install core packages"]
    C --> D["4. Launch Jupyter FROM notebooks/"]
    D --> E["Open 09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb"]
    E --> F["Run all 3 cells"]
    F --> G{"number_of_mdSAMs_per_protein.svg<br/>appears in notebooks/ ?"}
    G -- Yes --> H["Environment verified ✓"]
    G -- No --> I["Consult troubleshooting table"]
```

**Step 1 — Clone.** Standard clone of the `main` branch. Both data pickles come with the clone; no separate download step is needed for the smoke test.

**Step 2 — Create an environment.** Any workflow works (conda, venv, pyenv); the only hard constraint is Python 3.9 to match the author kernel:

```bash
conda create -n mdsam python=3.9 -y
conda activate mdsam
```

**Step 3 — Install the smoke-test package set** (extend later per notebook):

```bash
pip install jupyter pandas numpy scipy scikit-learn matplotlib seaborn tqdm Levenshtein
```

**Step 4 — Launch Jupyter from `notebooks/`, not the repo root.** This is the single most important detail in the whole setup. The notebooks load every shared table with the relative path `../files/<name>`, which only resolves when the notebook's working directory is `notebooks/`:

```bash
cd mdSAM/notebooks
jupyter lab   # or: jupyter notebook
```

> [!TIP]
> Launching Jupyter from the repo root instead of `notebooks/` is the #1 cause of `FileNotFoundError: '../files/...'` in this repository. Every shared table is addressed relative to `notebooks/`, by design.

Sources: [files/README.md](files/README.md#L11-L14), [README.md](README.md#L248), [notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb](notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb#L35-L36)

## Your First Run: the Three-Cell Smoke Test

Notebook `09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb` is the smallest notebook in the repository and the fastest end-to-end verification of your setup. It reproduces Figure 2E (mdSAMs per protein) in exactly three cells:

1. **Cell 1 — imports.** Loads only the core stack plus `tqdm` and `Levenshtein`; nothing exotic.
2. **Cell 2 — data load.** Reads the two shipped tables: `pd.read_pickle('../files/hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl')` and `pd.read_pickle('../files/dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl')`.
3. **Cell 3 — plot.** Counts proteins carrying 1, 2, or ≥3 mdSAMs and writes `number_of_mdSAMs_per_protein.svg` into `notebooks/`.

Run all three cells (*Run → Run All Cells*). **Success criterion:** the SVG file appears in `notebooks/` and the bar chart renders inline — your environment, working directory, data paths, and plotting stack are all confirmed at once.

> [!TIP]
> Notebook 09 doubles as a data-integrity check: if either shipped pickle fails to load here, the problem is your pandas version or working directory — not the notebook. Fix this before attempting any other notebook.

Sources: [notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb](notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb#L10-L25), [notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb](notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb#L35-L36), [notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb](notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb#L65), [README.md](README.md#L62-L63)

## Understanding the Data: Three Tiers

Not every notebook can run out of the box, and the reason is a clean three-tier data model. Knowing which tier a notebook depends on tells you exactly how much setup it needs:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph T1["Tier 1 · Shipped in files/ — ready now"]
        A["dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl<br/>(mdSAM motifs, AAseq column)"]
        B["hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl<br/>(human TM proteins + topology)"]
    end
    subgraph T2["Tier 2 · Regenerated by the early pipeline"]
        C["AF2_with_ENSG.pkl<br/>(created by notebook 02)"]
        D["Trained RF classifier<br/>(saved by notebook 01)"]
    end
    subgraph T3["Tier 3 · External downloads at hardcoded paths"]
        E["WALTZ-DB export CSV"]
        F["UniProt keyword / id-mapping TSVs"]
        G["IUPred2A library"]
    end
    T3 --> T2
    T1 --> R1["Notebook 09 and friends:<br/>run immediately"]
    T2 --> R2["Full pipeline:<br/>reproduces every figure"]
```

| Tier | Files | Status | Needed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1 — Shipped** | `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl`, `hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl` | In `files/` after cloning | Notebooks 05–09, 15, 18, 20, 21, 23 |
| **2 — Regenerated** | `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` (by notebook 02), trained classifier (by notebook 01) | Appears only after running 01/02 | Notebooks 03, 05–08, 11, 15, 18–21, 23 |
| **3 — External** | WALTZ-DB export, UniProt TSVs, IUPred2A library | Not in repo; fetched by author-local absolute paths | Notebooks 01, 02, 05 |

Tier 3 is the practical surprise for newcomers: the early pipeline notebooks contain author-local paths such as `/Users/aelazar/Downloads/waltzdb_export.csv` (notebook 01), `/Users/aelazar/Downloads/keywords_all_2023_10_27.tsv` (notebook 05), and `sys.path.append('/Users/aelazar/Downloads/iupred2a/')` (notebook 02). To run Tier 2/3 notebooks you either edit those paths to your own downloads or restructure them into the expected format — the data sources are named in the code comments (e.g., WALTZ-DB at `waltzdb.switchlab.org`).

A safety note applies to all tiers: **pickle files can execute code when loaded** and are sensitive to the pandas version used to write them. Load them only from this repository, with a compatible pandas.

Sources: [files/README.md](files/README.md#L5-L9), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L13-L14), [notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L113), [notebooks/05_uniprot_keyword_enrichment.ipynb](notebooks/05_uniprot_keyword_enrichment.ipynb#L33-L36), [notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L18-L19)

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Root cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `FileNotFoundError: '../files/...'` | Jupyter launched from repo root | `cd notebooks/` and relaunch — all table paths are relative to it |
| `ModuleNotFoundError` on first import | Missing package, or pip-name mismatch | Install from the package table (e.g., `umap-learn` not `umap`) |
| Unpickling / version error on `read_pickle` | pandas version differs from the one that wrote the tables | Use a pandas version compatible with the authors' (Python 3.9 environment) |
| `FileNotFoundError: /Users/aelazar/...` | Tier 3 external data not present on your machine | Download the named source (e.g., WALTZ-DB export) and edit the path in the cell |
| Plots missing after running a notebook | Expected behavior | Notebooks ship with outputs cleared; running regenerates them |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L244-L250), [README.md](README.md#L246-L247), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L13-L14), [notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L113)

# Repository Layout and Notebook Map



This page is your orientation map for the **mdSAM** repository — the analysis code behind the manuscript *Discovery of self-assembly motifs regulating membrane-protein organization and function* (Elazar, Trivedi, et al., Babu lab, St. Jude). The repo is deliberately minimal: a root `README.md`, one directory of **23 numbered Jupyter notebooks**, and one directory of **shared pickled data tables**. If you understand these three pieces, you can navigate every result in the paper. This page covers what lives where, how the pieces connect, and which notebook produces which figure panel.

An **mdSAM** (membrane-disordered Self-Assembly Motif) is a short 7–9 residue peptide in a disordered, solvent-exposed region of a transmembrane protein, predicted to self-assemble via beta-strand-mediated, amyloid-like interactions. Keep that definition in mind — every notebook, table, and figure in this repository ultimately traces back to finding or validating these motifs.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L21)

## The Two-Directory Layout

The repository has exactly three top-level entries: the root README, `notebooks/`, and `files/`. The actual tree on disk is:

```
.
├── README.md            # project overview, notebook descriptions, figure-to-notebook map
├── files/               # shared input tables (pickled pandas DataFrames)
│   ├── README.md        # documents each pickle: contents, producer, consumers
│   ├── dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl
│   └── hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl
└── notebooks/           # 23 notebooks, numbered 01–23 in pipeline order
    ├── 01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb
    ├── 02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb
    ├── ⋮
    └── 23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb
```

The README's *Repository contents* block summarizes this structure in three lines: `notebooks/` holds the 23 analysis notebooks numbered in pipeline order (with outputs cleared), `files/` holds shared input tables, and it also lists a `FIGURE_MAP.csv` described as a "machine-readable map: paper panel → notebook → cell." Note that `FIGURE_MAP.csv` does **not** appear in the current repository tree — the same panel→notebook→cell mapping is available as human-readable tables in the README itself (see [Tracing Paper Figures Back to Notebooks](#tracing-paper-figures-back-to-notebooks) below). Similarly, `files/` ships two of the three pickles its README describes; the third, `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl`, is generated at runtime by notebook 02.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L23-L29), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L1-L9)

The two directories have clearly separated roles:

| Directory | Role | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| `notebooks/` | All analysis logic | 23 `.ipynb` files, two-digit prefix = pipeline order, outputs cleared |
| `files/` | Shared data layer | Pickled pandas DataFrames read with `pd.read_pickle`; ships `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl` and `hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl` |
| `README.md` (root) | Documentation hub | Project abstract, per-notebook task tables, complete figure→notebook→cell map, run instructions, package list |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L25-L29), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L5-L13)

## Architecture at a Glance

Before reading the notebook map, it helps to see the data flow. The central pattern of this repository is a **shared-table hub**: notebooks don't pass data to each other directly. Instead, a few notebooks *write* pickle tables into `files/`, and most later notebooks *read* them back with relative paths like `../files/<name>`. Three tables form this hub:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P["mdSAM identification pipeline<br/>(STAR Methods, external to these notebooks)"]
    N02["notebook 02<br/>AlphaFold residue table"]
    N03["notebook 03<br/>sequence logos"]
    NA["notebooks 04–23<br/>analysis notebooks"]
    subgraph F["files/ — shared data tables"]
        D["dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl<br/>mdSAM motifs, AAseq column"]
        A["AF2_with_ENSG.pkl<br/>AlphaFold annotations + ENSG"]
        H["hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl<br/>human TM proteins + topology"]
    end
    P --> D
    N02 --> A
    N03 --> H
    A --> N03
    A --> NA
    D --> NA
    H --> NA
```

Reading the diagram left to right: the mdSAM identification pipeline (described in the paper's STAR Methods, not part of these notebooks) produces the main mdSAM motif table. Notebook 02 builds the AlphaFold-derived per-residue table, notebook 03 builds the human transmembrane-protein table, and notebooks 04–23 consume all of these. For beginners, the practical consequence is that **notebook 02 is a prerequisite for nearly everything else**, because it writes the most widely consumed table.

Sources: [files/README.md](files/README.md#L5-L9), [README.md](README.md#L40-L41)

## The Notebook Map: 23 Notebooks in Pipeline Order

Every notebook filename follows the same convention: a two-digit prefix (`01`–`23`) indicating pipeline order, followed by a topic slug. The root README groups the notebooks into six thematic stages that mirror the manuscript's figure sequence — from data preparation, through motif discovery and characterization, into experimental validation, and finally evolutionary analysis. The tables below condense each notebook's task and the paper panels it produces. Cell numbers referenced in the README are 0-based indices into each notebook's `cells` list.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L31-L33), [README.md](README.md#L26)
