## The Shared Data Tables in `files/`

The `files/` directory is the data backbone of the repository. Its three tables are pickled pandas DataFrames — Python objects serialized to disk — that notebooks load with `pd.read_pickle`. One critical convention governs all of this: notebooks reference the tables as `../files/<name>`, so you must **run every notebook with `notebooks/` as your working directory**, or the relative paths will break.

> [!TIP]
> The single most common failure mode for newcomers is launching Jupyter from the repository root. Because notebooks hard-code `../files/` paths, always start your session from inside `notebooks/` (e.g., `cd notebooks && jupyter lab`).

| File | Contents | Created by | Read by notebooks |
|---|---|---|---|
| `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl` | The mdSAM table loaded by the analysis notebooks; motif sequence in the `AAseq` column | mdSAM identification pipeline (STAR Methods) | 05, 06, 07, 08, 09, 15, 18, 20, 21, 23 |
| `hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl` | Human transmembrane proteins with UniProt topology annotation | `03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb` | 03, 05, 06, 07, 08, 09, 15, 18, 20, 21, 23 |
| `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` | AlphaFold-derived per-protein annotations with Ensembl gene IDs (ENSG) | `02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb` | 02, 03, 05, 06, 07, 08, 11, 15, 18, 19, 20, 21, 23 |

> [!TIP]
> `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` is *not* shipped in the repository — it only exists after you run notebook 02, which writes it via `AF2.to_pickle`. Since it is the most widely consumed table (14 notebooks), running notebook 02 first is effectively mandatory. Also handle pickles with care: they can execute code when loaded and depend on the pandas version used to write them, so only load them from this repository.

Sources: [files/README.md](files/README.md#L3-L14), [README.md](README.md#L244-L248)

## Tracing Paper Figures Back to Notebooks

A distinguishing feature of this repository is its **figure traceability**: the README contains complete tables mapping every notebook-produced figure panel to the exact notebook and cell that draws it, covering Figure 1 through Figure 7 plus supplementary figures S1, S2, S3, S6, and S7. For example, Fig 1D (RF classifier performance) comes from `01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb` cell 26, and Fig 2D (distance to nearest membrane leaflet) comes from `08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb` cell 45. Two caveats keep these tables honest: cell indices are 0-based into the notebook's `cells` list, and panels that are schematics, microscopy/EM images, NMR, or mass-photometry data are deliberately excluded because they were produced outside these notebooks.

Notebooks are distributed with their outputs cleared — running a notebook regenerates its plots locally. The full per-figure breakdown deserves its own reference page, which the catalog provides at [Figure-to-Notebook Reproducibility Map](9-figure-to-notebook-reproducibility-map); the same information also exists in machine-readable form per the README's `FIGURE_MAP.csv` entry, though that file is not present in the current tree.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L88-L242)

## Naming and Terminology Conventions

Three conventions will save you confusion when reading code and file names. First, the **two-digit prefixes are pipeline order**, not arbitrary IDs — `05` means notebook 05, and `files/README.md` uses these same numbers in its consumer lists. Second, older notebooks use the term **dSAM** (disordered Self-Assembly Motif) and its structured-region counterpart **mSAM/sSAM/msSAM**; per the README, "dSAM" in any file name or variable name means **mdSAM** — hence the shipped file `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl` is the mdSAM table. Third, the notebooks were written for interactive sessions rather than as a formal package: there is no `src/` module or entry-point script, just 23 self-contained notebooks plus the shared pickle tables, which is why the README also enumerates the imported Python packages (`Bio`, `Levenshtein`, `logomaker`, `gseapy`, `fcsparser`, `localcider`, and others) rather than shipping a dependency file.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L21), [README.md](README.md#L244-L250), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L11)

## Suggested Reading Path

With the map above in hand, a logical progression through the rest of the catalog is: solidify the big picture with [Overview](1-overview) and get the environment running via [Quick Start](2-quick-start). Then follow the pipeline in execution order: [Notebook Pipeline Architecture](5-notebook-pipeline-architecture) explains how the 23 notebooks depend on each other, [WALTZ-DB Random-Forest Classifier](6-waltz-db-random-forest-classifier) deep-dives notebook 01, and [AlphaFold-Based Disorder Filtering](7-alphafold-based-disorder-filtering) covers notebook 02 — the table-builder you must run first. For the data layer, keep [Shared Data Tables Reference](8-shared-data-tables-reference) open as a lookup companion to this page, and use [Figure-to-Notebook Reproducibility Map](9-figure-to-notebook-reproducibility-map) whenever you want to jump straight from a paper panel to its generating cell. When you are ready to adapt the methods to your own data, finish with [Reusing the Analysis Toolkit](27-reusing-the-analysis-toolkit).


# mdSAM Concept and Discovery Rationale



This page explains the central scientific idea behind the mdSAM repository: what an mdSAM is, why the discovery approach was designed the way it was, and how the evidence for the concept was assembled across 23 notebooks. It is a conceptual companion to the implementation-focused pages — the classifier mechanics live in [WALTZ-DB Random-Forest Classifier](6-waltz-db-random-forest-classifier), the disorder gate in [AlphaFold-Based Disorder Filtering](7-alphafold-based-disorder-filtering), and the shared input tables in [Shared Data Tables Reference](8-shared-data-tables-reference).

## From biological question to postulate

The work starts from an open problem: cell-surface clustering of membrane proteins is central to many cellular processes, yet the molecular determinants that drive this clustering remained elusive. The authors' postulate was that short peptide motifs inside **disordered regions** of transmembrane proteins — the flexible tails and loops flanking transmembrane helices — could drive self-association and clustering through amyloid-like interactions. Everything in this repository exists to test that one hypothesis systematically across the human membrane proteome.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L5-L7)

## What exactly is an mdSAM?

An **mdSAM** (membrane-disordered Self-Assembly Motif) is a short peptide motif — typically 7–9 residues with a median of 8 — located in an intrinsically disordered, solvent-exposed region of a transmembrane protein, predicted to self-assemble through beta-strand-mediated, amyloid-like interactions. The definition is deliberately two-part: the motif must pass an *assembly* test (sequence-level amyloid propensity) and a *context* test (disorder, exposure, and non-transmembrane localization). Both parts are essential; either alone would describe a different biological object.

The identification logic reflects this two-part definition, executed as a three-stage screen:

1. A random-forest classifier trained on WALTZ-DB 2.0 (1,402 hexapeptides: 510 amyloid-forming, 892 non-forming), using one-hot-encoded sequence plus summed beta-strand free energy (F1 = 0.77 under stratified 5-fold cross-validation).
2. Every hexapeptide window across human membrane proteins is scored; positive windows are called **Self-Assembly Motifs (SAMs)**.
3. A SAM becomes an **mdSAM** only if it lies in a disordered region: AlphaFold pLDDT < 70, non-helical and solvent exposed, excluding transmembrane segments and signal peptides. A ROC-derived threshold on consecutive positive windows defines the high-confidence set.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L9-L17)

The prerequisite for reading the diagram below: the classifier is a per-hexapeptide scorer, so it produces many isolated positive windows; the disorder gate and consecutive-window threshold are what convert noisy per-window scores into a biologically meaningful motif set.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Human membrane protein<br/>(4,886 analysed)"] --> B["Hexapeptide scan<br/>every 6-residue window"]
    B --> C{"RF classifier<br/>WALTZ-DB 2.0 trained"}
    C -->|"positive"| D["SAM<br/>Self-Assembly Motif"]
    C -->|"negative"| E["discarded"]
    D --> F{"Disorder gate:<br/>pLDDT < 70, non-helical,<br/>solvent exposed,<br/>no TM / signal peptide"}
    F -->|"passes"| G["mdSAM candidate"]
    F -->|"fails"| H["SAM kept as<br/>structured-region motif"]
    G --> I["Consecutive-window<br/>ROC threshold"]
    I --> J["High-confidence mdSAM set<br/>(1,425 motifs / 945 proteins)"]
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L11-L17)

### Why this design rather than energy-based prediction alone

The rationale is visible in the validation notebook: the pipeline's primary engine is the WALTZ-DB-trained classifier because WALTZ-DB provides *labeled* experimental hexapeptides (downloaded from waltzdb.switchlab.org), while energy-only tools have no per-motif trained decision boundary. PASTA 2.0 and Aggrescan hot spots were deliberately positioned as **independent cross-checks**, not as the discovery engine — notebook 04's header states its purpose is supplemental information on the window cutoff, PASTA, and Aggrescan, and its main plot cross-references PASTA pairing energies against Aggrescan hot-spot counts for the discovered motifs.

Sources: [notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](/notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L10-L12), [README.md](/README.md#L47)

A telling conceptual anchor appears at the very top of the classifier notebook: the beta-strand free-energy scale (AAindex `MUNV940103`) is immediately applied to two sequences side by side — the APP amyloid core `YEVHHQKLVFFA` (the canonical positive control) and the HTR7 motif `VSVWVLQS` (a candidate). This calibration-against-known-amyloid pattern is the intellectual seed of the whole approach: treat motifs in membrane-protein tails as testable analogs of known amyloid cores.

Sources: [notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](/notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L22-L24), [notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](/notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L34-L38)

| Strategy | Evidence basis | Role in this study |
|---|---|---|
| RF classifier (one-hot + summed beta-strand energy) | 1,402 labeled WALTZ-DB 2.0 hexapeptides; F1 = 0.77 | Primary genome-wide scan engine |
| PASTA 2.0 pairing energy | Physicochemical beta-pairing energies | Independent validation of discovered motifs (S1J) |
| Aggrescan hot-spot count (nHS) | Aggregation hot-spot density | Independent validation of discovered motifs |
| Consecutive-window ROC threshold | ROC over window counts per region | Sets the high-confidence boundary (S1I) |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L15-L17), [README.md](/README.md#L183-L185), [notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](/notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L189-L195)

## What the screen found

The concept survived its first contact with the proteome with striking statistics. The screen yielded **1,425 high-confidence mdSAMs in 945 membrane proteins** — roughly 20% of the 4,886 human membrane proteins analysed carry at least one. The localization signature is strongly non-random: 91% of mdSAMs sit in N- or C-terminal tails rather than internal loops, and 72% of mdSAM-containing proteins carry exactly one motif, suggesting motifs are a targeted, not ubiquitous, feature. Critically, the concept was testable at the peptide level: of 44 synthesized mdSAM peptides, 36 (81%) gave a Thioflavin-T signal — in vitro assembly rates far above what a random motif set would produce.

| Quantity | Value | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| High-confidence mdSAMs | 1,425 | The discoverable motif population |
| mdSAM-containing proteins | 945 (~20% of 4,886) | Widespread, not rare |
| Motif length | 7–9 residues (median 8) | Hexapeptide windows aggregate into short motifs |
| Tail localization | 91% N- or C-terminal | Tails are the preferred regulatory position |
| Single-motif proteins | 72% | Motifs are specific features, not generic clutter |
| Peptide validation | 36/44 (81%) ThT-positive | In vitro assembly confirms prediction quality |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L11-L19)

## The evidence chain: how the rationale was validated

The discovery rationale is structured as a tiered argument, and the notebook numbering mirrors it exactly. Each tier answers a distinct question and would stand as evidence even without the later tiers; together they move from *prediction* to *physics* to *cell biology* to *function* to *evolution*.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P["Postulate:<br/>disordered motifs drive clustering"] --> A["Tier 1<br/>Computational discovery<br/>Fig 1; S1"]
    A --> B["Tier 2<br/>Diversity and localisation<br/>Fig 2; S2"]
    B --> C["Tier 3<br/>Peptide self-assembly<br/>Fig 3; S3"]
    C --> D["Tier 4<br/>Cellular clustering<br/>Figs 4-5; S5-S6"]
    D --> E["Tier 5<br/>Function: HTR7 signalling<br/>Fig 6"]
    E --> F["Tier 6<br/>Evolutionary conservation<br/>Fig 7; S7"]
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L43-L86)

| Tier | Question answered | Notebooks | Paper figure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Discovery | Do mdSAMs exist genome-wide? | 01, 02, 04, 05 | Fig 1; S1 |
| Diversity | Where do they sit and how varied are they? | 06, 07, 08, 09 | Fig 2; S2 |
| In vitro | Do the peptides physically assemble? | 10, 11, 12 | Fig 3; S3 |
| In cells | Do they cluster full-length proteins? | 13, 14, 15, 16 | Figs 4–5; S5–S6 |
| Function | Does motif disruption change signalling? | 17, 18, 19 | Fig 6 |
| Evolution | Are motifs evolutionarily maintained? | 20, 21, 22, 23 | Fig 7; S7 |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L35-L86)

Two design choices in this chain deserve emphasis. First, the diversity tier (notebooks 06–09) characterizes the sequence space *before* any experiment: physicochemical embedding, charge-archetype clustering, organelle enrichment via hyperLOPIT, and topology analysis — this established that mdSAMs are a coherent, non-random class worth experimental investment. Second, the functional tier is anchored by a single deep case study (HTR7): proline mutants (which break beta-strand assembly) serve as the causal perturbation across every assay from peptide ThT through dSTORM nanoscale clustering to cAMP dose-response and RNA-seq. The logic is that one mutation, V451P, breaks motif assembly and everything downstream if — and only if — the mdSAM concept is correct.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L43-L52), [README.md](/README.md#L71-L77)

> [!TIP]
> The shared motif table is named `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new.pkl` with the **dSAM** prefix, not mdSAM. When grepping notebooks for the central object, search for `dSAM` — searching for `mdSAM` will miss every load site (e.g., notebook 05 reads `../files/dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl`).

## Terminology you will meet in the code

The vocabulary shifted over the course of the project, and the notebooks preserve that history. Reading the terminology map below first will prevent most confusion when you open the notebooks.

| Term | Meaning | Where encountered |
|---|---|---|
| mdSAM | Current paper term: membrane-disordered Self-Assembly Motif | README, manuscript context |
| dSAM | Older in-code name for the same object (disordered SAM) | File names and variables, e.g. `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl` |
| SAM | Any classifier-positive hexapeptide window, no disorder requirement | Sequence-logo comparisons (S1H) |
| mSAM / sSAM / msSAM | Structured-region counterpart motifs in older notebooks | Legacy variable names |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L21), [notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](/notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L36), [files/README.md](/files/README.md#L7)

The SAM-versus-mdSAM distinction is not pedantry — it is the operationalization of the concept. The supplementary sequence logos explicitly compare mdSAMs against all SAMs, which is how the study quantifies what the disorder context *adds* to the amino-acid composition signature beyond raw amyloid propensity. The discovered motifs are all stored in the shared table with their sequence in the `AAseq` column, read by ten downstream notebooks.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L181-L182), [files/README.md](/files/README.md#L7-L9), [notebooks/05_uniprot_keyword_enrichment.ipynb](/notebooks/05_uniprot_keyword_enrichment.ipynb#L33-L34)

## Where to go next

If the concept convinced you, the natural progression through this catalog follows the evidence chain itself. [Notebook Pipeline Architecture](5-notebook-pipeline-architecture) maps how the 23 notebooks interconnect as a system. To understand the two-stage screen in depth, continue to [WALTZ-DB Random-Forest Classifier](6-waltz-db-random-forest-classifier) and [AlphaFold-Based Disorder Filtering](7-alphafold-based-disorder-filtering). For the characterizations that justified experimental investment, see [Sequence Logos and Composition](10-sequence-logos-and-composition) and [hyperLOPIT Organelle Enrichment](14-hyperlopit-organelle-enrichment); for the causal tests, start with [Thioflavin-T and Amytracker Screens](16-thioflavin-t-and-amytracker-screens) and then the [HTR7 End-to-End Case Study](21-htr7-end-to-end-case-study), which integrates every tier in one protein. The evolutionary closure of the argument is documented under [Alignment-Based Conservation Metrics](24-alignment-based-conservation-metrics).

# Notebook Pipeline Architecture



This page explains how the 23 numbered notebooks in `notebooks/` are organized, how they exchange data through the shared tables in `files/`, and where the real execution dependencies lie. The central architectural fact is that this repository is a **publishing checkpoint**, not a self-contained executable pipeline: the heavy lifting (classifier training artifacts, the genome-wide hexapeptide scoring sweep) was performed off-repo, and the repo ships canonical *result tables* that downstream notebooks consume. Understanding this producer/consumer topology is the key to reading, re-running, or extending any notebook in the series.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L23-L33), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L3)

## The Three-Tier Architecture

The repository separates concerns into three tiers: an off-repo computation tier (classifier training and the full sweep over every hexapeptide window in human membrane proteins, described in the paper's STAR Methods), a canonical data tier (the pickled tables in `files/`), and a presentation/analysis tier (the 23 notebooks that generate figure panels). Only tiers two and three live in this repository; the notebooks in tier three deliberately *start from* frozen results rather than re-deriving them.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L35-L52), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L5-L9), [notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L528-L529)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph OFFREPO["Tier 1 - Off-repo computation (not shipped)"]
        RF["Random-forest training<br/>(WALTZ-DB 2.0, 1,402 hexapeptides)"]
        SWEEP["Hexapeptide scoring sweep<br/>(all human membrane proteins)"]
        AF["AlphaFold disorder annotation<br/>(pLDDT, IDR definition)"]
    end
    subgraph FILES["Tier 2 - Canonical tables (files/)"]
        DSAM["dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl<br/>(1,425 high-confidence mdSAMs)"]
        HTMS["hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl<br/>(human TM proteins + topology)"]
        AF2["AF2_with_ENSG.pkl<br/>(per-residue AlphaFold annotations)"]
    end
    subgraph NB["Tier 3 - Notebooks (notebooks/)"]
        LOGOS["03 sequence logos"]
        CHAR["04-08 characterization"]
        VALID["09-23 per-protein + assays"]
    end
    RF --> SWEEP
    SWEEP --> DSAM
    AF --> AF2
    LOGOS --> HTMS
    DSAM --> CHAR & VALID
    HTMS --> CHAR & VALID
    AF2 --> LOGOS & CHAR & VALID
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L13-L19), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L5-L9)

The off-repo tier explains the single most confusing artifact in notebook 01: the notebook evaluates the classifier via cross-validation, but the *trained* model that actually produced the shipped mdSAM table is persisted to an external volume (`joblib.dump(rf, '/Volumes/aelazar/.../RandomForestClassifier_model.sav')`), and notebooks later reload that same artifact to re-score new sequences. The scoring logic that turned classifier outputs into the mdSAM call set ran outside this repository; `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl` is its frozen output.

Sources: [notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L528-L529), [README.md](README.md#L15-L19)

> [!TIP]
> When auditing reproducibility, treat `files/*.pkl` as the ground truth, not notebook outputs. Notebooks are distributed with outputs cleared and would rebuild only their own intermediate frames — never the canonical tables — if re-run as-is.

## The Shared Tables: the Inter-Notebook Data Bus

Notebooks never pass data to each other directly through cell state. The only sanctioned exchange mechanism is the pickle bus in `files/`, read with `pd.read_pickle` via relative paths like `../files/AF2_with_ENSG.pkl`. This requires running every notebook with `notebooks/` as the working directory — a hard convention documented in both READMEs. Two of the three bus tables are notebook-producible (`hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl` from notebook 03, `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` from notebook 02 at cell 205); the third, the mdSAM call set itself, arrives from the off-repo pipeline and is the widest fan-in input.

Sources: [files/README.md](files/README.md#L3-L9), [notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L39), [README.md](README.md#L40-L41)

| Table | Contents | Producer | Consumers (notebook numbers) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl` | The mdSAM call set; motif sequence in the `AAseq` column | Off-repo identification pipeline (STAR Methods) | 05, 06, 07, 08, 09, 15, 18, 20, 21, 23 |
| `hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl` | Human transmembrane proteins with UniProt topology annotation | `03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb` (`TMs.to_pickle`) | 03, 05, 06, 07, 08, 09, 15, 18, 20, 21, 23 |
| `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` | AlphaFold-derived per-residue annotations + Ensembl gene IDs | `02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb` (cell 205, `AF2.to_pickle`) | 02, 03, 05, 06, 07, 08, 11, 15, 18, 19, 20, 21, 23 |

Sources: [files/README.md](files/README.md#L5-L9)

The consumer matrix reveals the join keys that matter for integration: `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` carries both UniProt accessions (`acc`) and Ensembl gene IDs (`ENSG`), which is why notebook 03 uses it to map `ENSG` keys in its local `topology_df` frame onto accessions before building the topology table. Any notebook that needs to reconcile mdSAM coordinates with gene-level annotations routes through this one table.

Sources: [notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L39), [notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L62-L64), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L9)

> [!TIP]
> Pickle files execute code on load and are pandas-version sensitive. The repo's own guidance is to load them only from this repository and match the pandas version used to write them — do not "upgrade" the bus tables casually.

## Notebook Numbering as Pipeline Order

The `NN_` prefixes encode a deliberate funnel: broad sequence-space characterization narrows into per-protein analysis, then into controlled experiments, then into a single-protein case study (HTR7), and finally into evolutionary generality checks. The numbering is also the execution order assumed by the figure map: every paper panel in the README resolves to a `(notebook, 0-based cell index)` pair, making the numbering the primary traceability key across the whole repo.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L31-L33), [README.md](README.md#L88-L90)

| Stage | Notebooks | Role in the funnel |
|---|---|---|
| Foundation | 01, 02, 03 | Train/evaluate RF classifier; build `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl`; build logos, `hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl`, `AF_IDR_v3.pkl` |
| Discovery & diversity | 04–08 | PASTA/threshold validation, UniProt keyword enrichment, sequence-space embedding & GMM clustering, hyperLOPIT organelles, topology & membrane distance |
| Per-protein census | 09 | mdSAMs-per-protein histogram |
| In vitro assembly | 10–12 | ThT 96-well screen, GPCR peptide ThT, Amytracker |
| Cell-based clustering | 13–16 | TIRF puncta Poisson GLM, flow cytometry gating, BioGRID interactomics, dSTORM clusters |
| HTR7 case study | 17–19 | cAMP dose-response, RNA-seq PCA/volcano, DE + GSEA |
| Evolution | 20–23 | Alignment-based and ESM conservation, ortholog peptide ThT, LARKS/WIRS/FINCHES overlap |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L35-L86)

## The Dependency Topology in Practice

Reading order and execution order agree on the foundation, but the dependency edges are *star-shaped around the bus*, not a chain. Notebook 03, for instance, depends on notebook 02's output (it reads `../files/AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` as its second cell) while simultaneously reading the mdSAM table and re-scoring gnomAD variants by reloading the classifier artifact from the external volume — the same feature schema (one-hot hexapeptide + summed MUNV940103 beta energy) that notebook 01 defines. This is why notebook 01's feature engineering is worth studying even though its model artifact lives off-repo: downstream notebooks re-instantiate the scoring function locally.

Sources: [notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L39), [notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L2776-L2790), [notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L22-L25), [notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L2824-L2830)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    N01["01 RF classifier<br/>(model saved off-repo)"]
    N02["02 AlphaFold residue table<br/>→ AF2_with_ENSG.pkl"]
    N03["03 logos + hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl<br/>+ AF_IDR_v3.pkl"]
    BUS1[("dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl")]
    N04["04-09 discovery & diversity"]
    N15["15 BioGRID"]
    N18["18 RNA-seq"]
    N20["20-23 evolution"]
    N01 -.->|model artifact<br/>reloaded at /Volumes| N03
    N02 --> N03
    BUS1 --> N04 & N15 & N18 & N20
    N03 --> N04 & N15 & N18 & N20
    N02 --> N04 & N15 & N18 & N20
```

Sources: [notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L2776-L2778), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L5-L9)

Two friction points in this topology deserve explicit acknowledgment. First, several notebooks still reference the original author's machine paths (`/Volumes/aelazar/...` for background tables, model artifacts, and gnomAD data, plus notebook-local side files like `enumerate/enumerate.pkl` and `topology_df`), which the root README itself flags as a caveat for re-running. Second, the README references a machine-readable `FIGURE_MAP.csv` that is not present in the shipped tree — the README's panel tables are the de facto figure map. Neither breaks the read path for the shipped tables, but both affect a from-scratch re-execution attempt.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L27-L29), [README.md](README.md#L248-L250), [notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L49-L51)

## Notebook Anatomy: A Representative Pattern

Across the catalog, notebooks share a recognizable skeleton: an import cell (often duplicating the `MUNV940103` energy scale and helper functions like `adjust_box_widths`), followed by reads from `../files/`, followed by analysis cells and `plt.savefig` calls that emit figure assets. Notebook 02's anatomy is the extreme case: it begins with the same import block family (including `iupred2a_lib`, `pyaaisc.Aaindex`, UMAP/t-SNE) and ends with a long tail of exploratory PTM-enrichment plots that the README explicitly labels as earlier versions not tied to final panels. The shipped figure panels are pinned to specific cell indices, so a notebook's *position* in its cell list — not its narrative flow — is what the reproducibility contract depends on.

Sources: [notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L9-L25), [notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L9-L28), [README.md](README.md#L40), [README.md](README.md#L33)

For intermediate developers, the practical contract when touching any notebook is therefore: preserve cell ordering (or update the map), keep reads pointing at `../files/`, and treat `01`'s feature definitions as the canonical scoring schema. The classifier design itself — one-hot-encoded hexapeptide plus summed beta-strand free energy, F1 = 0.77 under stratified 5-fold CV — is detailed on the dedicated classifier page, and the disorder-filtering rules that turn SAMs into mdSAMs are covered on the AlphaFold page.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L15-L17)

## Suggested Reading Progression

To build a working mental model in three steps: start with the catalog-level map to locate each notebook's role, then study the two producer notebooks (02 and 03) since everything downstream hangs off their tables, and finish with the shared-table reference before attempting any re-runs. From here, the natural deep-dive order follows the funnel.

1. [Repository Layout and Notebook Map](3-repository-layout-and-notebook-map) — inventory of what lives where
2. [mdSAM Concept and Discovery Rationale](4-mdsam-concept-and-discovery-rationale) — the biology behind the call set
3. [WALTZ-DB Random-Forest Classifier](6-waltz-db-random-forest-classifier) — notebook 01's training and evaluation in depth
4. [AlphaFold-Based Disorder Filtering](7-alphafold-based-disorder-filtering) — notebook 02's residue table and IDR rules
5. [Shared Data Tables Reference](8-shared-data-tables-reference) — schemas of the three bus tables
6. [Figure-to-Notebook Reproducibility Map](9-figure-to-notebook-reproducibility-map) — the panel → `(notebook, cell)` contract


# WALTZ-DB Random-Forest Classifier



This page documents `notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb`, the notebook that trains, validates, and persists the binary amyloid-forming classifier at the root of the mdSAM discovery pipeline. It covers the WALTZ-DB 2.0 training data, the feature construction (positional one-hot encoding plus summed beta-strand free energy), the hyperparameter search, the stratified cross-validated evaluation behind paper figures Fig 1D, S1F, and S1G, and the persisted artifacts that downstream notebooks consume. All references are to the notebook JSON line ranges unless otherwise noted.

## Role in the mdSAM Discovery Pipeline

Notebook 01 is **stage one of a two-stage discovery cascade**. The random forest it produces scores every hexapeptide window of human membrane proteins for amyloid-forming potential; a window labeled positive is a Self-Assembly Motif (SAM), and only SAMs that additionally sit in a disordered, solvent-exposed region — a determination made later by notebook 02 using AlphaFold confidence — become mdSAMs. Of the 4,886 human membrane proteins analysed, this cascade ultimately yields 1,425 high-confidence mdSAMs across 945 proteins. Understanding the classifier's exact training contract is therefore prerequisite to interpreting every downstream result in the repository.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["WALTZ-DB 2.0 hexapeptides<br/>(1,402: 510 amyloid, 892 non)"] --> B["Notebook 01<br/>train + validate RF classifier"]
    B --> C["Persisted model + feature schema"]
    C --> D["Hexapeptide scan of human<br/>membrane proteins"]
    D --> E["SAM = positive window"]
    E --> F["Notebook 02: AlphaFold<br/>disorder / exposure filter"]
    F --> G["mdSAM table<br/>dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl"]
```

The prerequisite to read this diagram: the classifier operates on **fixed-length hexapeptides**, so "window scoring" means sliding a 6-residue frame across each protein sequence and predicting class per frame. The final table above is the shared input read by ten analysis notebooks (05, 06, 07, 08, 09, 15, 18, 20, 21, 23).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L13-L21), [README.md](README.md#L19), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L7)

## Training Data: the WALTZ-DB 2.0 Export

The notebook ingests a CSV export from [waltzdb.switchlab.org](http://waltzdb.switchlab.org/), consisting of **1,402 experimentally characterised hexapeptides — 510 amyloid-forming and 892 non-forming** — and immediately enforces uniqueness by dropping duplicate `Sequence` rows before resetting the index. Each entry carries a `Classification` field (the label source) and a `UniProt ID` (retained as provenance). The export itself is a local download, referenced by a hardcoded user path rather than being bundled in the repository.

| Property | Value | Role in training |
|---|---|---|
| Unit of data | Hexapeptide sequence | One feature vector per peptide |
| Positive class | `Classification == 'amyloid'` (510) | Encoded as `classification = 1` |
| Negative class | all other classifications (892) | Encoded as `classification = 0` |
| Deduplication | `drop_duplicates(subset=['Sequence'])` | Prevents sequence leakage across folds |
| Provenance | `UniProt ID` column | Carried through as `acc` metadata |

Sources: [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L113-L117), [README.md](README.md#L15)

## Feature Engineering: One-Hot Sequence Plus Summed Beta-Strand Free Energy

Each hexapeptide is converted into a **121-dimensional vector**: 120 positional one-hot columns (6 positions × 20 amino acids) generated by `pd.get_dummies(waltzdb['Sequence'].apply(lambda x: pd.Series(list(x))))`, plus one scalar feature `beta` — the sum of per-residue values from the AAindex scale **MUNV940103**, a beta-sheet free-energy scale where lower values indicate residues that favor beta-strand conformation. Because the canonical export is uniformly hexameric, the positional encoding is well-formed with no ragged padding.

The scale's key behaviour is worth internalising: hydrophobic, beta-branched residues sit at the low end (V = 0.546, I = 0.583, Y = 0.665, F = 0.685) while proline and charged/polar residues sit at the high end (P = 1.412, D = 1.266, N = 1.197). This is why the summed feature is interpretable as a **pseudo free energy ΣΔG_β** — amyloid-forming peptides accumulate low (favorable) values. The notebook demonstrates this directly by plotting per-residue propensity profiles for the HTR7 motif `VSVWVLQS` against the canonical amyloid core `YEVHHQKLVFFA` from APP, establishing the physiological intuition before any model is fit.

| Feature block | Construction | Dimensions |
|---|---|---|
| Positional one-hot | `get_dummies` over per-position residue identity | 120 binary columns |
| `beta` | `Σ MUNV940103[residue]` over the sequence | 1 scalar |
| Label | `1` if amyloid else `0` | target |
| Metadata | `AAseq`, `acc` (UniProt ID) | carried alongside, not trained on |

The finished matrix is shuffled, written to `waltzdb_Random_Forest_input.csv` as an archival intermediate, and the `beta` distributions of the two classes are compared by a t-test and plotted as a notched boxplot annotated `p = 10⁻¹¹²` — this panel is paper figure S1G.

> [!TIP]
> When porting or retraining, **preserve the exact column order** of the feature matrix — positional one-hot columns are order-sensitive, and downstream window scoring must present vectors in the same layout. The notebook guards this by persisting the fitted DataFrame itself (`RandomForestClassifier_DataFrame.sav`, cell 28) as the canonical schema reference rather than relying on column names alone.

Sources: [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L22-L24), [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L149-L171), [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L34-L47), [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L182-L233)

## Model Selection: From Baseline to the Final Hyperparameters

The notebook documents a deliberate, three-step selection trajectory that a reproducer should recognise as **exploration history, not a required sequence**. A `RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=24)` baseline first establishes signal and prints top-10 feature importances (with the summed beta energy typically leading). A `RandomizedSearchCV` over a broad grid — 200–2000 trees, `auto`/`sqrt` feature sampling, depths 10–110 or unlimited, split/leaf minimums, bootstrap on/off — runs 100 iterations at 3-fold CV, followed by a narrowed `GridSearchCV` (bootstrap `False`, `max_features` 2–3, `n_estimators` 550–2000). The final production configuration that the evaluation cells use is:

| Hyperparameter | Final value |
|---|---|
| Model class | `RandomForestClassifier` |
| `n_estimators` | 700 |
| `max_features` | 3 |
| `min_samples_split` | 2 |
| `min_samples_leaf` | 1 |
| `max_depth` | None (unlimited) |
| `bootstrap` | False |

Sources: [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L268-L294), [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L613-L632), [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L654-L661), [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L687-L724), [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L314)

## Cross-Validated Evaluation (Figure S1F)

The headline evaluation is a **5-fold StratifiedKFold loop** that refits the 700-tree classifier per fold, overlays per-fold ROC curves, and plots the interpolated mean ROC with a ±1 standard-deviation band against the chance diagonal — the figure exported as S1F. Each fold's metrics are accumulated independently: accuracy, binary precision, recall, F1 (reported as mean ± std across folds; the paper reports **F1 = 0.77**), the ravelled confusion matrix, and the held-out indices. Critically for reproducibility, **each fold's fitted model is persisted immediately** via `joblib.dump(rf, 'models/rf_%d.sav')`, so the evaluation leaves behind five artefacts, not just plots.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    W["waltzdb_export.csv"] --> DEDUP["Dedup on Sequence"]
    DEDUP --> FE["Cell 8: label + ΣΔG_β + positional one-hot"]
    FE --> CSV["waltzdb_Random_Forest_input.csv"]
    CSV --> SHUF["Cell 10: shuffle"]
    SHUF --> EDA["Cell 12: t-test + boxplot → S1G"]
    SHUF --> BASE["Cell 14: RFR baseline + importances"]
    SHUF --> HP["Cells 34–40: Randomized → Grid search"]
    HP --> FINAL["Cell 15: RF(700) × StratifiedKFold-5 → S1F"]
    FINAL --> PER["models/rf_0.sav … rf_4.sav"]
    PER --> R4["Cell 18: reload rf_4.sav"]
    R4 --> TEST["Cells 20–22: fold-4 predictions,<br/>confusion matrix, MCC"]
    TEST --> F1D["Cell 26: Fig 1D test-set plot"]
    FINAL --> PROD["Cell 28: production .sav dumps"]
    PROD --> ENST["Cells 29–32: per-transcript<br/>window tables (≥3 windows)"]
```

Read the diagram top-to-bottom as the notebook's executable spine: the branch through `rf_4` is the held-out characterisation, and the bottom branch is the hand-off to proteome scanning.

Sources: [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L311-L365), [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L384-L392), [README.md](README.md#L15), [README.md](README.md#L179-L180)

## Held-Out Test-Set Characterisation (Figure 1D)

After cross-validation, the notebook designates **fold 4's model (`rf_4.sav`) with fold 4's test indices** as the canonical held-out characterisation. Predictions are collected row-by-row into `RF_regression` (true class vs. score), from which the notebook prints the confusion matrix decomposition (`TN/FP/FN/TP`), computes the **Matthews correlation coefficient** as a class-imbalance-robust summary, and draws the score-separation count plot. The final Fig 1D panel is rendered from a curated tab-separated file (`confusion_matrix_bar_plot.csv`) grouping test peptides by RF classification and ground truth — an example row comment records the fold-4 decomposition as `TN=160; FP=18; FN=26; TP=76`.

| Evaluation layer | Output | Figure / consumer |
|---|---|---|
| Mean ROC over 5 folds ± std | `aucs`, interpolated `tprs` | S1F |
| Per-fold ACC/Precision/Recall/F1 | mean ± std printed | notebook log |
| Fold-4 confusion matrix + MCC | TN/FP/FN/TP, `matthews_corrcoef` | notebook log |
| Score separation count plots | `RF_classifier_test_set.svg`, `_v2.svg` | Fig 1D |

Sources: [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L401-L450), [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L468-L508), [README.md](README.md#L96)

## Artefact Persistence and Downstream Consumption

The notebook's real product is the set of serialised objects at its end. Per-fold models land in a local `models/` directory during evaluation; the **production pair** — the fitted classifier (`RandomForestClassifier_model.sav`) and its feature DataFrame (`RandomForestClassifier_DataFrame.sav`) — is dumped to the project volume for the proteome scan. The final cells then load per-transcript pickle tables (e.g. `ENST00000000233.pkl`) and count transcripts whose `WT_Windows_above_thershold` column reaches **≥ 3 consecutive positive hexapeptide windows** — exactly the consecutive-window criterion whose ROC-derived threshold is calibrated in notebook 04. The discovered motifs ultimately flow into `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl` (with motif sequences in the `AAseq` column), the shared table behind ten downstream notebooks; note the repository's naming convention that **"dSAM" in filenames and variables means mdSAM**.

| Artefact | Produced at | Consumed by |
|---|---|---|
| `waltzdb_Random_Forest_input.csv` | cell 9 | archival feature matrix |
| `models/rf_0.sav` … `rf_4.sav` | cell 15 | cell 18 reloads `rf_4.sav` |
| `RandomForestClassifier_model.sav` + `_DataFrame.sav` | cell 28 | proteome-wide window scoring |
| `RF_classifier_test_set*.svg` | cells 24, 26 | Fig 1D |
| `ENST*.pkl` per-transcript window tables | external scan step | cells 29–32 threshold check |

Sources: [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L340), [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L528-L529), [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L538-L547), [README.md](README.md#L17-L21), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L7)

## Reproducing the Notebook Today: Environment Caveats

The notebook is a research artefact written against an earlier scientific-Python stack, and a faithful re-run requires mapping several legacy usages. Beyond API drift, the file mixes executable spine with superseded cells: cell 10 reads `set(df['type'])` before the `type` column is created (cell 12), cell 25 references `RF_for_plot` one cell before it is defined (cell 26), and a duplicate CV loop with 100-tree settings (cells 33) exists alongside the production 700-tree loop. Execution order therefore matters, and the notebook must be run in cell-index order for the documented figures to regenerate.

| Legacy usage | Issue | Modern replacement |
|---|---|---|
| `df.append(...)` | Removed in pandas ≥ 2.0 | `pd.concat` |
| `plot_roc_curve` | Removed in scikit-learn ≥ 1.2 | `RocCurveDisplay.from_estimator` |
| `max_features='auto'` | Removed in scikit-learn ≥ 1.2 | explicit `'sqrt'` or integer |
| `/Users/aelazar/...` and `/Volumes/...` paths | Host-specific, non-portable | download WALTZ-DB export; local output dirs |
| `models/` target of `joblib.dump` | Directory must pre-exist | create before running cell 15 |
| `! open .` (cell 23) | macOS shell | remove on other platforms |

External dependencies declared in the import cell include `localcider` and an appended path to a local `iupred2a` installation (its import is commented out), so a minimal environment is `pandas`, `numpy`, `scikit-learn`, `scipy`, `seaborn`, `matplotlib`, `biopython`, `joblib`, and `localcider`.

> [!TIP]
> The `p = 10⁻¹¹²` annotation on the S1G boxplot is a **hardcoded string**, while the live `stats.ttest_ind` result is printed separately one line above — treat the printed statistic as ground truth when regenerating the panel, since re-sampling or re-deduplicating WALTZ-DB will not update the annotation.

Sources: [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L9-L25), [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L113-L117), [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L159), [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L215-L230), [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L328), [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L586-L603)

## Key Takeaways and Where to Go Next

The classifier itself is deliberately simple — a 700-tree random forest over 121 features derived from sequence position and beta-strand energetics — and its strength lies in the engineering discipline around it: stratified evaluation with per-fold persistence, a held-out fold for figure-grade characterisation, and serialisation of both model and feature schema for proteome-scale application. To continue the discovery narrative, the natural progression is: [AlphaFold-Based Disorder Filtering](7-alphafold-based-disorder-filtering) for the second stage that converts SAM predictions into mdSAMs; [PASTA Comparison and Window Thresholds](12-pasta-comparison-and-window-thresholds) for the consecutive-window threshold calibration (S1I–J); [Notebook Pipeline Architecture](5-notebook-pipeline-architecture) for how notebook 01 sits among all 23 notebooks; [Shared Data Tables Reference](8-shared-data-tables-reference) for the schemas of `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl` and friends; and [Figure-to-Notebook Reproducibility Map](9-figure-to-notebook-reproducibility-map) to trace Fig 1D, S1F, and S1G back to their exact generating cells. For how the HTR7 motif used in this notebook's demo profile becomes a full experimental case study, see [HTR7 End-to-End Case Study](21-htr7-end-to-end-case-study), and for the composition-level view of what the classifier labels, see [Sequence Logos and Composition](10-sequence-logos-and-composition).


# AlphaFold-Based Disorder Filtering



This page documents the AlphaFold-driven order/disorder stratification implemented in `02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb` — the computational stage that converts raw per-residue amyloidogenicity calls from the WALTZ-DB random-forest stage ([WALTZ-DB Random-Forest Classifier](6-waltz-db-random-forest-classifier)) into biophysically interpretable mdSAM candidates. The notebook's core contribution is threefold: a **three-class residue stratification** built on AlphaFold pLDDT confidence, a **two-factor objective function** that fuses amyloidogenic window counts with pLDDT, and a **matched-background validation layer** that benchmarks candidate segments against gnomAD allele-frequency distributions. All logic verified below resides in the single notebook file.

Sources: [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L8-L27)

## Position in the Discovery Pipeline

Notebook 02 is the *adjudication layer* of the mdSAM pipeline: notebook 01 produces per-residue counts of classifier windows above threshold (`WT_Windows_above_thershold`), and notebook 02 decides which of those residues actually live in protein contexts where amyloidogenicity is structurally plausible. The AlphaFold table (`DataFrame_AF2_drop_duplicates_classifier.pkl`) carries the per-residue features used for that decision — `AF2_pLDDT_max`, `AF2_accessibility`, and `AF2_SS_helix_count` — keyed by `ENSG`/`ENST`. From this one table, three independent analyses branch out: class stratification with KS-tested ECDFs, the objective-function scoring surface, and gnomAD percentile matching against IDR or structured backgrounds.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    RF["Random-forest window counts<br/>WT_Windows_above_thershold"] --> TBL["AF2 residue table<br/>DataFrame_AF2_drop_duplicates_classifier.pkl"]
    AF2["AlphaFold per-transcript predictions<br/>AF2_with_ENSG.pkl + per-ENST WT/gnomAD pickles"] --> TBL
    TBL --> SPLIT{"pLDDT_max vs 70"}
    SPLIT -->|"gt 70"| ST["Structured"]
    SPLIT -->|"lt 70"| IDR["IDR"]
    SPLIT -->|"lt 70 + masked accessibility<br/>+ no helices"| IDE["IDR_expo"]
    ST --> VAL["ECDF + KS-2samp"]
    IDR --> VAL
    IDE --> VAL
    TBL --> OBJ["Objective function<br/>Score = sigma_Agg(x) * sigma_pLDDT(y)"]
    OBJ --> PLOTS["pLDDT-vs-Score panels<br/>ojb_f_new.svg"]
    TBL --> GN["gnomAD percentile matching<br/>IDR / Structured-Exposed / Structured-Buried"]
    GN --> STATS["Percentile box plots"]
```

Sources: [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L289-L308), [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L1349-L1350)

## The Three-Class pLDDT Stratification

The notebook operationalizes disorder as a hard threshold on per-residue maximum pLDDT: **`AF2_pLDDT_max > 70` → `Structured`**, **`AF2_pLDDT_max < 70` → `IDR`**. A third, stricter class `IDR_expo` intersects the pLDDT condition with two structural guards: a fully masked accessibility string (`AF2_accessibility == '*********'`, nine wildcard characters) and absence of modeled helical secondary structure (`AF2_SS_helix_count < 1`). This stratification is immediately stress-tested: a Kolmogorov–Smirnov two-sample test compares `WT_Windows_above_thershold` distributions between the `Structured` and `IDR_expo` classes, and three overlaid ECDFs (blue/red/orange, `#04A1D5`/`r`/`#ED8453`) visualize the separation under the title "Human ORFs".

| Class | Mask (verbatim) | Biophysical reading |
|---|---|---|
| `Structured` | `df.AF2_pLDDT_max > 70` | residue sits in a well-resolved fold |
| `IDR` | `df.AF2_pLDDT_max < 70` | low-confidence, disordered context |
| `IDR_expo` | `accessibility=='*********'` **and** `pLDDT_max<70` **and** `SS_helix_count<1` | disordered with no modeled secondary structure and masked solvent-accessibility state |

The 70 boundary is used symmetrically elsewhere: the per-transcript loop selects IDR residues with `df_WT.AF2_pLDDT_max <= 70` (line 433) and background residues with `>= 70` (line 485), confirming that the same cutoff governs both candidate selection and matched-background construction. This mirrors AlphaFold's documented interpretation of pLDDT as a local-resolution/confidence proxy, applied here as the sole disorder oracle — no external disorder predictor is needed for the primary filtering (although IUPred2A is imported at module level for auxiliary sequence analyses).

Sources: [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L298-L326), [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L422-L433), [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L474-L485)

## The mdSAM Objective Function

The quantitative heart of the page is a closed-form objective function evaluated on every residue:

```
Score = 1 / (1 + exp(-2*(Agg_value - 2)))  ×  1 / (1 + exp(0.5*(pLDDT - 70)))
```

defined at lines 1349–1350 as `def f(pLDDT, Agg_value)`. Each factor is a logistic sigmoid, and their product yields a score in the open interval (0, 1):

| Factor | Formula | Midpoint | Slope behavior | Reward direction |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Amyloidogenic support | `1/(1+e^(-2(x-2)))` | x = 2 windows | rising | ≥2 classifier windows per residue |
| Disorder weight | `1/(1+e^(0.5(y-70)))` | y = pLDDT 70 | falling (in y) | low pLDDT maximizes weight |

The notebook renders this surface twice: first as a 3D scatter over the meshgrid x∈[0,6], y∈[0,100] with the axes labeled "Windows classified as amyloidogenic", `pLDDT^max`, and `Score`, exported to `obj_f.svg`; then as 2D `pLDDT`-vs-`Score` scatter panels faceted by `Agg` count (0, 1, 2, 3, ≥4) with a `cividis_r` color ramp normalized to `hue_norm=(0,1)`, exported to `ojb_f_new.svg` with the ylabel "Objective function score".

> [!TIP]
> The sigmoid midpoint x = 2 is not arbitrary: the companion artifact `Agg_len_RF_at_least_2.pkl` is commented as "Agg = windows with at least 2 RF windows as classified; as used in the IDR search" (line 261). The objective function simply recodes that empirical ≥2-window rule into a differentiable form, so scoring and segment-calling share one consistent threshold.

Sources: [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L83-L149), [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L1348-L1350), [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L1384-L1474), [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L260-L281)

## Background Construction: WT and gnomAD per-Transcript Tables

To prove that amyloidogenic-in-disorder residues are not a trivial consequence of local sequence composition, the notebook builds matched null distributions from gnomAD variant annotations. For each transcript `ENST`, it loads a WT prediction pickle and a gnomAD variant pickle from the cluster paths `/home/aelazar/higher_order_assemblies/classifier/human_ORfs/AF2/WT_RFR/pkls_RandomForestClassifier_9_9_21/pkls/%s_WT.pkl` and `.../gnomAD_AF2/pkls/%s_gnomAD.pkl`. Candidate aggregate stretches are pulled from positions falling inside the IDR interval (`IDRs.loc[i,'start']` to `'end'`), filtered to `MUT_Windows_above_thershold < 2` so the query stretch is amyloidogenic while the background is not, then `stats.percentileofscore(..., 'weak')` ranks the candidate's summed `exome_af` against matched stretches sampled from the rest of the protein. Two structural guards discipline the match: the background pool must be at least twice the query length (`len(df_IDR) > 2 * len(pos)`), and only contiguous position runs of exactly `len(pos)` residues qualify.

The loop exists in two symmetric variants — `AF2_pLDDT_max <= 70` (IDR background) and `>= 70` (Structured background) — persisting results to `gnomAD_allele_count_new_v4.pkl` and `gnomAD_allele_count_new_v4_v_Structured.pkl` respectively. A later refinement (v5) splits the structured control by solvent exposure into `Structured^{Buried}` and `Structured^{Exposed}` pickles (`gnomAD_allele_count_new_v5_SB_random.pkl`, `..._SE_random.pkl`, `..._IDR*.pkl`), enabling the three-way IDR / Exposed / Buried box plots that anchor the disorder-specific enrichment claim.

> [!TIP]
> Both loops embed the class logic directly: changing the pLDDT comparison at lines 433/485 re-tasks the identical gnomAD machinery between disorder-enrichment and structured-control analyses. The buried/exposed split (v5) then reuses the same percentile pipeline a third time — one matching engine, three experimental arms.

Sources: [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L422-L465), [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L474-L517), [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L692-L708)

## Statistical Validation Layer

Every filtering decision in this notebook is paired with a falsification test. The validation battery operates at three levels:

| Level | Comparison | Method / statistic | Output artifact |
|---|---|---|---|
| Classifier sanity | RF classification vs ground truth | confusion-matrix bar chart (TN=160, FP=18, FN=26, TP=76 annotated at L158) | `RF_classifier_test_set_v2.svg` |
| Class separation | Structured vs IDR vs IDR_expo window counts | ECDF overlay + `stats.ks_2samp` (L308) | ECDF panels, "Human ORFs" |
| IDR vs Globular prior | fraction of residues by windows above RF threshold | grouped bar chart (Globular `#0088DC` vs IDR `#FF8B00`) | `Fraction_residues_IDR_V_Globular_AF2_RF_classifier.svg` |
| Evolutionary constraint (IDR) | aggregate stretch vs matched IDR stretches | percentile-of-score box plot, annotated p = 10⁻¹⁷⁵ | `gnomad_all.svg` |
| Evolutionary constraint (Structured) | same on structured background | annotated p = 6·10⁻³⁶ | `gnomad_all_structed.svg` |
| Exposure control | IDR / Structured^{Exposed} / Structured^{Buried} | three-way box plots of `percentileofscore` | `gnomad_new.svg`, `precentile_new.svg` (commented) |

Two supporting analyses round out the picture: a scatter of IDR length against aggregating-residue count (`Agg_len_RF_at_least_2.pkl`) reports Spearman r = 0.51 on a log-x axis, showing that aggregation propensity scales sub-linearly with IDR length; and the membrane-specific slice restricts the IDR arm to bitopic proteins via `ENSG_type.protein_type == 'Bitopic'` joined through `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl`, with CD22 (ENST00000085219) developed as the worked single-gene example in `gnomAD_CD22.svg`. Sequence-level redundancy of IDR stretches is additionally probed with a pairwise Levenshtein distance matrix over `AAseq` values.

Sources: [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L157-L207), [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L298-L326), [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L536-L585), [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L644-L685), [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L977-L979), [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L1492-L1499)

## Artifact Inventory and Reproducibility Notes

The notebook reads and writes a large artifact graph. The table below consolidates every verified path, its role in the disorder-filtering logic, and where it enters the code.

| Artifact | Role | Code anchor |
|---|---|---|
| `waltzdb_export.csv` (waltzdb.switchlab.org) | amyloid/non-amyloid labels for ΔG_β box plot (ΣMUNV940103, t-test p = 10⁻¹¹²) | L215–L253 |
| `Agg_len_RF_at_least_2.pkl` | residues with ≥2 classifier windows, IDR-search standard | L261 |
| `DataFrame_AF2_drop_duplicates_classifier.pkl` | central per-residue AF2 feature table | L290 |
| `../files/AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` | ENST↔ENSG join table for protein-type filtering | L403 |

| `gnomAD_allele_count_new_v4.pkl`, `_v_Structured.pkl`, `_v5_{IDR,SE,SB}*.pkl` | percentile-match results per background arm | L536, L645, L693–L702 |
| `obj_f.svg`, `ojb_f_new.svg`, `gnomad_*.svg` | figure exports for the reproducibility map | L149, L1473, L584, L684 |

Three reproducibility caveats follow directly from the code. First, data paths are split between relative (`../files/`), local-author (`/Users/aelazar/PycharmProjects/PhaseSep/...`), and cluster (`/home/aelazar/higher_order_assemblies/...`) locations, so a faithful re-run requires the cluster filesystem. Second, the environment appends a personal IUPred2A install to `sys.path` and imports `localcider`, `pyaaisc`, and `umap` beyond the scientific core stack. Third, the notebook uses the long-deprecated `DataFrame.append` idiom and mutates shared DataFrames in place (e.g., assigning `d1['type']='Structured'` on slices), meaning cells are order-sensitive and idempotent only when executed top-to-bottom — deviations will silently alter class membership in the stratification table.

Sources: [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L215-L253), [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L289-L291), [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L402-L404), [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L8-L27), [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L149-L149)

## Where This Fits and What to Read Next

Within the catalog, this page is the hinge between statistical discovery and biological interpretation. Upstream, the classifier mechanics and training set belong to [WALTZ-DB Random-Forest Classifier](6-waltz-db-random-forest-classifier); the exact provenance and schema of the pickle artifacts consumed here are catalogued in [Shared Data Tables Reference](8-shared-data-tables-reference), and the figure exports (`obj_f.svg`, `ojb_f_new.svg`, `gnomad_all.svg`, `Fraction_residues_IDR_V_Globular_AF2_RF_classifier.svg`) are traceable through [Figure-to-Notebook Reproducibility Map](9-figure-to-notebook-reproducibility-map). Downstream, the IDR/Structured classes defined here become the population frames for sequence-composition and enrichment analyses ([Sequence Logos and Composition](10-sequence-logos-and-composition), [UniProt Keyword Enrichment](13-uniprot-keyword-enrichment)), while the bitopic-membrane restriction of the gnomAD arm previews the topology analysis in [Topology and Membrane-Leaflet Distance](15-topology-and-membrane-leaflet-distance). The recommended reading order is classifier → this page → shared tables, then any domain-specific downstream page.


# Shared Data Tables Reference



`files/` is the shared-data contract of the mdSAM repository: a small set of pickled pandas DataFrames that every analysis notebook reads as its common starting point. This page is a **reference document** — it catalogs each table, its producer, its verified column schema, its join semantics, and the notebooks that depend on it. Everything documented here was verified directly in the shipped files and notebooks; where the repository shows an inconsistency (a documented table missing from the shipped tree, or a notebook reading a local variant), that is flagged explicitly rather than papered over.

Sources: [files/README.md](files/README.md#L3-L11), [README.md](README.md#L33-L40)

## The files/ Directory at a Glance

The directory is deliberately small: three tables form the entire inter-notebook data plane. Two are shipped as `.pkl` artifacts (`dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl`, `hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl`); a third (`AF2_with_ENSG.pkl`) is documented in `files/README.md` and is loaded by thirteen notebooks, but is **not present in the shipped `files/` tree** — you must regenerate it with notebook 02 before running most consumers. Notebooks reference the tables with the relative prefix `../files/<name>`, which means every notebook must be executed with `notebooks/` as the working directory.

Sources: [files/README.md](files/README.md#L7-L11), [notebooks/05_uniprot_keyword_enrichment.ipynb](notebooks/05_uniprot_keyword_enrichment.ipynb#L33-L34)

| File | Contents | Producer | Verified key columns | Shipped? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl` | The mdSAM catalog (one row per motif); motif sequence in `AAseq` | mdSAM identification pipeline (offline, STAR Methods) | `AAseq`, `acc`, `start_new`, `end_new` | Yes |
| `hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl` | Human transmembrane proteins with UniProt topology annotation (one row per TM segment) | `03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb` (`TMs.to_pickle`) | `acc`, `start`, `end` | Yes |
| `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` | AlphaFold-derived per-protein annotations with Ensembl gene IDs | `02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb` (`AF2.to_pickle`, cell 205) | `acc`, `AAseq`, `ENSG`, `pLDDT`, `SS`, `accessibility`, `enst` | **No — regenerate via notebook 02** |

Sources: [files/README.md](files/README.md#L7-L9), [README.md](README.md#L36-L38)

The dependency flow is one-directional: producers write into `files/`, consumers only read. Notebook 08 is the most complete example of the consumer pattern — its first cell loads all three tables in a single block:

```python
hTMs = pd.read_pickle('../files/hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl')
AF2 = pd.read_pickle('../files/AF2_with_ENSG.pkl')
mdSAMs = pd.read_pickle('../files/dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl')
mdSAMs = mdSAMs.drop_duplicates('AAseq')
```

Sources: [notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb](notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb#L27-L30)

**Architecture note (prerequisite: the three tables above)** — the following diagram shows the verified producer→table→consumer graph. Solid arrows are load/write calls verified in notebook source; the dashed arrow marks the offline pipeline that produced the mdSAM table outside this repository.

