## Table 1: `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl` — The mdSAM Catalog

This is the central result table of the study: one row per predicted mdSAM (membrane-disordered Self-Assembly Motif). The paper reports **1,425 high-confidence mdSAMs across 945 membrane proteins** (~20% of the 4,886 human membrane proteins analyzed), with motifs typically 7–9 residues (median 8). The filename suffix `new_locs` refers to the `_new` location columns — `start_new`/`end_new` — that encode each motif's coordinate window within its parent protein.

Sources: [files/README.md](files/README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L19-L19)

| Column | Type | Meaning | Evidence in notebooks |
|---|---|---|---|
| `AAseq` | `str` | The 7–9 residue motif sequence (the join-free identity used for de-duplication) | `mdSAMs.drop_duplicates('AAseq')`; `mdSAMs[mdSAMs.AAseq=='GSSVFLNRS']` |
| `acc` | `str` | Parent protein UniProt accession — the foreign key into the other two tables | `mdSAMs.acc.isin(SSTM_topology.From)`; `AF2[AF2.acc==dSAMs.loc[i,'acc']]` |
| `start_new` | `int` | 0-based start coordinate of the motif in the parent protein | `int(mdSAMs[...].start_new.values[0])` |
| `end_new` | `int` | Exclusive end coordinate of the motif | `for j in range(int(mdSAMs.loc[i,'start_new']), int(mdSAMs.loc[i,'end_new']))` |

Sources: [notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb](notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb#L30-L57), [notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb](notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb#L161-L165), [notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb](notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb#L255-L259), [notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L52-L54)

Consumers apply two canonical patterns against this table. Notebook 08 de-duplicates on motif sequence before topology analysis (`drop_duplicates('AAseq')`), because the same motif string can appear in multiple proteins; and notebook 20 treats the table as a pure seed list, iterating rows to extract `acc` + `AAseq` pairs for conservation scoring.

Sources: [notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb](notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb#L30-L30), [notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L52-L54)

> [!TIP]
> Coordinate frames differ between consumers: notebook 08 trusts the shipped `start_new`/`end_new` columns directly, while notebook 20 deliberately **re-derives** positions by running `AF2.AAseq.str.find(motif)` against the AlphaFold sequence table before computing `start`/`end`. If your analysis is sensitive to coordinate frame consistency, follow notebook 20's re-derivation pattern rather than assuming `start_new` aligns with the AF2 sequence index.

Sources: [notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb](notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb#L57-L57), [notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L52-L54)

## Table 2: `hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl` — Human TM Proteins with Topology

This table is the universe definition for the study: all human transmembrane proteins with UniProt topology annotation. Unlike the mdSAM table, it is **long-shaped** — one row per transmembrane segment, so a polytopic protein contributes multiple rows with the same `acc`. Notebook 08 exploits this shape directly: `hTMs.acc.value_counts()` with a count of exactly 1 identifies single-pass (bitopic) proteins, the population used for the membrane-leaflet distance analysis.

Sources: [files/README.md](files/README.md#L8), [notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb](notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb#L77-L82)

| Column | Type | Meaning | Evidence in notebooks |
|---|---|---|---|
| `acc` | `str` | UniProt accession (repeated once per TM segment) | `set(TMs.acc)`; `hTMs[hTMs.acc==acc].start.values[0]` |
| `start` | `int` | TM segment start residue | `range(TMs.loc[i,'start'], TMs.loc[i,'end']+1)` |
| `end` | `int` | TM segment end residue | `hTMs[hTMs.acc==acc].end.values[0] - mdSAM_s` (leaflet distance) |

Sources: [notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L2663-L2669), [notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb](notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb#L135-L145)

Per `files/README.md`, the table is produced by notebook 03 via `TMs.to_pickle`. The verified read-back in notebook 03's late gnomAD cell (`TMs = pd.read_pickle('../files/hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl')`) confirms the round-trip: the same notebook both writes and re-consumes the table in different sections. Consumers use `start`/`end` to mask transmembrane regions — for example, notebook 03 builds the set of all TM-segment residue positions per accession to exclude membrane-embedded hexapeptides from disorder analyses.

Sources: [files/README.md](files/README.md#L8), [notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L2824-L2824), [notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L2665-L2669)

## Table 3: `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` — AlphaFold Per-Protein Annotations

This is the widest and most-consumed table (thirteen notebooks per `files/README.md`): one row per protein, carrying the full AlphaFold-derived annotation vector set plus cross-database identifiers. Its columns are the substrate for the disorder-filtering logic that defines what makes a SAM an mdSAM.

Sources: [files/README.md](files/README.md#L9), [README.md](README.md#L36-L38)

| Column | Type | Meaning | Evidence in notebooks |
|---|---|---|---|
| `acc` | `str` | UniProt accession (primary key) | `AF2[AF2.acc=='Q8IX19']` |
| `AAseq` | `str` | Full protein sequence; indexed by `str.find` to locate motifs | `AF2[AF2.acc==dSAMs.loc[i,'acc']].AAseq.str.find(...)` |
| `ENSG` | `str` | Ensembl gene ID — bridge from UniProt space to Ensembl space | `AF2[AF2.ENSG==topology_df.loc[i,'ENSG']].acc.values[0]` |
| `pLDDT` | array-like | Per-residue AlphaFold confidence; `<70` marks disordered residues | `AF2[AF2.acc=='Q6DN72']['pLDDT'].values[0][329:434]`; `pLDDT...if i>70` |
| `SS` | array-like | Per-residue secondary structure (`'H'` = helix) | `AF2...SS.values[0][pos-6:pos+6] if i=='H'` |
| `accessibility` | array-like | Per-residue solvent accessibility (`'*'` = exposed) | `accessibility.values[0][pos-6:pos+6] if i=='*'` |
| `enst` | `str` | Ensembl transcript ID (used in downstream joins) | `dSAM_df.ENST.isin(AF2[...].enst)` |

Sources: [notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L62-L63), [notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L2686-L2689), [notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L2830-L2830), [notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb](notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb#L225-L225), [notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L53-L53)

**Verification caveat**: `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` is documented and loaded everywhere, but the repository's `files/` directory currently ships only the two other pickles. Concretely, this means the pipeline is **not** runnable end-to-end until notebook 02 regenerates this table first — notebook 02 is therefore not merely the earliest notebook, it is a hard build dependency for twelve others. Its producer cell (cell 205, per the README) executes `AF2.to_pickle`, closing the loop.

Sources: [files/README.md](files/README.md#L9), [README.md](README.md#L36-L38)

## Join Semantics and Identifier Space

The three tables interlock through a deliberate identifier hierarchy. `acc` (UniProt accession) is the **universal join key** present in all three tables; `ENSG` and `enst` exist only in the AF2 table and act as outbound bridges into Ensembl space. Notebook 03 demonstrates the canonical resolution pattern when a foreign table speaks Ensembl: look up the accession through AF2 first (`AF2[AF2.ENSG==x].acc.values[0]`), then join everything else on `acc`. The relationship structure:

Sources: [notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L62-L63), [notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L2830-L2830)

```mermaid
erDiagram
    AF2_WITH_ENSG ||--o{ DSAM_MPS_V_PAPER_V2 : "acc (1 protein : N motifs)"
    AF2_WITH_ENSG ||--o{ HTMS_UNIPROT_V1 : "acc (1 protein : N TM segments)"
    DSAM_MPS_V_PAPER_V2 }o--|| HTMS_UNIPROT_V1 : "acc (motif sits outside TM start..end)"
    AF2_WITH_ENSG {
        string acc PK "UniProt accession"
        string AAseq "full protein sequence"
        string ENSG "Ensembl gene ID bridge"
        string enst "Ensembl transcript bridge"
        array pLDDT "per-residue confidence"
        array SS "per-residue secondary structure"
        array accessibility "per-residue solvent exposure"
    }
    DSAM_MPS_V_PAPER_V2 {
        string AAseq "motif sequence"
        string acc FK "parent protein"
        int start_new "motif start"
        int end_new "motif end"
    }
    HTMS_UNIPROT_V1 {
        string acc FK "protein, repeated per segment"
        int start "TM segment start"
        int end "TM segment end"
    }
```

Sources: [notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb](notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb#L124-L149), [notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb](notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb#L255-L259)

Two multiplicity rules follow from this schema. First, `dSAM → hTMs` joins must use `isin`-style filtering, not positional lookup, because mdSAM-containing proteins can be polytopic (multiple TM rows). Second, `AF2 → anything` is strictly one-to-many keyed on `acc`, which is why every consumer indexes AF2 with boolean masks (`AF2[AF2.acc==x]`) and extracts with `.values[0]` — a pattern that silently assumes unique accessions and will break loudly on duplicates.

Sources: [notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb](notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb#L135-L141), [notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb](notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb#L67-L68)

## Provenance, Conventions, and Safety

The repository enforces three conventions around these tables. **Path convention**: all loads use `../files/<name>`, so notebooks fail unless run from `notebooks/` as the working directory. **Provenance convention**: derived tables stay *local* to the notebook that computes them — notebook 08, after annotating leaflet distances, writes `mdSAMs.to_pickle('mdSAM_loacation.pkl')` into `notebooks/`, not back into `files/`; only the three tables above earned shared status. **Version convention**: consumers may pin specific snapshots, and this is where a lineage trap exists.

Sources: [files/README.md](files/README.md#L3-L11), [notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb](notebooks/08_mdsam_topology_and_membrane_distance.ipynb#L175-L175)

> [!TIP]
> Notebook 03's late LARKS/WIRS overlap cell loads `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2.pkl` — a **local file without the `new_locs` suffix** — rather than the shared `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl`. When tracing which mdSAM snapshot a figure was built from, check the exact filename in the loading cell, not the table's conceptual identity.

Sources: [notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L2824-L2830)

Finally, the pickle format itself carries a standing warning in `files/README.md`: pickles **execute arbitrary code on load** and are sensitive to the pandas version that wrote them. Load them only from this repository, and match your pandas version to the one used at write time. This also explains the design decision to keep `files/` minimal — fewer serialized blobs, fewer compatibility and trust surfaces.

Sources: [files/README.md](files/README.md#L13-L13)

| Convention | Rule | Why it exists |
|---|---|---|
| Working directory | Run notebooks from `notebooks/`; paths are `../files/<name>` | All load calls use relative parent paths |
| Derivatives | Annotation tables derived from shared pickles stay local to the notebook | Keeps `files/` as a minimal, auditable contract |
| Naming | `dSAM` in filenames/variables == mdSAM; structured-region counterpart is `mSAM`/`sSAM` | Historical naming preserved for lineage with the paper |
| Safety | `pd.read_pickle` only on tables from this repo; pin pandas version | Pickle deserialization is code execution |

Sources: [files/README.md](files/README.md#L3-L13), [README.md](README.md#L21-L21)

## Reading Progression

This reference sits between the pipeline description and the notebook-specific deep dives. A logical continuation path: understand how these tables feed the analysis flow in [Notebook Pipeline Architecture](5-notebook-pipeline-architecture), then see how the classifier that produced the mdSAM table was built in [WALTZ-DB Random-Forest Classifier](6-waltz-db-random-forest-classifier), how the `pLDDT`/`SS`/`accessibility` columns gate motif calls in [AlphaFold-Based Disorder Filtering](7-alphafold-based-disorder-filtering), and how specific notebook cells map back to paper figures in [Figure-to-Notebook Reproducibility Map](9-figure-to-notebook-reproducibility-map).


# Figure-to-Notebook Reproducibility Map



Every quantitative panel in the mdSAM manuscript can be traced to a specific notebook and a specific cell. This page is the reference for that trace: it consolidates the panel → notebook → cell mapping distributed in the repository's README, explains the conventions the map uses, documents which panels are intentionally not mapped, and shows how to regenerate any mapped panel locally. The map covers main Figures 1–7 and Supplementary Figures S1, S2, S3, S6 and S7; the notebooks are distributed with outputs cleared, so plots only exist after execution.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L88-L90), [README.md](README.md#L244-L248)

## Where the Map Lives and Its Conventions

The authoritative map is the **"Where the paper figures come from"** section of the root README, organized as one table per paper figure. Each row names the panel, describes its content, and points to the notebook plus the cell that draws it. The README's repository-contents block also advertises a `FIGURE_MAP.csv` ("machine-readable map: paper panel -> notebook -> cell"), but that file is not present in the current repository tree — the README tables are the operative reference on this branch.

Four conventions govern how to read the map. First, cell numbers are **0-based indices** into the notebook's `cells` list — they are positional, not Jupyter execution counts. Second, notebook filename prefixes (`01`–`23`) reflect pipeline order, not figure order: Figure 2 panels, for example, come from notebooks 06, 07, 08 and 09. Third, a panel may list **multiple cells**; these are alternative or iterative renderings of the same content, and any of them reproduces the panel. Fourth, one cell may serve **multiple panels** (e.g., notebook 11 cells 16–17 are cited jointly as "4C / 5B"). The README also establishes the naming bridge you will hit in the code: older notebooks call the motifs **dSAM** in filenames and variables — this means mdSAM.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L88-L90), [README.md](README.md#L26-L33), [README.md](README.md#L21), [README.md](README.md#L137-L142)

| Convention | Meaning for reproducibility |
|---|---|
| Cell index | 0-based position in the `.ipynb` `cells` list (e.g., "cell 2" = third cell), as stated in the README |
| Notebook numbering | `01`–`23` prefixes = pipeline order; figure order is independent |
| Multiple cells per panel | Iterative/alternative renderings — any listed cell reproduces the panel |
| Shared cells | One cell can be cited for several panels (e.g., `4C / 5B`, `4D / S5C`) |
| Outputs cleared | `.ipynb` files ship with `"outputs": []`; plots appear only after a run |
| Naming | `dSAM` in filenames/variables = **mdSAM** (e.g., `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl`) |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L31-L33), [README.md](README.md#L21), [notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb](notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb#L39-L67)

I verified the indexing convention by direct inspection rather than trusting the prose. Notebook 09 has exactly three cells; its third cell (index 2) draws the barplot and saves `number_of_mdSAMs_per_protein.svg` — precisely the README's Fig 2E row ("`09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb` (cell 2)"). Notebook 12's cell 3 saves `Amytracker_100uM.svg`, matching the cited "4C" and "S3D" rows, and a late cell of notebook 01 saves `RF_classifier_test_set_v2.svg`, consistent with its Fig 1D citation at cell 26.

Sources: [notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb](notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb#L39-L67), [notebooks/12_amytracker_peptides.ipynb](notebooks/12_amytracker_peptides.ipynb#L37-L52), [notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L489-L509), [README.md](README.md#L92-L98), [README.md](README.md#L134)

> [!TIP]
> When a panel cites several cells (e.g., Fig 2A → cells 79, 87, 89), the numbers are not sequential refinement steps of one plot — they are independently runnable renderings. To reproduce a paper panel, running any single listed cell after its notebook's setup cells is sufficient.

## Resolving a Panel: Panel → Notebook → Cell

The map is consumed in a fixed four-step flow, and the resolution chain matters because the two index systems differ. A paper panel is looked up in the README table by its label (e.g., `2E`), which yields a notebook filename and a 0-based cell index; you then execute the notebook from its own working directory so relative paths resolve, and the figure emerges as an SVG file written into the notebook directory. The paper's final rendering remains the visual reference — the notebooks reproduce the analysis and the plot, not the typeset composite.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Paper panel<br/>(e.g. Fig 2E)"] --> B["README figure table<br/>row lookup"]
    B --> C["Notebook + 0-based cell<br/>09_...ipynb (cell 2)"]
    C --> D["Run from notebooks/ cwd<br/>tables read from ../files/"]
    D --> E["SVG written to cwd<br/>number_of_mdSAMs_per_protein.svg"]
    E --> F["Panel reproduced<br/>(paper = final rendering)"]
```

The working-directory requirement is structural, not stylistic: notebook code reads shared tables via relative paths such as `pd.read_pickle('../files/hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl')`, and figure exports use relative filenames (`plt.savefig('number_of_mdSAMs_per_protein.svg', ...)`, `plt.savefig('Amytracker_100uM.svg', ...)`). Running from the wrong directory fails the table load or writes the SVG elsewhere.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L88-L90), [README.md](README.md#L244-L248), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L1-L3), [notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb](notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb#L35-L36), [notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb](notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb#L65), [notebooks/12_amytracker_peptides.ipynb](notebooks/12_amytracker_peptides.ipynb#L50)

## Architecture: Notebooks Grouped by Figure Theme

Before reading the per-figure tables, it helps to see the production topology. The 23 notebooks fall into six thematic stages, and figures are generally assembled from one notebook per stage — Figure 2 is the notable exception, drawing on four notebooks because it spans organelle enrichment, topology, per-protein counts and sequence-space embedding. Notebooks 02 and 19 occupy supporting positions: 02 produces the shared AlphaFold residue table rather than panels, and 19 re-runs differential expression and gene-set enrichment that supports Fig 6E without a dedicated map row.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph prep["Data preparation &amp; classifier"]
        NB01["01 RF classifier<br/>(WALTZ-DB)"]
        NB02["02 AlphaFold<br/>residue table"]
        NB03["03 Sequence<br/>logos"]
    end
    subgraph div["Discovery &amp; diversity"]
        NB04["04 PASTA<br/>comparison"]
        NB05["05 UniProt<br/>keywords"]
        NB06["06 Sequence-space<br/>embedding"]
        NB07["07 hyperLOPIT<br/>organelles"]
        NB08["08 Topology &amp;<br/>leaflet distance"]
        NB09["09 mdSAMs<br/>per protein"]
    end
    subgraph inv["In vitro self-assembly"]
        NB10["10 ThT<br/>96-well"]
        NB11["11 GPCR ThT<br/>proline mutants"]
        NB12["12 Amytracker"]
    end
    subgraph cb["Cell-based clustering"]
        NB13["13 TIRF<br/>Poisson GLM"]
        NB14["14 Flow<br/>cytometry"]
        NB15["15 BioGRID<br/>interactions"]
        NB16["16 dSTORM<br/>HTR7"]
    end
    subgraph sig["HTR7 signalling"]
        NB17["17 cAMP Emax/EC50"]
        NB18["18 RNA-seq<br/>PCA/volcano"]
        NB19["19 GSEA<br/>(support)"]
    end
    subgraph ev["Evolution"]
        NB20["20 Alignment<br/>conservation"]
        NB21["21 ESM<br/>conservation"]
        NB22["22 Ortholog ThT"]
        NB23["23 LARKS/WIRS/<br/>FINCHES"]
    end
    NB01 --> F1("Fig 1")
    NB06 --> F1
    NB05 --> F1
    NB07 --> F2("Fig 2")
    NB08 --> F2
    NB09 --> F2
    NB06 --> F2
    NB10 --> F3("Fig 3")
    NB12 --> F4("Fig 4")
    NB11 --> F4
    NB13 --> F4
    NB11 --> F5("Fig 5")
    NB13 --> F5
    NB16 --> F5
    NB17 --> F6("Fig 6")
    NB18 --> F6
    NB19 -.-> F6
    NB21 --> F7("Fig 7")
    NB20 --> F7
    NB22 --> F7
```

The supplementary figures reuse the same notebooks rather than introducing new ones: S1 is served by 01/03/04/05 (validation of the prediction), S2 by 06/07 (diversity and localisation), S3 by 10/12 (peptide assembly), S6 by 14/15/17 (expression controls and BioGRID), and S7 by 20/22/23 (conservation). This is why the notebook count (23) exceeds the figure count — each notebook typically feeds both a main figure and a supplementary one.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L35-L86), [README.md](README.md#L175-L206), [README.md](README.md#L207-L213), [README.md](README.md#L215-L240), [README.md](README.md#L40), [README.md](README.md#L77)

### Figure 7: Evolutionary conservation

Conservation is measured two independent ways — alignment-based (20) and protein-language-model embedding-based (21) — both feeding panel 7B, with ortholog peptide ThT (22) supplying 7D.

## Coverage Boundaries: What the Map Omits

The map is explicitly partial, and its exclusions are as documented as its inclusions. The README states that panels that are schematics, microscopy or EM images, NMR or mass-photometry data, or produced outside these notebooks are not listed — so the absence of an S4/S5 section and of imaging-micrograph rows is by design, not an omission to be fixed. Within the notebooks themselves, several analyses are documented as beyond the paper: notebook 03 contains additional gnomAD analyses, notebook 15 contains further interaction analyses, and notebook 16 holds earlier analysis versions — none of these appear in the figure tables.

For intermediate developers the practical consequence is a triage rule: if a plot appears in a notebook but not in the map, treat it as exploratory or superseded; if a paper panel is absent from the map, check whether it belongs to an excluded category before searching for missing code.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L242), [README.md](README.md#L41), [README.md](README.md#L68-L69)

> [!TIP]
> The "task" tables in the earlier README section and the figure map section are mutually consistent but not identical in scope — notebook 11's task row lists S3C, while the S3 map section attributes S3C's cited cells to notebook 10. When in doubt, the per-figure map section (panel → cell) is the operative reference for reproduction; the task tables describe notebook intent.

## Regenerating a Panel

A mapped panel is reproduced by executing its notebook in place. The repository ships the three shared input tables as pickled pandas DataFrames in `files/` — `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl` (the mdSAM table with motifs in the `AAseq` column), `hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl` (human transmembrane proteins with UniProt topology), and `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` (AlphaFold-derived annotations with Ensembl IDs). Notebooks reference them as `../files/<name>`, so the run must start from `notebooks/` as the working directory. Then execute the notebook's cells top-to-bottom (imports and table loads come first in the `cells` list) and stop at the cited index; the panel is exported as an SVG into the notebook directory. Because the notebooks were written for interactive sessions, some read additional intermediate files not stored in `files/` — the README flags this for specific notebooks.

Two cautions from the repository's own documentation apply. First, pickle files execute code on load and are pandas-version dependent — load them only from this repository with a compatible pandas version. Second, cells above the cited index are required context, not optional: the target cell consumes variables defined upstream (e.g., notebook 09's cell 2 uses `dSAMs` loaded in cell 1).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L244-L248), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L5-L13), [notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb](notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb#L34-L37), [notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb](notebooks/09_mdsams_per_protein.ipynb#L39-L65)

| Step | Action | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `cd notebooks/` (working directory requirement) | Relative pickle paths `../files/<name>` |
| 2 | Confirm `../files/` contains the three shared `.pkl` tables | `files/README.md` table |
| 3 | Run notebook cells 0 → target index (inclusive) | Cell indices are 0-based positions |
| 4 | Collect the exported SVG from the notebook directory | e.g., `number_of_mdSAMs_per_protein.svg` |
| 5 | Compare against the paper panel (final typeset rendering) | Notebooks reproduce analysis, not composite layout |

For deeper setup (environment, package imports spanning `Bio`, `Levenshtein`, `logomaker`, `fcsparser`, `gseapy`, and more) see [Quick Start](2-quick-start) and [Reusing the Analysis Toolkit](27-reusing-the-analysis-toolkit); for the full contents and provenance of the three pickles see [Shared Data Tables Reference](8-shared-data-tables-reference).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L250), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L5-L13)

# Sequence Logos and Composition



This page documents `notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb` — the notebook that characterizes *what mdSAMs look like* at the sequence level. It renders Shannon-information sequence logos of mdSAM hexapeptides versus all predicted SAMs in membrane proteins (paper panel **Fig. S1H**), tests whether amyloid-positive windows are statistically over-represented in disordered regions, and persists two shared artifacts consumed by most later notebooks: the human transmembrane-protein table `hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl` and the disordered-window table `AF_IDR_v3.pkl`. It also carries exploratory mutation-robustness and gnomAD analyses that never became paper figures. Throughout, note the naming convention: older code calls mdSAMs **dSAM** and their structured-region counterparts **mSAM/sSAM**.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L41), [README.md](README.md#L21), [03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L9-L29)

## Pipeline Position and Data Flow

The notebook sits third in the numbered pipeline: it consumes the AlphaFold residue table built by notebook 02 (`AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` with per-protein sequence, pLDDT, secondary structure and accessibility arrays) and the WALTZ-DB random-forest classifier scores attached to every enumerated hexapeptide. From these it derives the disordered/structured window populations, renders the logos, and exports reference tables that notebooks 05–09, 15, 18, 20, 21 and 23 later read back from `files/`.

Before reading the diagram: `enumerate.pkl` holds every hexapeptide window of the analyzed proteins together with the RF classifier verdict (`classifier` = 1 means amyloid-forming), while `topology_df` supplies membrane-protein ENSG identifiers used to restrict analysis to the membrane proteome.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph inputs["Inputs"]
        NB02["02: AF2_with_ENSG.pkl<br/>(pLDDT, SS, accessibility)"]
        RF["01: RF classifier scores<br/>(classifier ∈ {0,1})"]
        TOP["topology_df<br/>(membrane-protein ENSGs)"]
    end
    subgraph nb03["notebook 03"]
        POP["Population tables<br/>AF_IDR_v2/v3, AF_Stru_v2/v3"]
        LOGO["Sequence logos<br/>(logomaker, cells 35/37)"]
        STAT["Enrichment tests<br/>chi-square / Fisher / hypergeometric"]
    end
    subgraph outputs["Persistent artifacts"]
        HTM["files/hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl"]
        AIDR["AF_IDR_v3.pkl"]
        SVG["Fig S1H SVGs"]
    end
    NB02 --> POP
    RF --> POP
    TOP --> POP
    POP --> LOGO
    POP --> STAT
    POP --> HTM
    POP --> AIDR
    LOGO --> SVG
    HTM --> DN["Notebooks 05, 06, 07, 08, 09,<br/>15, 18, 20, 21, 23"]
    AIDR --> DN
```

Sources: [03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L38-L53), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L8-L9), [README.md](README.md#L41)

## Constructing the Comparison Populations

The logos are only meaningful relative to a contrast, and the notebook builds four window populations from a single filter grammar: membership in disordered vs. structured regions, solvent accessibility (six `*` characters marks fully accessible), secondary structure (any `H` excludes a window), and removal of hexapeptides overlapping transmembrane segments (`TM_hexa`).

| Table | Definition | Role in the logos |
|---|---|---|
| `AF_IDR_v2` | Windows in IDR regions, non-helical, accessibility `******`, in membrane proteins (`TMs.acc`) | Source of mdSAM hexapeptides |
| `AF_Stru_v2` | Windows with `IDR=='Structure'` in the same proteins | Structured counterpart (mSAM host) |
| `AF_IDR_v3` / `AF_Stru_v3` | v2 tables after dropping `TM_hexa` sequences | TM-contamination-free final populations |

> [!TIP]
> Cell 35's mdSAM logo draws from `AF_IDR_v3[AF_IDR_v3.classifier==1]` — i.e., motifs that are simultaneously classifier-positive *and* in disordered, solvent-exposed context. This is the operational definition of an mdSAM at hexapeptide granularity, mirroring the discovery criteria (pLDDT < 70, non-helical, solvent-exposed, non-TM) described on the [AlphaFold-Based Disorder Filtering](7-alphafold-based-disorder-filtering) page.

Sources: [03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L125-L136), [03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L148-L149), [03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L169-L191)

## Building the Sequence Logos (Fig. S1H)

The logo construction is deliberately transparent — no black-box logo utility does the counting. Two counting cells (33 and 36) loop over the six hexapeptide positions × the 20 standard amino acids, tallying occurrences in the positive-class windows; the result is pivoted into a 6×20 count matrix. The accompanying `seqlogo.fa` cell (cell 34) writes all mdSAM hexapeptides to FASTA for external tools.

The rendering cells then delegate to **logomaker** with an explicit information transform:

| Parameter | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `transform_matrix` | `counts → information` | Per-position Shannon information in **bits** (Rₛₑ𝵪₝ₑₙcₑ formula) — stack height = conservation |
| `color_scheme` | `NajafabadiEtAl2017` | Physicochemical AA coloring |
| `font_name` | `Stencil Std` | Glyph font for the letter stacks |
| Y-axis | `Information (bits)` | 0–~4.2 bit scale |
| X-axis | positions 1–6 | Hexapeptide window coordinates |

Two figures result, and the README's figure map pins them exactly to paper panel S1H: cell 35 saves `seqlogo_membrane_all_dSAMs_membrane.svg` (title *mdSAM*) and cell 37 saves `seqlogo_membrane_all_SAMs.svg` (title *SAMs*, counting **all** classifier-positive windows in membrane proteins regardless of disorder). The visual contrast between the two stacks is the point: SAMs overall vs. their disordered-context subset.

Sources: [03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L562-L585), [03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L597-L616), [03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L653-L673), [README.md](README.md#L181-L182)

## Statistical Context: Are Disordered SAMs Enriched?

The logos are framed by three significance tests that justify comparing mdSAM composition against the structured baseline. A 2×2 contingency table (IDR/Structure × classifier 1/0) feeds a chi-square test and a two-sided Fisher exact test; an "expected vs. observed" bar plot (`chi_anaysis_MPs_SAMs_human.svg`) visualizes the chi-square decomposition with dSAM/sSAM axis labels. Hypergeometric CDF curves — written with the authors' "team A runners/winners" metaphor — quantify enrichment from both the disordered (`human_disordered.svg`) and structured (`human_ordered.svg`) sides. A small pie chart quantifies what fraction of the 4,886 analyzed membrane proteins harbor a predicted SAM in disordered context.

Sources: [03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L233-L263), [03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L287-L288), [03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L340-L361), [03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L373-L388), [03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L476-L536)

## Persistent Artifacts and Downstream Consumers

Beyond figures, notebook 03 is a *producer* notebook: it pickles the population tables it computes and the transmembrane-protein reference table that the rest of the pipeline depends on.

| Artifact | Producer evidence | Read by |
|---|---|---|
| `hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl` | `TMs.to_pickle` (per `files/README.md`) | Notebooks 03, 05, 06, 07, 08, 09, 15, 18, 20, 21, 23 |
| `AF_IDR_v3.pkl` | v3 tables derived after `TM_hexa` exclusion | Downstream diversity/conservation notebooks |
| `AF_IDR_v2.pkl`, `AF_Stru_v2.pkl` | explicit `to_pickle` calls in cell 17 | Local reuse within the notebook |
| `gnomAD_no_TM_v_2_1._with_ele.pkl` | cell 15 | Off-paper gnomAD extension |

`hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl` — human transmembrane proteins with UniProt topology annotation — is one of only two data files committed under `files/`, which is why the catalog's [Shared Data Tables Reference](8-shared-data-tables-reference) treats this notebook as its upstream source.

Sources: [03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L222-L223), [03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L201-L203), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L5-L9)

## Beyond the Paper: Mutation Robustness and gnomAD

The README explicitly flags that this notebook "contains additional gnomAD analyses that are not part of the paper figures." Two exploratory blocks follow the logos:

**Single-mutation robustness.** Loading `enumerate_one_away.pkl` (all hexapeptides one substitution away from an observed window), the notebook computes how many mutations are needed to *create* or *maintain* a SAM, stratified by IDR vs. structured vs. random context, producing the "Creating a mSAM" and "Maintaining a mSAM" cumulative-frequency curves.

**gnomAD variant impact.** Population variants (`gnomAD_mutations_with_WT_and_CADD.pkl`) are classified by re-scoring wild-type and mutant hexapeptides with the RF classifier: `destroy` (WT_RF ≥ 1, MUT_RF = 0), `create`, `maintain`, or `None`. A geometric helper (`seqlocmembrane_IDR_balant`, with a ballantine `0.52·(70n)^(1/3)` correction) estimates each variant's signed distance to the membrane boundary, which is then plotted against CADD-PHRED deleteriousness — asking whether variants that destroy mdSAMs are under constraint near the lipid bilayer.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L41), [03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L706-L718), [03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L783-L812), [03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L953-L956), [03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L1001-L1035)

## Reproducibility Caveats

Two practical facts matter if you re-run this notebook. First, several inputs are **not shipped with the repository**: `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` must be regenerated by notebook 02, and `enumerate/enumerate.pkl`, `topology_df`, the SSTM boundary tables, and gnomAD pickles reference local paths or an external volume (`/Volumes/aelazar/...`) — only the derived tables in `files/` are committed. The `files/README.md` warns that pickle files execute code on load and are pandas-version sensitive. Second, the committed notebook carries a mechanical text artifact: the token `ax` was globally replaced by `ax[0]`, corrupting identifiers such as `Max[0]NLocator`, `ax[0]is` (for `axis`), and `ww_logo.ax[0]` in the logo cells. Cells must have these reverted to their original identifiers before execution — the analytical logic is intact, only identifiers are affected.

> [!TIP]
> Cell numbers in this documentation are 0-based indices into the notebook's `cells` list, matching the README's figure map convention — so "cell 35" means the 36th cell object in the `.ipynb` JSON, not a display index in Jupyter.

Sources: [03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L49-L52), [03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L25), [03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L663-L668), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L13), [README.md](README.md#L33)

## Where to Go Next

The logos answer *what* mdSAMs look like; the rest of the "Sequence Space Characterization" section answers *how they relate to each other*. Continue to [Physicochemical Embedding and Clustering](11-physicochemical-embedding-and-clustering) for the GMM/Levenshtein/charge-archetype treatment of the same sequence space, or to [PASTA Comparison and Window Thresholds](12-pasta-comparison-and-window-thresholds) for how consecutive positive windows set the high-confidence mdSAM threshold. For the schema of `hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl` and the other shared tables this notebook produces, see [Shared Data Tables Reference](8-shared-data-tables-reference); for the classifier whose `classifier==1` labels feed every logo stack, see [WALTZ-DB Random-Forest Classifier](6-waltz-db-random-forest-classifier).


# Physicochemical Embedding and Clustering



This page documents `notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb`, the notebook that maps the mdSAM peptide collection into a low-dimensional physicochemical feature space and partitions it into interpretable clusters. It is the quantitative bridge between the compositional characterization of [Sequence Logos and Composition](10-sequence-logos-and-composition) and the functional annotation performed in [UniProt Keyword Enrichment](13-uniprot-keyword-enrichment): it converts each unique amino-acid sequence into a compact vector of IDR-theory descriptors, projects those vectors with UMAP and t-SNE, fits a Gaussian Mixture Model on the projected coordinates, and then validates that the clusters carry biological meaning via hypergeometric keyword enrichment.

Sources: [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L20-L39)

## Position in the Pipeline and Data Inputs

Architecturally, notebook 06 consumes the two shared intermediate tables defined in the [Shared Data Tables Reference](8-shared-data-tables-reference): the mdSAM motif table `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl` (motif sequence in the `AAseq` column) and the human transmembrane protein table `hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl`. It also reads `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` (produced by notebook 02) to reconcile UniProt accessions with Ensembl transcripts before embedding. The first structural operation is a strict deduplication on the motif sequence — `dSAM_df.drop_duplicates(subset='AAseq')` — which guarantees that the embedding describes the *sequence space* rather than the redundant occurrence space; the deduplicated count (`len(mdSAMs)`) is the effective population of every subsequent analysis.

Sources: [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L49-L51), [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L297-L297), [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L374-L376), [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L476-L479), [README.md](files/README.md#L5-L9)

The notebook also produces contextual context figures early on: a 70×70 dot matrix (4,900 grid points truncated to the 4,887 membrane proteins) distinguishing the 945 mdSAM-harboring membrane proteins from the remaining 3,978, and a motif-length distribution histogram covering lengths 7 through ≥13. These establish the population statistics that motivate the embedding analysis, and are exported as `mdSAMs_in_membrane_proteins_high_con_dot_matrix.svg` and `mdSAMs_length_distribution.svg` for the figure pipeline mapped in [Figure-to-Notebook Reproducibility Map](9-figure-to-notebook-reproducibility-map).

Sources: [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L341-L349), [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L359-L400), [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L457-L466)

## Stage 1 — Physicochemical Feature Engineering with localcider

The analytical core of the notebook is a per-sequence feature table (`umap_dff`) built by iterating over every deduplicated motif and calling the `localcider.sequenceParameters.SequenceParameters` API — the reference implementation of Uversky/Das-Pappu IDR physics. Each sequence is reduced to eight scalar descriptors: Uversky hydropathy, mean net charge (NCPR), the AAindex `MUNV940103` residue scale aggregated as `beta`, and four grouped residue-class fractions — `Aromatic` = F(Y)+F(W)+F(F), `Posetive` = F(H)+F(R)+F(K), `Negitive` = F(D)+F(E), plus hydrophobic and polar classes (`Hydro` starting from V/I/L, `Polar` from T/S/N).

Sources: [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L498-L512)

| Feature | Definition | Source API | Biological semantics |
|---|---|---|---|
| `beta` | Mean of AAindex `MUNV940103` values per residue | Hard-coded dict (L31–33) | β-aggregation coupling potential (rendered as $\sum\Delta G_{\beta}$ in figures) |
| `hydropathy` | Uversky hydropathy | `get_uversky_hydropathy()` | Promotes inter-peptide association |
| `mean_net_charge` | NCPR | `get_mean_net_charge()` | Electrostatic repulsion / salt-bridge balance |
| `Aromatic` | F(Y)+F(W)+F(F) | `get_amino_acid_fractions()` | π-stacking and hydrophobic core formation |
| `Posetive` | F(H)+F(R)+F(K) | `get_amino_acid_fractions()` | Cationic motif density |
| `Negitive` | F(D)+F(E) | `get_amino_acid_fractions()` | Anionic motif density |
| `Hydro` | F(V)+F(I)+F(L)+… | `get_amino_acid_fractions()` | Aliphatic hydrophobicity |
| `Polar` | F(T)+F(S)+F(N)+… | `get_amino_acid_fractions()` | H-bonding side-chain density |

Sources: [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L31-L33), [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L504-L512)

A second, richer annotation pass reconstructs the full descriptor matrix (`UMAP_plot`): besides the eight embedding features, it computes `get_delta()`, `get_fraction_disorder_promoting()`, `get_FCR()`, `get_Omega()`, motif length, all twenty per-residue fractions, and the *summed* `beta` variant (`np.sum` of `MUNV940103` values, matching the $\sum\Delta G_{\beta}$ axis title). Note the deliberate asymmetry: the **8-column matrix feeds the projection**, while the **40+ column table annotates the projected points** — a separation of concerns that keeps the embedding low-dimensional but the interpretation high-dimensional. The membrane-relevant subset `df_membrane` is then isolated by dropping rows with null `acc` and de-duplicated again by `AAseq`.

Sources: [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L556-L604), [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L601-L603)

> [!TIP]
> The two `beta` aggregations are not redundant — `umap_dff` uses the **mean** flexibility value as an embedding coordinate, while `UMAP_plot` uses the **sum**, which couples motif length into the quantity displayed as $\sum\Delta G_{\beta}$ in the paper panels. Choosing which one to visualize changes the geometric gradient you read off the embedding.

## Stage 2 — Dimensionality Reduction: Standardize, Then UMAP and t-SNE

Both projections follow the same discipline: z-normalize the 8-column feature matrix with `StandardScaler().fit_transform()` before projecting. Two reducers are instantiated and cross-checked:

1. **UMAP** — `umap.UMAP(random_state=120, n_neighbors=5)`, a fine-grained local-manifold view seeded for determinism (L532–533).
2. **t-SNE** — `TSNE(n_components=2, learning_rate='auto', init='random', perplexity=30, random_state=2)` (L556).

The paper-grade figure (`all_tsne_colors_paper_v2.svg`) uses the **t-SNE** coordinates — every panel axis is labeled `t-SNE`, and the earlier UMAP export exists only as a commented-out call (`all_UMAP_madan_colors_paper_not_rasterized_v3.svg`). A hierarchical clustermap of the standardized features (`sns.clustermap`) provides a third, independent sanity check of feature-space structure before projection.

Sources: [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L522-L522), [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L532-L533), [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L556-L556), [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L707-L712)

| Aspect | UMAP path | t-SNE path |
|---|---|---|
| Call | `umap.UMAP(random_state=120, n_neighbors=5)` | `TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=30, random_state=2, learning_rate='auto', init='random')` |
| Input | Standardized 8-feature matrix | Standardized 8-feature matrix |
| Role in notebook | Exploratory manifold view | Paper-figure geometry (`all_tsne_colors_paper_v2.svg`) |
| Downstream use | Superseded | Feeds `df_membrane['x','y']` and GMM clustering |

Sources: [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L532-L533), [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L556-L570)

The embedding workflow can be summarized as follows:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl<br/>(mdSAM motifs, AAseq)"] --> B["drop_duplicates(AAseq)<br/>unique sequence space"]
    B --> C["localcider feature loop<br/>8 descriptors per sequence"]
    C --> D["StandardScaler<br/>z-normalization"]
    D --> E["UMAP<br/>rs=120, n_neighbors=5"]
    D --> F["t-SNE<br/>rs=2, perplexity=30"]
    F --> G["df_membrane<br/>(x, y) + 40-column annotation"]
    G --> H["GaussianMixture<br/>k=3, full, rs=42"]
    H --> I["gmm_dSAMs labels"]
    I --> J["Hypergeometric keyword enrichment<br/>+ FDR per cluster"]
    G --> K["3x2 t-SNE color panels<br/>all_tsne_colors_paper_v2.svg"]
```

Sources: [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L498-L533)

## Stage 3 — The Paper Figure: Color-Encoded Feature Gradients

The canonical figure is a 3×2 scatter grid over `df_membrane`, coloring the same t-SNE point cloud by six orthogonal gradients: `Negitive`, `Posetive`, `Aromatic`, `Hydro`, `Polar`, and `beta`. Each panel uses a custom two-stop `LinearSegmentedColormap` (light gray `#DEE0E3` to a signature accent color per class, with the beta panel running `#B9A84B → #000832`), a shared `Normalize(vmin=0, vmax=100)` color scale, and per-panel colorbars — since a single seaborn `hue` cannot span multiple colormaps in one figure, the code loops over `(feature, colormap)` pairs with `fig.colorbar(sm, ...)` attached to each subplot. Panel titles use the compact residue-class notation: `Negative(DE)`, `Positive(RKH)`, `Aromatic(YWF)`, `Hydrophobic(GAVILM)`, `Polar(TSNQC)`, and `$\sum\Delta G_{\beta}$`.

Sources: [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L649-L712)

A companion set of five zoom-in "test" figures validates that color gradients correspond to real sequence families at specific coordinates: each figure draws a `Rectangle` over a quadrant of the global t-SNE (e.g., the cationic block at `(-15, 20, 25, 25)`), then re-plots the magnified window with four hand-selected indices highlighted as white points and their raw `AAseq` strings annotated via `adjust_text`. The exported artifacts — `tnse_RK_test.svg`, `tnse_DE_test.svg`, `tnse_YWF_test.svg`, `tnse_Hydro_test.svg`, `tnse_PLOAR_test.svg` — demonstrate that, e.g., the RK-rich region genuinely contains lysine/arginine-dense motifs and the YWF region aromatic ones. These figures exemplify the notebook's verification pattern: **claim a spatial gradient, then magnify and label the sequences that instantiate it**.

Sources: [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L715-L755), [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L814-L844), [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L991-L1060)

## Stage 4 — Gaussian Mixture Clustering on Embedded Coordinates

The clustering stage is deliberately simple and *post-hoc*: after reloading the annotated projection (`df_membrane = pd.read_pickle('HTS/umap.pkl')`), a `mixture.GaussianMixture(n_components=3, covariance_type="full", random_state=42)` is fitted on the **2-D t-SNE coordinates** (`['x','y']`), and soft-assignment predictions are written back into a `gmm_dSAMs` column. This is a key architectural decision worth internalizing: **the mixture model partitions the embedding manifold, not the original 8-D feature space** — clusters therefore correspond to visually coherent regions of the published figure, and their interpretation inherits the usual t-SNE caveat that only local neighborhoods are trustworthy. An adjacent exploratory cell sweeps the hyperparameters (`n_components=10, covariance_type="diag", random_state=157`) for robustness comparison before settling on k=3.

Sources: [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L1079-L1086), [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L1106-L1113)

| GMM parameter | Value | Rationale in this context |
|---|---|---|
| `n_components` | 3 | Minimal partition matching the three dominant visual lobes of the t-SNE cloud |
| `covariance_type` | `"full"` | Allows anisotropic cluster shapes on the manifold |
| `random_state` | 42 | Deterministic EM initialization for reproducibility |
| Fit coordinates | `['x','y']` (t-SNE) | Clusters are defined on the published geometry, not raw features |
| Exploration sweep | k=10, `diag`, rs=157 | Sensitivity check on over-segmentation |

Sources: [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L1082-L1086)

## Stage 5 — Statistical Validation: Per-Cluster Keyword Enrichment

To show the clusters are not geometric artifacts, the notebook runs a hypergeometric enrichment of UniProt keywords within each `gmm_dSAMs` label. The `hypergeom(keyword, cluster)` function computes observed vs. expected keyword counts over the `df_membrane` population, using `stats.hypergeom.cdf` with a one-sided correction (`p = 1-p` when observed exceeds expected). Candidate keywords are pre-filtered to those with ≥10 mdSAM-bearing members across the `Disease`, `Molecular function`, and `Biological process` categories of a UniProt keyword table (`KeyWord_df`). Multiple-testing pressure is handled by a rankdata-based Benjamini–Hochberg-style `fdr()` helper, and results are plotted as per-cluster and combined volcano panels (`obs-exp` vs. `-log10 FDR`), exported as `obs_exp_Keywords_gmm_cluster_%d.svg` and `obs_exp_Keywords_gmm.svg`.

Sources: [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L1122-L1139), [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L1205-L1248), [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L1258-L1291)

This closes the analytical loop: geometry → clusters → function. Spot checks in the notebook (e.g., querying `enrich[enrich.keyword_ID=='Cell adhesion']` and `'Neurodegeneration'`) indicate the clusters differentiate mdSAM-bearing proteins by functional family. The methodological details of the keyword machinery itself — the UniProt annotation tables and genome-wide enrichment strategy — are covered on [UniProt Keyword Enrichment](13-uniprot-keyword-enrichment); here it serves only as the interpretive endpoint of clustering.

Sources: [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L1335-L1336), [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L1399-L1399)

## Reusable Utilities: Publication-Grade Convex Hulls

Beyond the pipeline proper, notebook 06 ships three plotting utilities that are candidates for extraction into the shared toolkit described in [Reusing the Analysis Toolkit](27-reusing-the-analysis-toolkit): `calculate_hull()` builds a scale-based-padded convex hull (a `StandardScaler → MinMaxScaler(-1,1)` pipeline times a `scale` factor, `scipy.spatial.ConvexHull`, then periodic quadratic B-spline interpolation via `scipy.interpolate.splev(..., per=True, k=4)`); `draw_hull()` wraps it for matplotlib; and `draw_rounded_hull()` renders hulls with true rounded corners by offsetting hull edges along their normals and inserting `matplotlib.patches.Arc` segments. These are the mechanism for drawing cluster/membership boundaries around scattered embedding points in publication figures.

Sources: [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L79-L171), [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L212-L277)

## Reproducibility Notes for Advanced Users

Three environment realities matter when re-running this notebook. First, two inputs are external to the repository: the UniProt id-mapping TSV (`/Users/aelazar/notebooks_for_paper/idmapping_reviewed_true_2024_02_05.tsv`) used for gene-name mapping, and the keyword TSV (`/Users/aelazar/Downloads/keywords_all_2023_10_27.tsv`) — these author-local paths must be replaced with fresh UniProt downloads to reproduce `df_membrane['gene_name']` and the enrichment. Second, the clustering stage re-reads a serialized state (`HTS/umap.pkl`) rather than recomputing from the in-memory t-SNE, so the exact published cluster partition depends on that snapshot; regenerating it requires rerunning the t-SNE cell with `random_state=2` first. Third, all stochastic components (UMAP `random_state=120`, t-SNE `random_state=2`, GMM `random_state=42`) are pinned — preserve them if you need bit-exact figure reproduction. The dependency set (`localcider`, `umap`, `adjustText`, sklearn, seaborn) plus the `Arial` font family via `plt.rcParams` are declared at the top of the notebook.

Sources: [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L612-L618), [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L1079-L1079), [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L1123-L1123), [06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/06_mdsam_sequence_space_embedding.ipynb#L34-L39)

> [!TIP]
> Because GMM labels are fit on t-SNE coordinates, do not treat cluster assignment as a stable function of the 8 input features across reruns — small t-SNE drift propagates into label flips. If you need stable, transferable cluster identity, refit the GMM directly on the standardized `umap_dff` matrix and only *visualize* the labels on the t-SNE plane.

The natural reading order around this page: upstream compositional context in [Sequence Logos and Composition](10-sequence-logos-and-composition); how the same embedding coordinates reappear with per-protein aggregation and localization overlays in [hyperLOPIT Organelle Enrichment](14-hyperlopit-organelle-enrichment) and [Topology and Membrane-Leaflet Distance](15-topology-and-membrane-leaflet-distance); the full statistical machinery behind the keyword enrichment in [UniProt Keyword Enrichment](13-uniprot-keyword-enrichment); and notebook-level orchestration details in [Notebook Pipeline Architecture](5-notebook-pipeline-architecture). For adapting the feature-engineering loop to your own peptide sets, see [Reusing the Analysis Toolkit](27-reusing-the-analysis-toolkit).


# PASTA Comparison and Window Thresholds



Notebook `04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb` answers a skepticism question that any reviewer of a *de novo* aggregation predictor should ask: **do mdSAM motifs look like aggregation hot spots to independent, physics-based methods?** The notebook performs two coupled analyses — a round trip to the PASTA 2.0 and Aggrescan web servers for orthogonal scoring of every deduplicated mdSAM motif, and a calibration study that sweeps the "minimum number of windows above threshold" decision rule against the WALTZ-DB ground truth. Its opening comment states the agenda plainly: *supplemental information on cutoff of windows*, citing both tools.

Sources: [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L10-L12)

## Pipeline Position and Data Flow

Conceptually this notebook is the **external validation wing** of the sequence-space characterization section. It consumes the mdSAM motif table, ships sequences out to two tools that are not reimplemented anywhere in the repository, joins the returned scores back by sequence string, and then turns to the WALTZ-DB table to ask how many positive windows a sequence must contain before calling it amyloid. The two halves share no data — only a theme — which is why the notebook reads like two mini-pipelines back to back.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["dSAM table<br/>deduplicated AAseq motifs"] -->|"FASTA export"| B["batch FASTA files"]
    B --> C["Aggrescan<br/>hot-spot scan"]
    B --> D["PASTA 2.0<br/>pairing energy"]
    C --> E["dSAMs_aggrescan.txt"]
    D --> F["one .best_pairings_list.dat<br/>per peptide"]
    E --> G["join on AAseq<br/>adds nHS and PASTA columns"]
    F --> G
    G --> H["swarm plot<br/>PASTA energy vs hot-spot count"]
    I["waltzdb_extend.pkl"] --> J["window-count threshold sweep"]
    J --> K["ROC curves<br/>operating point: 2 windows"]
```

The staged hand-off through web servers means several inputs exist only as local files on the original author's machine; the table below is the complete inventory of what the notebook touches.

| Stage | Artifact referenced | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Motif source | `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2.pkl` | mdSAM table; motifs in the `AAseq` column |
| Export | printed FASTA records | input batch for both web tools |
| Aggrescan return | `dSAMs_aggrescan.txt` | per-sequence hot-spot count (`nHS`) |
| PASTA return | `*.fasta.seq.best_pairings_list.dat` | per-sequence best pairing energy (`PASTA`) |
| Threshold study | `waltzdb_extend.pkl` | WALTZ-DB labels + `WT_Windows_above_thershold` |

Sources: [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L36), [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L235), [README.md](files/README.md#L3-L9)

## Round Trip to External Predictors

### A Self-Describing FASTA Export

The export loop deduplicates the table on `AAseq` and prints FASTA records whose *headers embed the sequence itself*: `>acc_AAseq` on the header line, with `AAseq` repeated as the sequence line. This redundancy is deliberate — because PASTA names its output files after the input FASTA header, the sequence ends up encoded in the returned filename, so the notebook can re-join scores without maintaining a separate manifest.

> [!TIP]
> When you re-run this notebook against your own PASTA/Aggrescan batches, keep the `>acc_seq` header convention intact. The join-back expressions (`split('_')[1]` for PASTA, `split('_')[-1]` for Aggrescan) parse the sequence out of filenames and column names — any change to the header format silently breaks the match and leaves `NaN` scores rather than raising an error.

Sources: [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L62-L66)

### Ingesting Aggrescan Hot-Spot Counts

The Aggrescan result is a single tab-delimited table where **each column is one sequence** (its name ends with the motif string) and each row is one Aggrescan metric. The ingestion loop walks the columns from index 1 onward, extracts the trailing token of each column name, looks up the matching row in `dSAMs` by `AAseq`, and writes the value at row index 1 into a new `nHS` column. The downstream figure legend labels this quantity as the Aggrescan hot-spot count, which anchors its interpretation.

Sources: [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L75), [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L86-L89), [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L195)

### Ingesting PASTA 2.0 Pairing Energies

PASTA returns **one small space-delimited file per peptide**, exemplified by `Q5VU65_LQHWLWS.fasta.seq.best_pairings_list.dat`. Three consecutive `glob` loops cover the run's output batches — directories `predictions1_1000`, `predictions10001_2000` (spelled exactly so in the code), and `predictions2001_end` — and each iteration parses the motif out of the filename via `split('_')[1].split('.')[0]`, then reads the value at row 0, column 5 into the `PASTA` column. The figure's axis label names this quantity the *PASTA energy (best)*, i.e., the best pairing energy PASTA found for the motif.

Sources: [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L140), [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L150-L161), [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L194)

### The Comparison Figure

Both ingested scores meet in one swarm plot: **`PASTA energy(best)` on the y-axis, colored by Aggrescan hot-spot count (`nHS`)** using the `cividis` palette, over the deduplicated motif set. The plot is produced twice at different figure sizes, saving `PASTA_nHS_mdSAMs_v2.svg` and `PASTA_nHS_mdSAMs.svg`; a `value_counts()` cell on `nHS` beforehand serves as a sanity check on how many sequences received each hot-spot count. A quick mental model of the two external scores:

| Aspect | Aggrescan | PASTA 2.0 |
|---|---|---|
| Input artifact | printed FASTA batch | same FASTA batch |
| Return format | one TSV, sequence-per-column | one `.dat` file per peptide |
| Extraction expression | `dSAMs_aggrescan.loc[1, i]` | `read_csv(...).loc[0, 5]` |
| Filename/column parse | `i.split('_')[-1]` | `split('_')[1].split('.')[0]` |
| Stored column | `nHS` (hot-spot count) | `PASTA` (best pairing energy) |
| Figure role | color (`hue`) | y-axis value |

Sources: [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L171), [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L183-L199), [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L208-L225)

## Calibrating the Window-Count Threshold

The second half of the notebook loads `waltzdb_extend.pkl` — the WALTZ-DB peptide table (curated from `waltzdb_export.csv` in [WALTZ-DB Random-Forest Classifier](6-waltz-db-random-forest-classifier)) extended with a per-sequence `WT_Windows_above_thershold` column (the repository's own spelling, preserved here so you can search for it). That column **counts how many sliding windows of the sequence the trained random forest scored above its amyloid threshold**; it is computed upstream of these notebooks in the identification pipeline and merely consumed here.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S["WALTZ-DB peptide"] --> W["per-window RF scores"]
    W --> N["WT_Windows_above_thershold<br/>count of positive windows"]
    N --> D{"count >= c ?"}
    D -->|"yes"| AMY["predicted amyloid"]
    D -->|"no"| NON["predicted non-amyloid"]
    D -.->|"c = 2 selected<br/>in both ROC sweeps"| OP["pipeline operating point"]
```

Two distribution views establish the raw material: notch-boxplots of the window count split by WALTZ-DB `Classification` (gray for non-amyloid, maroon `#9D282B` for amyloid, with a light strip-overlay of individual points), rendered at both the start and end of this notebook section.

Sources: [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L235), [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L245-L257), [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L426-L438), [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L113-L117)

## Two Sweeps Toward One Operating Point

### Coarse Sweep: Normalized Frequency Tables

The first threshold scan works entirely from **normalized frequency distributions** of the window count per class: `n` for non-amyloid sequences and `a` for amyloid sequences. For each cut `c` from 0 to 8, the false-positive rate is `1 − cumsum(n[:c])` (the non-amyloid share with count ≥ c) and the true-positive rate is `a[c:].sum()` (the amyloid share with count ≥ c), assembled into a cut-vs-rates DataFrame. One literal quirk is worth knowing before you extend the range: the `cut = 1` row hardcodes `TP` to 1 rather than deriving it from `a`.

Sources: [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L267-L268), [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L290-L298)

### Exact Sweep: Confusion-Matrix Counts

The second scan re-encodes `Classification` into a binary `class` column and computes **exact confusion-matrix counts** for cuts 1 through 4: sequences with count ≤ c−1 are predicted non-amyloid (contributing `TN`/`FN`), sequences with count between c and 10 are predicted amyloid (contributing `TP`/`FP`), then `TPR = TP/(TP+FN)` and `FPR = FP/(FP+TN)` are collected into a small DataFrame. Both sweeps are plotted as ROC scatter plots with the cut value encoded as color, and **both place an empty red circle at the same spot — c = 2** — via `ax.plot(..., markerfacecolor='none', markeredgecolor='red')`; the exact sweep is saved as `ROC_extneded_waltzdb.svg` (again, spelling preserved for searchability).

> [!TIP]
> The c = 2 operating point highlighted in this notebook is not an isolated choice: elsewhere in the pipeline the same "at least 2 RF-positive windows" rule is explicitly annotated (the `Agg_len_RF_at_least_2.pkl` comment defines *Agg* as windows with at least two RF-classified windows, "as used in the IDR search"). Treat 2 as the pipeline-wide convention when reusing the scoring logic on new sequences.

Sources: [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L346-L357), [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L379-L389), [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L311-L336), [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L398-L416), [02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L258-L281)

### Reading the Two Sweeps Side by Side

| Property | Coarse sweep | Exact sweep |
|---|---|---|
| Cut range | 0 – 8 | 1 – 4 |
| Rate basis | normalized `value_counts` cumsums | per-cut confusion-matrix counts |
| Binary labels | implicit (n vs a) | explicit `class` 0/1 column |
| Cut encoded by | `hue='cut'`, `cividis` | `hue='c'`, `RdGy` + connecting line |
| Operating point | red circle at c = 2 | red circle at `ll.loc[1]` (c = 2) |
| Known quirk | `TP` hardcoded to 1 at cut = 1 | counts capped at `between(i, 10)` |

The agreement between an approximate frequency-based curve and an exact count-based curve is the notebook's implicit argument that **the operating point is robust to how you compute the rates** — and the `≥ 3` queries on per-transcript window counts in [WALTZ-DB Random-Forest Classifier](6-waltz-db-random-forest-classifier) show the same column being filtered even more conservatively in other contexts.

Sources: [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L308-L336), [04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb](notebooks/04_pasta_aggregation_comparison.ipynb#L398-L416), [01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L560-L572)
