# dSTORM Cluster Analysis



This page dissects `notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb` — an 11,700-line spatial-statistics notebook that converts raw ThunderSTORM single-molecule localization exports into biologically interpretable receptor-cluster measurements. The methodological core is a **Voronoi-tessellation density threshold calibrated against a Monte Carlo spatial null**, followed by **HDBSCAN cluster assignment** on threshold-passing localizations. The notebook operates in two dataset phases: an APP/dAPP (WT vs. mutant transmembrane peptide) development phase, and the HTR7 GPCR phase (basal vs. stimulated, WT vs. MUT) that feeds the end-to-end HTR7 case study. It sits between [Flow Cytometry Surface Gating](18-flow-cytometry-surface-gating) and [cAMP Dose-Response Mixed Models](20-camp-dose-response-mixed-models) in the Experimental Assay Analytics track.

Sources: [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L9-L53), [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L114-L150)

## Why Voronoi Before Clustering: The Core Concept

Direct density-based clustering of SMLM localizations is confounded by local labeling density: a region with 500 localizations/µm² may look "clustered" under a fixed epsilon even when it is spatially random, purely because fluorophore density is high. This notebook's central insight is to invert the problem — measure *local crowding per localization* via Voronoi cell area, then decide "what counts as crowded" **empirically per ROI** rather than by a global constant. Each localization's Voronoi cell area is converted to a density score `vol_invers = log10(1/vol)` (smaller cell → higher score), and the cut between "random" and "clustered" is set at the 1st percentile of Voronoi areas drawn from uniform-random point patterns matched to the ROI's point count. Only points below this adaptive threshold enter the clusterer.

The dependency chain of this concept is worth internalizing before reading the code:

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[ThunderSTORM CSV export<br/>x, y, frame, uncertainty nm] --> B[Localization filtering<br/>uncertainty &lt; 20nm, frame &gt;= 200]
    B --> C[ROI cropping<br/>4,000 nm x 4,000 nm rectangle]
    C --> D[Voronoi tessellation<br/>per-localization cell area]
    D --> E[Monte Carlo null<br/>n uniform-random trials, same N, same grid]
    E --> F[Adaptive threshold<br/>mean of 1st-percentile random cell areas]
    F --> G[Density gate<br/>keep points with vol &lt; threshold]
    G --> H[HDBSCAN min_cluster_size=5<br/>labels; -1 = noise]
    H --> I[Cluster metrics<br/>count, size, radius, % clustered]
    I --> J[Statistical validation<br/>Fisher exact, hypergeometric, BH-FDR]
```

Sources: [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L399-L431), [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L340-L366)

## Ingestion Layer: `ThnderSTORM2df`

The entry point `ThnderSTORM2df(file, squre_size, x1, y1, parent, element, cell, rectangle, replicate)` reads localization tables from `csv/v2/<file>.csv` and applies two physics-motivated filters before any spatial analysis: localizations with fitting **uncertainty ≥ 20 nm** are discarded (they are too imprecise to support nanoscale cluster claims), and **frame < 200** localizations are dropped — early frames of a dSTORM acquisition carry transient high-density blinking artifacts. The function then crops the requested rectangle (production calls use 4,000 nm squares; the function default is a full 50,000 nm field), renders a two-panel QA figure (full field with ROI rectangle overlay, zoomed ROI), exports it as SVG and 600-dpi PNG, and returns a tidy DataFrame with unified column names (`x`, `y`, `intensity`) plus experimental metadata (`parent`, `element`, `cell`, `rectangle`, `replicate`, `name`).

| Filter / Parameter | Value | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| `uncertainty [nm]` | `< 20` | Reject imprecise localizations that blur cluster boundaries |
| `frame` | `>= 200` | Skip early-frame acquisition artifacts |
| `squre_size` | `4000` nm | Standard ROI (4 µm membrane patch) in all production calls |
| Output columns | `x, y, intensity, parent, element, cell, rectangle, replicate, name` | Schema consumed by every downstream function |

Sources: [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L114-L150), [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L165-L169)

## The Adaptive Threshold Engine: `voronoi_thershold_v2`

This is the notebook's intellectual center. Given a point array, it runs `n` Monte Carlo trials, each drawing `len(points)` uniform-random coordinates over the same `size_of_grid` (4,000 nm in practice). For every trial it computes Voronoi cell volumes via `voronoi_volumes` (which wraps `scipy.spatial.Voronoi` and returns `ConvexHull(...).volume` per cell, `inf` for open boundary cells), records the **1st percentile** of each trial's volume distribution, and averages the percentiles into a single threshold. The intuition: under complete spatial randomness, ~1% of localizations will occupy cells smaller than the threshold — so labeling real points below it yields a controlled ~1% false-density rate regardless of ROI-level localization count. The real pattern's cells are then gated, and `HDBSCAN(min_cluster_size=5)` is fit on the survivors; labels are written back to the full frame (`-1` and `NaN` retained for noise). Notably, the function retains a commented-out `DBSCAN(eps=50, min_samples=3)` variant, documenting the migration from fixed-epsilon to hierarchical-density clustering. It returns five objects: the annotated point DataFrame, the random-trial volume table, the scalar threshold, per-cluster size probabilities, and the concatenated random-point table used in threshold visualization.

> [!TIP]
> The threshold is recomputed **per ROI** because it depends on `len(points)` and `size_of_grid` — never cache thresholds across ROIs with different localization counts, or the false-positive calibration silently breaks.

| Design decision | Implementation | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Null model | `np.random.uniform(0, size_of_grid, size=(len(points), 2))` | Matches the ROI's point count exactly |
| Threshold statistic | `np.mean` of per-trial `np.percentile(random_dist, 1)` | Reduces Monte Carlo variance across trials |
| Density score | `vol_invers = log10(1/vol)` | Log-scaled crowding, stable for violin/threshold plots |
| Clusterer | `HDBSCAN(min_cluster_size=5)` | No fixed eps; adapts to varying cluster scales |
| Legacy alternative | `DBSCAN(eps=50, min_samples=3)` (commented) | Fixed 50 nm radius rejected for density robustness |

Sources: [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L399-L431), [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L103-L112)

## Per-ROI Orchestration: `voro2cluster` and `roi2df`

Two wrappers standardize the workflow. `voro2cluster` is the **publication-figure generator**: a three-panel layout showing (1) raw filtered localizations with the teal ROI rectangle, (2) Voronoi cells colored by `vol_invers` under a viridis density scale with tessellation edges overlaid, and (3) HDBSCAN-assigned points colored per cluster with noise faintly black underneath. It embeds the threshold call (`n=1` for speed) and saves 600-dpi PNGs per cell/rectangle. `roi2df` is the **metrics-oriented wrapper** used in batch statistics: it runs the heavier calibration (`n=30` trials), bins each clustered localization's `cluster_size` into ranges `5-10`, `11-50`, `51-100`, `>100`, flags `binary_theshold` per point, and propagates ROI identity columns (`name`, `cell`, `rectangle`, `replicate`) into the returned frame so that every localization row is traceable to its source image.

Sources: [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L240-L306), [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L1586-L1607)

## Metric Functions and Batch Execution

A utility block defines the measurement vocabulary applied to every labeled ROI. `df2clustersize` computes each cluster's **maximal pairwise extent** via `scipy.spatial.distance.pdist` (nanometers, since coordinates are in nm), `area2clusters` produces cluster-size distributions as tidy records tagged with element and square number, `cluster_fraction` relates each cluster's size to unclustered-spot counts, and `precent_clustered` returns the fraction of Voronoi-gated points plus total localization count — the notebook's headline "percent clustered" statistic. Geometric annotation is handled by `cluster2rad_for_fig`, which computes each cluster's centroid, its **max radial distance R (nm)**, draws proportional circles on the scatter, and annotates `R=…nm / n=…` for exemplar clusters.

The batch loop then iterates over ~29 WT (`apps_v2`) and ~17 MUT (`dapp_v2`) ROI DataFrames, and — critically — additionally tiles each ROI into **500 nm × 500 nm sub-squares**, recording per-tile `all_points`, `db_points`, `vor_points`, `clusters_in_roi`, and cluster-size aggregates into a records list that later becomes the density-controlled `grid_df`. This sub-sampling layer is what enables the density-bin analyses described below.

| Function | Metric produced | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| `df2clustersize` | Max pairwise distance within cluster | nm |
| `area2clusters` | Cluster-size distribution records | localizations/cluster |
| `cluster_fraction` | Cluster size relative to free spots | dimensionless |
| `precent_clustered` | % localizations below threshold | % + count |
| `cluster2rad_for_fig` | Centroid-to-farthest-point radius R | nm |

Sources: [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L73-L112), [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L2318-L2399), [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L1642-L1662), [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L2232-L2298)

## Statistical Validation Layer

Because single-molecule cluster claims are easy to overstate, the notebook wraps its point estimates in three complementary tests. **Fisher exact tests** run on 2×2 contingency tables partitioning cluster anatomy by `cluster_size_log` and `dens_log` cutoffs, independently for APP and dAPP, with `scipy.stats.contingency.expected_freq` printed alongside observed-minus-expected residuals. **Hypergeometric radius enrichment** (`G_hypergeom_radii` over radius quantiles q = 1–4 for both elements) asks whether large-R clusters are over-represented relative to expectation; p-values pass through a hand-rolled **Benjamini–Hochberg FDR** (`fdr`) that scales p by `len(p_vals)/rankdata(p)` with values capped at 1, and results are plotted as `log2(observed/expected)` enrichment barplots. Finally, Tukey-style outlier bounds (`calculate_upper_bound`, Q3 + 1.5×IQR) bound "compatibly sized high-density" cluster populations before medians are reported.

> [!TIP]
> The Fisher-exact cutoffs (`cluster_size_log >= 1`, `dens_log >= -3`) are strata definitions, not significance thresholds — they define the high-size/high-density quadrant of the contingency table, so changing them changes the tested hypothesis, not just its power.

Sources: [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L6808-L6833), [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L5201-L5208), [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L5238-L5255), [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L5313-L5326)

## Density Normalization: Controlling the Dominant Confound

Cluster-size statistics co-vary trivially with localization density, so the notebook normalizes comparisons by construction. Using the 500 nm tile records (`grid_df`), cluster-level means are regrouped into **density bins** — `0–300`, `301–900`, `901–1500` localizations per tile for the APP phase — and `cluster_sizes_full_vals_nm_mean` is plotted per bin as strip + mean-marker point plots on a log y-axis (`Localizations_per_clsuter_SNAPtm_v2_dAPP.svg`). The notebook even catalogs hand-picked exemplar tiles at matched point counts (e.g., 53, 140, 295 localizations) to render like-for-like Voronoi panels for WT and MUT. This design means any WT/MUT cluster-size difference reported downstream survives a same-density comparison — the strongest form of evidence this pipeline produces.

Sources: [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L7800-L7858), [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L7895-L7944)

## The HTR7 Phase: `voro2cluster_v4` and Basal/Stimulated Design

The final notebook section reapplies the matured pipeline to the HTR7 receptor. A refined wrapper, `voro2cluster_v4`, is invoked over dozens of `HTR7_MUT_Basal_1_*` / `HTR7Mut_B_2_*` ThunderSTORM files — parent `HTR7`, element `MUT`, cells 2–10, replicates 1–2, all with 4,000 nm ROIs — following the identical call pattern established in the APP phase. Files are referenced from the author's local figure directory (`dSTORM/figures/HTR7_Science/`) via `glob` sampling for the main-figure composites. The terminal analysis joins clusters back into `bins_df` split by functional **state** (`basal` vs. stimulated) and **element** (`WT` vs. `MUT`), with density re-binned to HTR7-appropriate ranges (`0-70`, `71-150`), and produces the log-scaled "localizations per cluster" violin/strip comparisons (`Localizations_per_clsuter_HTR7_high_dens.svg`) that summarize HTR7 clustering phenotypes.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph Phase 1 - Development
        A[APP WT ROIs] --> C[Adaptive Voronoi+HDBSCAN]
        B[dAPP MUT ROIs] --> C
        C --> D[grid_df density tiles]
        D --> E[Fisher / hypergeometric / FDR]
    end
    subgraph Phase 2 - HTR7 Case Study
        F[HTR7 Basal WT/MUT] --> H[voro2cluster_v4]
        G[HTR7 Stimulated WT/MUT] --> H
        H --> I[bins_df: state x element x density]
        I --> J[Cluster-size phenotypes]
    end
    E -.method transfer.-> H
```

Sources: [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L11400-L11511), [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L11521-L11542), [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L11554-L11583)

## Supporting Spatial-Statistics Tooling

Beyond the Voronoi/HDBSCAN core, the import block reveals the notebook's fuller spatial-analysis arsenal: `ripleyk` for Ripley's K second-order statistics, `rdfpy.rdf` for radial distribution functions, `OPTICS` as another density-based alternative, `shapely` geometries plus `ConvexHull` and an `intersection` helper for region algebra, and `NearestNeighbors` for neighbor-based computations. These are wired in alongside the DBSCAN-family clusterers, indicating the threshold calibration was cross-validated against classical point-pattern methods before settling on the Voronoi-percentile design. Reproducibility caveats for developers: raw localization CSVs live under a local `csv/v2/` path (not shipped in this repository — see [Repository Layout and Notebook Map](3-repository-layout-and-notebook-map) for what is versioned), several output paths point to the author's machine (`/Users/aelazar/...`), and cell outputs are stripped from the committed notebook, so a full reproduction requires the ThunderSTORM exports plus matching directory scaffolding.

| Dependency | Role in pipeline |
|---|---|
| `ripleyk` | Ripley's K spatial autocorrelation cross-check |
| `rdfpy` | Radial distribution function of localization patterns |
| `sklearn.cluster` (DBSCAN/OPTICS/HDBSCAN) | Density-based cluster assignment (HDBSCAN production) |
| `scipy.spatial` (Voronoi, ConvexHull, pdist) | Tessellation, cell areas, cluster extents |
| `shapely` + `intersect` | Polygon region logic for Voronoi visual overlays |

Sources: [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L9-L53), [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L114-L118)

## Where This Fits and What to Read Next

This notebook is the microscopy leg of the HTR7 evidence chain: its cluster phenotypes (percent clustered, localizations per cluster, radius distributions under matched density) quantify the membrane-organization consequences of the HTR7 constructs, which are then related to signaling output on [cAMP Dose-Response Mixed Models](20-camp-dose-response-mixed-models) and integrated into the narrative on [HTR7 End-to-End Case Study](21-htr7-end-to-end-case-study). For the upstream discovery context — why these membrane-proximal motifs were targeted for single-molecule imaging at all — see [mdSAM Concept and Discovery Rationale](4-mdsam-concept-and-discovery-rationale); for the imaging assays that precede dSTORM in resolution, see [TIRF Puncta Poisson GLM](17-tirf-puncta-poisson-glm). The figure-to-analysis mapping conventions it follows are cataloged in [Figure-to-Notebook Reproducibility Map](9-figure-to-notebook-reproducibility-map).


# cAMP Dose-Response Mixed Models



This page dissects `notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb`, the functional endpoint of the HTR7 assay chain. The notebook answers two coupled questions with one statistical engine: does the mdSAM-derived proline mutation change *how much receptor is expressed* as transfection DNA is titrated, and does it change *how well the receptor signals* (cAMP Emax and EC50)? The expression side is handled by per-construct **linear mixed models** with replicate-level random intercepts, while the cAMP side enters as a pre-computed summary layer. Understanding the division of labor between these two layers is the key to adapting the notebook correctly.

## Role in the Assay Analytics Chain

Within the *Experimental Assay Analytics* cluster, this notebook sits immediately after the single-cell imaging readouts and before the transcriptomic response. The mdSAM classifier proposes aggregation-prone membrane motifs; notebooks 13–16 test cellular phenotypes (puncta, surface gating, organelle clusters); notebook 17 closes the loop by testing whether the motif mutation alters receptor *expression* (Total), *trafficking* (Surface), and *function* (cAMP). Its outputs feed directly into the HTR7 end-to-end narrative.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["mdSAM motif discovery<br/>Notebooks 01–09"] --> B["Imaging phenotypes<br/>TIRF · Flow · dSTORM<br/>Notebooks 13–16"]
    B --> C["Notebook 17<br/>Expression LMMs +<br/>cAMP Emax/EC50 summary"]
    C --> D["Transcriptomic response<br/>PCA · Volcano · GSEA<br/>Notebooks 18–19"]
    C --> E["HTR7 case-study synthesis"]
```

The notebook's own header explicitly frames it as a plotting revision: log10-transformed values (not a log axis), statistics on the transformed scale, replicate trajectories grouped by `Element + Rep`, mean ± SEM, significant proteins split from the remainder, and SVG outputs. Every downstream design decision — the transforms, the trajectory keys, the figure split — follows from that stated contract.

Sources: [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L7-L17)

## The Data Contract: From Workbook to Model Frame

The raw input is a single Excel workbook read through two sheets, `Surface` and `Total`, using the `Geometric Mean` column as the measurement metric. Rows are filtered to the two conditions of interest, `Element ∈ {WT, MUT}`, then technical replicates are collapsed by taking the mean of the metric within each `(Construct, Element, DNA, Rep)` group — the four-column key that later feeds the merge between sheets. This groupby-then-mean step is deliberate: it removes well-level measurement noise *before* the model sees the data, so the mixed model's residual term reflects biological rather than technical variance.

Sources: [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L26-L49), [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L51-L61)

After merging, four derived columns define the entire analysis space: `logSurface`, `logTotal`, `DNAlog` (all log10), and `logTrafficking = logSurface − logTotal`. Two properties of this design deserve attention. First, transforming **before** plotting and statistics means every β coefficient is interpretable as a log10-fold change and every mean ± SEM ribbon is on the plotted scale — statistics and visuals never disagree. Second, the difference-of-logs `logTrafficking` is exactly log10(Surface/Total), so the trafficking panel is a ratio test expressed additively; a β on this column reads as a percent change in surface-per-total delivery.

Sources: [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L63-L69)

> [!TIP]
> The groupby key `(Construct, Element, DNA, Rep)` is simultaneously the merge key between sheets and the identity of one biological unit. If you add a condition (e.g., a second mutant), adding it to this key propagates automatically through averaging, merging, and model grouping — the only place to touch is the categorical `hue_order` used in plotting.

## Model Architecture: Two Live LMMs and One Imported Summary

The statistical core is a per-construct loop fitting two statsmodels linear mixed models, with the cAMP results arriving as constants rather than fits:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    XLSX["mdSAM_Constructs.xlsx<br/>Surface + Total sheets"] --> AVG["Mean technical replicates<br/>key: Construct·Element·DNA·Rep"]
    AVG --> LOG["log10 transforms<br/>logSurface · logTotal · DNAlog · logTrafficking"]
    LOG --> LMM1["Surface LMM<br/>logSurface ~ Element * logDNA + logTotal<br/>random intercept: Rep"]
    LOG --> LMM2["Total LMM<br/>logTotal ~ Element * logDNA<br/>random intercept: Rep"]
    LMM1 --> RES["results table<br/>Protein · Term · Estimate · StdErr · P-value"]
    LMM2 --> TOT["total_results table"]
    RES --> ANN["Panel annotations<br/>β and P per construct"]
    RES --> FOREST["Forest plot<br/>Element[T.MUT] ± 1.96·SE"]
    CAMP["Upstream cAMP nonlinear fits<br/>hardcoded Emax / EC50 constants"] --> BARS["Emax / EC50 bar charts<br/>with 95% CI"]
```

| Model | Fixed formula | Random effect | Optimizer | Status | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Surface LMM | `logSurface ~ Element * logDNA + logTotal` | intercept per `Rep` | lbfgs, REML | **Active** | Surface phenotype adjusted for expression |
| Surface-only LMM | `logSurface ~ Element * logDNA` | intercept per `Rep` | lbfgs, REML | Commented out | Archived pre-adjustment variant |
| Total LMM | `logTotal ~ Element * logDNA` | intercept per `Rep` | lbfgs, REML | **Active** | Expression-level dose response |

Sources: [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L893-L944), [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L1099-L1132), [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L774-L783)

## Fixed-Effects Logic: Why `Element * logDNA + logTotal`

The interaction `Element * logDNA` expands to four terms, and each has a precise geometric meaning on the dose-response plane. Because DNA dose enters as the continuous covariate `logDNA` rather than a categorical factor, the model estimates **slopes** instead of per-dose offsets — one degree of freedom per curve, and an interaction term that directly tests whether the mutant's dose-response *tilt* differs from WT's. `Element[T.MUT]` alone is the vertical offset at the reference dose, while `logTotal` is the adjustment covariate that asks the surface effect question *at equal expression*, which is what separates a trafficking phenotype from an expression artifact.

| Fitted term | Interpretation on the log-log plane |
|---|---|
| `Intercept` | WT baseline log10(Surface) at log10(DNA) = 0 |
| `Element[T.MUT]` | Vertical mutant offset at zero dose (log10 units) |
| `logDNA` | WT dose-response slope |
| `Element[T.MUT]:logDNA` | Differential slope — mutant vs WT sensitivity to transfection dose |
| `logTotal` | Δ log10(Surface) per log10 unit of total expression (the expression adjustment) |

Sources: [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L903-L907)

The commented-out cell preserves the notebook's analytical history: the original specification was `logSurface ~ Element * logDNA` with no adjustment, and the revision added `logTotal`. Keeping both in the file is useful archaeology — if a reviewer asks whether the adjustment drives a conclusion, the unadjusted comparison is one uncomment away. The same `results`-collection protocol (loop over `fit.params.index`, harvesting Estimate, `fit.bse`, and `fit.pvalues` into a tidy frame) is identical in both variants, so the downstream annotation code is agnostic to which specification ran.

Sources: [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L774-L811), [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L920-L943)

## Random-Effects and Estimation Choices

Every model uses `groups=sub["Rep"]`, which statsmodels implements as a random intercept per biological replicate — a compound-symmetry assumption stating that observations from the same replicate share a common shift. This is the correct minimal structure when each replicate contributes observations at multiple DNA doses: ignoring `Rep` would treat dose points within a replicate as independent and deflate standard errors. The loop also carries a defensive guard, skipping any construct with fewer than two unique replicates, since a single-group variance component is unidentifiable.

Estimation uses restricted maximum likelihood (`reml=True`) with the lbfgs optimizer. REML is the conventional default for a model whose purpose is fixed-effect inference on balanced-ish designs, and lbfgs avoids the convergence fragility of the default optimizer on small per-construct samples. Failures are caught per-construct and reported without halting the batch, so one pathological construct cannot silence the other twelve.

Sources: [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L894-L932), [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L1099-L1132)

> [!TIP]
> The random-intercept-only specification means all within-replicate correlation is assumed equal across doses and conditions. If you suspect replicate-specific slopes (e.g., one transfection batch titrates differently), the upgrade path is a random-slope model — `mixedlm(..., groups="Rep")` cannot express that in statsmodels' basic interface, so you would move to `GEE` or `MixedLM` with variance components via formula tricks.

## From Fit to Annotation: The `results` Table Protocol

The tidy `results` frame — columns `Protein`, `Term`, `Estimate`, `StdErr`, `P-value` — is the single source of truth for every figure annotation. Plotting code performs a two-key lookup, `results[(results["Protein"] == pro) & (results["Term"] == "Element[T.MUT")]`, then formats the p-value in mantissa-exponent LaTeX when it drops below 10⁻³. This is the notebook's second generation of statistics: an earlier legacy path embedded a hardcoded `mut_stats` dictionary (e.g., `"HTR7_SNAPtm": (1.040, 0.0001)`) directly in the source, which survives only inside the first `make_figure` helper. The model-driven lookup is strictly preferable — numbers can never drift from the fit that produced them.

Sources: [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L197-L212), [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L40-L46), [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L920-L940)

The forest plot reuses the same table for a cross-construct comparison: for each protein's `Element[T.MUT]` row it computes a Wald 95% interval as `Estimate ± 1.96 × StdErr`, sorts constructs by effect size, and draws the interval against a zero reference line. Because the estimates are on the log10 surface scale, a unit of β is a ten-fold trafficking shift — the APP construct's large positive β in `mut_stats` is exactly the kind of effect this panel is designed to rank.

Sources: [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L963-L1008)

## The cAMP Emax/EC50 Layer

The final cell renders the functional readout, and its architecture differs fundamentally from everything above it: **no model is fitted in this notebook**. The Emax and EC50 statistics arrive as literal constants — `emax_mean = [99.8, 75.3]` with CIs `[4.6, 4.8]` and `p_emax = 0.0003`; `ec50_mean = [2.69, 2.79]` nM with CIs `[0.94, 1.26]` and `p_ec50 = 0.95` — for the two groups labeled `Red` and `Black`, which inherit the WT/MUT color coding (`#AF3437` red, `#BDBEC0` gray) used throughout the notebook. The cell's job is purely presentational: twin bar charts with 95% CI whiskers and a `format_pvalue` helper that switches to scientific-notation LaTeX below 0.01.

| cAMP parameter | WT ("Red") | Proline mutant ("Black") | P value | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Emax (% max cAMP) | 99.8 ± 4.6 | 75.3 ± 4.8 | 3 × 10⁻⁴ | Mutant loses ~25% of maximal signaling |
| EC50 (nM) | 2.69 ± 0.94 | 2.79 ± 1.26 | 0.95 | Agonist potency unchanged |

The biological synthesis is in the contrast between the two rows: a significant Emax reduction with an unchanged EC50 is the signature of a *signaling-capacity* defect (fewer competent receptors at the surface) rather than a *binding/potency* defect — which is coherent with the surface-expression phenotype the LMMs quantify. The upstream nonlinear dose-response fits that produced these numbers live outside the repository, so this cell is a visualization contract, not an inference engine.

Sources: [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L1440-L1515)

> [!TIP]
> Re-running this notebook reproduces the Emax/EC50 figure exactly as published, but will **never** re-estimate those values — they are frozen constants. If the upstream cAMP fit changes, you must hand-edit `emax_mean`, `emax_ci`, `ec50_mean`, `ec50_ci`, and both p-values; there is no data dependency to warn you. Treat this cell as an import boundary and consider loading it from a CSV in any reusable version.

## Visualization Grammar and Output Artifacts

Every expression figure follows one shared grammar: `sns.pointplot` with `errorbar="se"` for the mean ± SEM trend, `native_scale=True` so log-spaced DNA doses sit at their true positions, and the fixed WT/MUT palette `['#AF3437', '#BDBEC0']` with `hue_order=['WT', 'MUT']`. The earlier generic helper adds replicate trajectory lines via `units="Trajectory"` with `estimator=None` — the `Trajectory = Element + "_Rep" + Rep` key created at transform time — so individual replicate curves stay visible beneath the summary points. The final total-expression figure switches to grouped bars with per-dose two-sided Student's t-tests drawn as significance brackets, a deliberately coarser summary view.

Sources: [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L70-L118), [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L63-L69), [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L1369-L1390)

All figures save as SVG at 900 dpi under a local reviewer-response directory, one file per analytical question:

| Artifact | Content |
|---|---|
| `total_vs_surface/{pro}.svg` | Three-panel Total/Surface/Trafficking per significant construct |
| `total_vs_surface/all_proteins.svg` | 3×3 grid, significant constructs, β/P annotations from `results` |
| `total_vs_surface/other_proteins.svg` | Grid for the remaining constructs |
| `total_vs_surface/all_beta_CI.svg` | Forest plot of `Element[T.MUT]` effects |
| `total_vs_surface/total_expression_only.svg`, `total_expression_barplot.svg` | Total-expression-only dose curves and bar+t-test summary |
| `HTR7_stats_emax_ec50.svg` | cAMP Emax/EC50 bar charts |

Sources: [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L240-L245), [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L1262-L1267), [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L1511-L1515)

## Adapting the Notebook: Known Friction Points

Three adaptation hazards are visible in the source. The data path is split across eras: the first loading block uses an absolute macOS path while the model block uses a bare relative filename (`file = "20270728_mdSAM_Constructs.xlsx"`), so a fresh clone requires normalizing both to one location. The file ends with a stray cell containing `plt.)()` — a syntax error that will break `nbconvert`/`jupyter execute` runs until deleted. And the metric is hardcoded as `"Geometric Mean"`; if the workbook's column naming changes, both the read and the groupby rename (`rename(columns={metric: "Surface"})`) must move together.

| Change | Where | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| New input location | Two `file =` assignments (absolute path L33, relative L830) | Silent `FileNotFoundError` in the later block only |
| Unadjusted surface model | Uncomment cell at L713–811 | Overwrites `df`/`results` from the adjusted run |
| Re-fit cAMP parameters | Not possible in-repo — constants at L1448–1455 | Stale functional claims if upstream fit changes |
| Batch execution | Delete trailing `plt.)()` cell | `nbconvert` hard-fails on syntax error |

Sources: [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L26-L49), [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L822-L831), [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L1444-L1455), [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L1524-L1526)

## Where This Connects

The LMM pattern here — log-transform first, dose as continuous covariate, replicate as random intercept — is the continuous-dose sibling of the count-based modeling in [TIRF Puncta Poisson GLM](17-tirf-puncta-poisson-glm), and the Total/Surface measurements it consumes are produced by the pipeline documented in [Flow Cytometry Surface Gating](18-flow-cytometry-surface-gating). The functional Emax/EC50 result is one pillar of the [HTR7 End-to-End Case Study](21-htr7-end-to-end-case-study), whose transcriptomic consequences continue in [RNA-seq Differential Expression and GSEA](22-rna-seq-differential-expression-and-gsea); for how this notebook maps to paper figures, see [Figure-to-Notebook Reproducibility Map](9-figure-to-notebook-reproducibility-map).


# HTR7 End-to-End Case Study



This page traces how a single predicted mdSAM — the amyloid-like motif in the serotonin 5-HT7 receptor (HTR7) — was taken from computational prediction through in-vitro peptide assays, cellular clustering measurements, nanoscale dSTORM imaging, signalling readouts, and finally transcriptomics. It is the repository's most complete worked example of the "motif → mechanism → consequence" logic, spanning notebooks 11–14 (upstream assays), 16–19 (the core case-study chain), and the shared figure map. Everything here is documented from the notebooks themselves; notebooks ship with outputs cleared, so all cell references are 0-based indices you can run to regenerate.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L21-L38), [README.md](README.md#L138-L166)

## Why HTR7: One Motif, Five Orthogonal Assays

An mdSAM is a short (7–9 residue) peptide motif in a disordered, solvent-exposed region of a transmembrane protein, predicted to self-assemble via beta-strand-mediated amyloid-like interactions. HTR7 carries such a motif, and the key experimental perturbation is a single-residue **proline substitution, V451P**, which breaks the beta-strand geometry that the assembly model requires. Because proline disrupts the motif without grossly altering the protein, every downstream difference between WT and V451P becomes attributable to the motif's self-assembly — provided expression and trafficking are controlled for, which is exactly what notebooks 14 and 17 quantify.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L21-L31), [README.md](README.md#L124-L128)

The evidence chain is deliberately layered: each stage tests the same hypothesis at a different physical scale, and each has a dedicated notebook with its own statistical model.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Prediction: WALTZ-DB RF classifier<br/>+ AlphaFold disorder filter"] --> B["HTR7 mdSAM identified<br/>perturbation: V451P"]
    B --> C["Peptide self-assembly<br/>ThT + Amytracker<br/>nb 11, 12"]
    C --> D["Cell-surface puncta<br/>TIRF Poisson GLM + flow cytometry<br/>nb 13, 14"]
    D --> E["Nanoscale organisation<br/>dSTORM Voronoi/HDBSCAN<br/>nb 16"]
    E --> F["Signalling<br/>cAMP Emax / EC50<br/>nb 17"]
    F --> G["Transcription<br/>RNA-seq PCA, volcano, GSEA<br/>nb 18, 19"]
```

The assay-to-notebook mapping below is the navigation table for the rest of this page; panel letters refer to the manuscript figures that the notebooks regenerate.

| Stage | Assay | Notebook | Paper panels | Key statistic |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Peptide | ThT spectra, GPCR peptides | `11_tht_gpcr_peptides_proline_mutants.ipynb` | Fig 4C / 5B | WT vs V451P fluorescence |
| Peptide | Amytracker 520 | `12_amytracker_peptides.ipynb` | Fig 4C | WT vs proline mutants |
| Cells | TIRF puncta density | `13_tirf_puncta_poisson_glm.ipynb` | Fig 4C-D, 5E | Poisson GLM rate ratio |
| Cells | Total vs surface expression | `14_flow_cytometry_total_vs_surface.ipynb` | S6A | percentile gating vs mock |
| Nanoscale | dSTORM clusters | `16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb` | Fig 5F-G | Voronoi/HDBSCAN + bootstrap skewness |
| Signalling | cAMP dose-response | `17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb` | Fig 6D, S6A | Emax/EC50 + mixed model |
| Transcriptome | PCA + volcano | `18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb` | Fig 6E | padj/log2FC thresholds |
| Transcriptome | GSEA | `19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb` | supports Fig 6E | KEGG prerank NES/FDR |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L114-L133), [README.md](README.md#L138-L166), [README.md](README.md#L215-L228)

## Stage 1 — Peptide-Level Self-Assembly (Notebooks 11–12)

The case study begins at the peptide level. Notebook 11 measures Thioflavin-T fluorescence of GPCR mdSAM peptides (HTR7, CCR4, DRD1) alongside their proline mutants, including HTR7 V451P, and produces the ThT spectra shown in Fig 4C/5B (cells 16–17, spectra figure at cell 32). Notebook 12 repeats the logic with Amytracker 520 at 100 µM peptide, providing a dye-independent confirmation that the wild-type motif assembles and the proline mutant does not.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L122-L128), [README.md](README.md#L209-L213)

## Stage 2 — Cell-Level Puncta and the Expression Confound (Notebooks 13–14)

Notebook 13 fits a **Poisson generalised linear model** to CellProfiler puncta tables and reports puncta-per-cell-area rate ratios (WT/mutant) for full-length APP and HTR7 in HEK and U2OS cells — HTR7 WT vs V451P TIRF puncta are Fig 5E (cell 25). Notebook 14 then runs flow cytometry on FCS files, computing total and surface SNAP signal for WT vs mutant constructs across DNA amounts with percentile gating against mock cells; these plots (cells 45, 98) become the S6A expression control that later stages lean on. The logic is important: a clustering phenotype is only interpretable if the mutant is expressed at comparable levels and reaches the surface at comparable rates.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L130-L134), [README.md](README.md#L215-L222)

## Stage 3 — Nanoscale Organisation: dSTORM Cluster Analysis (Notebook 16)

Notebook 16 is the largest HTR7-specific analysis (~480 cells) and the technical centrepiece of Fig 5. It starts from **ThunderSTORM localisation tables** exported as CSVs under `csv/v2/`, where the code comments `5000 pixes = 1micron` record the pixel-to-nanometre convention. The entry-point function `ThnderSTORM2df` applies two quality filters — localisation `uncertainty [nm] < 20` and `frame >= 200` (discarding the pre-stabilisation part of each movie) — then crops a `squre_size=4000` nm (4 µm) rectangle from the field and tags every localisation with `parent`/`element`/`cell`/`rectangle`/`replicate` metadata. HTR7 cells are loaded as WT and MUT (V451P) across multiple cells and replicates (e.g., `HTR7Mut_B_2_8`, `HTR7Mut_B_2_10` at nine and six ROI coordinates respectively).

Sources: [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L114-L150), [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L11500-L11511)

The clustering engine combines Voronoi tessellation with density-based clustering. `voro2cluster`/`voro2cluster_v4` tile each ROI with a Voronoi diagram (`scipy.spatial.Voronoi`), while `voronoi_volumes` computes each cell's area via `ConvexHull`, separating dense from sparse regions before cluster calls. Density-independent geometric descriptors come from helpers such as `df2clustersize` (cluster diameter = max pairwise distance via `pdist`) and `cluster_fraction`. The environment imports `HDBSCAN`, `OPTICS`, `DBSCAN`, `ripleyk` (Ripley's K), and `rdfpy` (radial distribution functions), so alternative cluster-callers and point-process statistics are all in scope.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["ThunderSTORM CSV<br/>csv/v2/*.csv"] --> B["Filter<br/>uncertainty &lt; 20 nm<br/>frame ≥ 200"]
    B --> C["Crop ROI<br/>4 × 4 µm rectangle"]
    C --> D["Voronoi tessellation<br/>+ ConvexHull cell areas"]
    D --> E["Density-based clustering<br/>HDBSCAN"]
    E --> F["Cluster size/density<br/>stratified summary"]
    F --> G["WT vs V451P tests<br/>t-test, Mann-Whitney,<br/>bootstrap skewness"]
```

Sources: [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L73-L112), [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L240-L259)

The figure-critical cells sit at the end of the notebook: Fig 5F (localisation map with Voronoi/cluster overlay) at cells 409–410, and Fig 5G (cluster stoichiometry by local density, bootstrap skewness) at cells 440–453. The analysis stratifies clusters by local density into bins `0-70` and `71-150`, then compares `cluster_sizes_full_vals_nm_mean` between WT (red `#C03830`) and MUT (grey `#B4B5B4`) with violin/strip plots; non-parametric confirmation uses `mannwhitneyu` alongside `stats.ttest_ind`.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L138-L152), [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L11554-L11583), [16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb](notebooks/16_dstorm_htr7_cluster_analysis.ipynb#L11648-L11665)

> [!TIP]
> The density stratification (`densitiy` bins 0-70 vs 71-150) exists because naive cluster-size comparisons confound cluster geometry with localisation density: dense regions mechanically produce larger apparent clusters. Comparing WT vs V451P within each density stratum isolates the motif effect from the sampling effect — replicate this pattern whenever you compare point-cloud clusters across conditions.

## Stage 4 — Signalling Readout: cAMP Dose-Response and Expression Controls (Notebook 17)

Notebook 17 closes the mechanistic loop: if V451P disrupts HTR7 clustering, does signalling change? Its header markdown states the design explicitly — total (left) and surface (right) plots on **log10-transformed** values (not log axes), statistics on the same transformed scale, replicate trajectories grouped by `Element + Rep`, mean ± SEM, SVG output. Input is `20270728_mdSAM_Constructs.xlsx` (sheets `Surface`/`Total`, metric `Geometric Mean`), and the derived quantity `logTrafficking = logSurface − logTotal` gives a per-construct trafficking index. Fig 6D (cell 18) summarises HTR7 cAMP Emax and EC50 between WT and V451P; S6A (cells 13, 17) holds the total-expression bar plots.

Sources: [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L4-L17), [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L26-L69), [README.md](README.md#L154-L166)

Statistical anchoring comes from a **linear mixed model** per construct: `smf.mixedlm("logSurface ~ Element * logDNA", groups=Rep)`, fit by REML with lbfgs, regressing surface expression on condition (WT/MUT) and DNA amount (a proxy for expression level) with replicate as random effect. The hard-coded `mut_stats` dictionary records the resulting β and p-values and annotates them onto the figures:

| Construct | β (Element=MUT effect) | p-value | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| HTR7 | −0.197 | 0.338 | No surface-expression deficit in full-length V451P |
| HTR7_SNAPtm | 1.040 | 0.0001 | Motif-swap construct shows strong surface effect |
| APP | 1.959 | 0.0001 | Positive control |
| A4 | 1.710 | 0.001 | Positive control |
| KCNE4_SNAPtm | 0.962 | 0.002 | Second motif-swap control |

Sources: [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L40-L46), [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L197-L239), [17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb](notebooks/17_htr7_camp_emax_ec50_and_expression_plots.ipynb#L823-L839)

> [!TIP]
> Notice that full-length HTR7 shows **no** significant surface effect (β = −0.197, p = 0.338) while the SNAPtm motif-swap constructs do. This is the analytical payoff of the design: any WT-vs-V451P differences in dSTORM clustering or cAMP signalling cannot be dismissed as a trafficking artefact, because surface delivery is statistically indistinguishable between full-length WT and V451P.

## Stage 5 — Transcriptional Consequences: RNA-seq (Notebooks 18–19)

The transcriptome stage asks whether a clustering/signalling defect propagates to gene expression. Notebook 18 is the figure notebook: it reads precomputed DESeq2 tables from `GPCR_ThT/RNAseq/ywang34_data/` and plots PCA (`PCA_data.tsv`, samples labelled `$WT$` rows 0–3, `$V451P$` rows 3–6, `$pCDNA$` empty-vector rows 6+) and a volcano for `deseq2_HTR7_MUT_vs_HTR7_WT.tsv` — these are Fig 6E (cells 3 and 8). Volcano thresholds are `padj_log > 2` (i.e., FDR < 0.01) combined with `|log2FC| > 0.4` for the MUT-vs-WT contrast, and a more permissive `|log2FC| > 1` for each construct vs the HEK pCDNA empty-vector control; `adjustText` de-overlaps gene labels and a `venn2` diagram contrasts the upregulated sets of V451P and WT versus pCDNA.

Sources: [18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb](notebooks/18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb#L10-L31), [18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb](notebooks/18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb#L40-L70), [18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb](notebooks/18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb#L120-L149), [18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb](notebooks/18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb#L169-L248)

Notebook 19 re-derives the differential expression from raw counts so the whole transcriptome stage is reproducible end-to-end. It reads the RSEM gene-count matrix (`BABU-301366-STRANDED_RSEM_gene_count...txt`), selects the nine samples (3× HTR7 WT basal, 3× HTR7 MUT basal, 3× HEK pCDNA), filters genes with total counts ≤ 10, and runs **pyDESeq2** with `DeseqDataSet(..., design_factors="Condition")` and `DeseqStats(contrast=('Condition','MUT','WT'))`. Genes with `baseMean >= 10` are ranked by the Wald statistic and fed to **gseapy prerank** GSEA against `KEGG_2021_Human` (seed=4, 1000 permutations); enriched sets are filtered at `FDR q-val < 0.2` with `|NES| > 1.5`, and the MAPK signalling pathway is inspected explicitly — consistent with HTR7 being a Gs-coupled receptor.

| Parameter | Value | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Contrast | MUT vs WT (basal) | `DeseqStats` call |
| Gene filter | sum > 10 counts; baseMean ≥ 10 | pre-DESeq2 / pre-ranking |
| Gene sets | KEGG_2021_Human | `gp.prerank` |
| Permutations / seed | 1000 / 4 | `gp.prerank` |
| Report thresholds | FDR q < 0.2, \|NES\| > 1.5 | results filtering |

Sources: [19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb](notebooks/19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb#L46-L92), [19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb](notebooks/19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb#L124-L155), [19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb](notebooks/19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb#L200-L224)

## Reproducing the Case Study

Run each notebook with `notebooks/` as the working directory; the shared input tables live in `files/` (`dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl`, `hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl`, and — for notebooks 18–19 — `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl`), as documented in `files/README.md`. Note that some stages depend on raw data not redistributed in this repository (ThunderSTORM CSVs under `csv/v2/`, the RNA-seq count matrix, and the cAMP Excel workbook referenced by absolute local paths), and notebook 18 additionally loads local pickles for an auxiliary phosphorylation-site analysis. The panel-to-cell mapping is fully specified in the README's figure tables, and notebooks call the motifs `dSAM` in filenames and variables — same concept as mdSAM.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L244-L248), [18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb](notebooks/18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb#L273-L301), [README.md](README.md#L119-L122)

## Where to Go Next

To go deeper on any single stage, follow the catalog: the dSTORM methods are elaborated in [dSTORM Cluster Analysis](19-dstorm-cluster-analysis), the mixed-model machinery in [cAMP Dose-Response Mixed Models](20-camp-dose-response-mixed-models), and the RNA-seq workflow in [RNA-seq Differential Expression and GSEA](22-rna-seq-differential-expression-and-gsea). The upstream assays that motivate this case study are covered in [Thioflavin-T and Amytracker Screens](16-thioflavin-t-and-amytracker-screens), [TIRF Puncta Poisson GLM](17-tirf-puncta-poisson-glm), and [Flow Cytometry Surface Gating](18-flow-cytometry-surface-gating). For the discovery logic that nominated HTR7's motif in the first place, start at [mdSAM Concept and Discovery Rationale](4-mdsam-concept-and-discovery-rationale), and for the complete panel-to-notebook index see [Figure-to-Notebook Reproducibility Map](9-figure-to-notebook-reproducibility-map).

# RNA-seq Differential Expression and GSEA



This page documents the transcriptional readout of the HTR7 case study: how the repository converts a 9-sample RNA-seq experiment into the Figure 6E panels and their supporting gene-set enrichment analysis. Two notebooks implement the layer, and they are deliberately different in kind. `18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb` is a publication-figure playback notebook that consumes precomputed DESeq2 result tables and renders the final panels (PCA, cell index 3; V451P-vs-WT volcano, cell 8). `19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb` is the full reanalysis engine: it re-fits the negative-binomial model from raw RSEM counts with **pyDESeq2**, then runs **GSEA pre-ranking** with **gseapy** over the KEGG 2021 human gene-set library, producing enrichment-score curves, pathway-similarity clustermaps, and pathway-annotated volcano plots. Together they form a two-tier architecture: a frozen, figure-exact layer on top of a re-runnable, statistically explicit layer.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L157-L163), [18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb](notebooks/18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb#L40-L80), [19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb](notebooks/19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb#L33-L36)

## Where This Layer Sits in the Pipeline

The RNA-seq notebooks are terminal nodes of the experimental-assay track. Everything upstream (classifier, motif discovery, ThT screens, dSTORM imaging) converges on HTR7; this layer measures what the V451P motif-disrupting mutation does to the transcriptome, complementing the cAMP dose-response and imaging measurements documented in [cAMP Dose-Response Mixed Models](20-camp-dose-response-mixed-models) and [dSTORM Cluster Analysis](19-dstorm-cluster-analysis). The notebooks load the shared pickled tables from `files/` (`hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl`, `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl`, `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl`) for identifier cross-referencing, but the transcriptional data itself lives in a project-local `GPCR_ThT/RNAseq/` directory with collaborator-provided inputs (`ywang34_data/` DESeq2 tables in notebook 18, a raw RSEM gene-count matrix in notebook 19).

Sources: [18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb](notebooks/18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb#L27-L30), [19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb](notebooks/19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb#L28-L36), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L1-L7)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph External inputs
        A[RSEM gene counts<br/>BABU-301366 STRANDED] --> B
        B[9 RNA-seq samples<br/>WT / V451P / pCDNA]
    end
    subgraph Notebook 19 — reanalysis engine
        C[pyDESeq2 DeseqDataSet<br/>design_factors = Condition]
        D[DeseqStats<br/>4 contrasts]
        E[Wald-stat ranking]
        F[gseapy prerank<br/>KEGG_2021_Human]
    end
    subgraph Notebook 18 — figure playback
        G[ywang34_data DESeq2 TSVs<br/>precomputed]
        H[PCA + volcano SVGs]
    end
    B --> C --> D --> E --> F
    B --> G --> H
    F --> I[ES curves, Jaccard<br/>clustermaps, annotated volcanoes]
```

## Experimental Design and Data Layer

The experiment is a 3 × 3 design: three conditions in triplicate, encoded in sample names with sequential numeric prefixes. Notebook 19 selects the nine columns explicitly — `2613875/76/77` are HTR7-WT basal replicates, `2613878/79/80` are HTR7-MUT (V451P) basal replicates, and `2613881/82/83` are HEK cells transfected with the empty pCDNA vector — then builds a `Sample`/`Condition` metadata frame with conditions labeled `WT`, `MUT`, `C` ([19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb](notebooks/19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb#L77-L92)). Three preprocessing rules precede modeling: counts are cast to `int64` (the pyDESeq2 integer requirement), genes with a total count sum ≤ 10 across all samples are dropped, and the matrix is transposed to the samples × genes orientation pyDESeq2 expects. Notebook 18 takes the opposite ingestion philosophy: it never touches raw counts, instead reading collaborator-precomputed DESeq2 tables (`deseq2_HTR7_MUT_vs_HTR7_WT.tsv`, `deseq2_HTR7_WT_vs_HEK_pCDNA.tsv`, `deseq2_HTR7_MUT_vs_HEK_pCDNA.tsv`) and precomputed PCA coordinates from `PCA_data.tsv`, where the first three rows are WT, the next three V451P, the rest pCDNA.

The key architectural distinction: notebook 18 guarantees bit-identical figure reproduction; notebook 19 guarantees statistical reproducibility and adds capabilities the precomputed tables lack (GSEA, arbitrary contrast re-fitting, pathway overlays). Both paths must agree on gene identity, so notebook 19 maintains a `geneID → geneSymbol` dictionary built from the count file itself and maps Ensembl IDs to symbols after every `DeseqStats` call.

Sources: [19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb](notebooks/19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb#L46-L92), [18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb](notebooks/18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb#L40-L53), [18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb](notebooks/18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb#L169-L172)

| Ingestion mode | Notebook | Input artifact | Preprocessing on load | Figure fidelity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frozen DESeq2 tables | 18 | `ywang34_data/*.tsv`, `PCA_data.tsv` | `padj_log = −log10(padj)` only | Exact panel playback (Fig 6E) |
| Raw RSEM counts | 19 | `BABU-301366-STRANDED_RSEM_gene_count.*.txt` | int64 cast, sum > 10 filter, transpose, metadata frame | Re-runnable; supports Fig 6E |

Sources: [18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb](notebooks/18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb#L100-L110), [19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb](notebooks/19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb#L77-L102)

## Notebook 18: Publication-Figure Playback (Fig 6E)

Notebook 18 contains 22 cells, of which cells 0–15 are the figure pipeline and cells 16–20 are trailing exploratory work. The PCA panel (cell 3) plots the precomputed coordinates with axis labels hard-coding the explained variance — PC1 at 60.7% and PC2 at 10.5% — and the fixed palette `['#C03830', '#B4B5B4', '#000080']` (red = WT, gray = V451P, navy = pCDNA), exporting `PCA_ywang34.svg` ([18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb](notebooks/18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb#L63-L70)). The volcano (cell 8) is the statistical centerpiece: it colors upregulated genes teal (`#18827E`) and downregulated genes magenta (`#B34F91`), draws dashed decision boundaries at log2FC = ±0.4 and −log10(FDR) = 2, and resolves overlapping labels with `adjustText`, exporting `volcano_ywang34.svg` ([18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb](notebooks/18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb#L120-L149)).

> [!TIP]
> Notebook 18 uses two different significance bands, and conflating them is the most common misreading of this layer. The V451P-vs-WT contrast — the biological comparison — uses the stricter band −log10(padj) > 2 (i.e., FDR < 0.01) with |log2FC| > 0.4 (cells 8–9), while the against-vector contrasts and the exploratory filter in cell 7 use −log10(padj) > 1.3 (FDR < 0.05). The against-vector volcanoes relax the fold-change boundary to |log2FC| > 1 because expression of the receptor itself generates large, expected shifts relative to pCDNA.

After the main volcano, cells 12–14 produce the two against-vector volcanoes and a `matplotlib_venn` overlap of the upregulated gene sets from V451P-vs-pCDNA and WT-vs-pCDNA, with the exact intersection printed in cell 15; cell 11 spot-checks the immediate-early gene JUNB across both contrasts as a sanity probe. Cells 16–20 are an unrelated side analysis intersecting predicted phosphorylation-site PTMs (iPTM score ≥ 3) with mdSAM-containing accessions — worth knowing for archaeology, but not part of any paper panel.

Sources: [18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb](notebooks/18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb#L120-L149), [18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb](notebooks/18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb#L186-L248), [18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb](notebooks/18_htr7_rnaseq_pca_volcano.ipynb#L266-L311), [README.md](README.md#L162-L163)

## Notebook 19: The End-to-End Reanalysis Engine

Notebook 19 executes a five-stage pipeline: fit → contrast → rank → enrich → visualize. The fit stage constructs a `DeseqDataSet` with `design_factors="Condition"` over the 9-sample count matrix and runs the dispersions/size-factor estimation with `dds.deseq2()` (cell 6). The contrast stage then calls `DeseqStats` four times against the same fitted object — `MUT` vs `WT` (cell 8), `WT` vs `C` (cell 44), `MUT` vs `C` (cell 49), and `WT` vs `MUT` (cell 51) — each with `n_cpus=8`, filtering to `baseMean >= 10` before any downstream use. The ranking stage converts the MUT-vs-WT result into a GSEA input: genes sorted by descending Wald statistic, deduplicated on both symbol and statistic to guarantee a strictly ordered rank vector. The enrichment stage runs `gp.prerank` with `gene_sets='KEGG_2021_Human'`, `seed=4`, and `permutation_num=1000`, extracting `res2d` and augmenting it with an `abs_NES` column.

> [!TIP]
> Cells 12 and 15 intentionally run the identical `gp.prerank` call twice with the same `seed=4`. This is a determinism audit, not dead code: with gene permutation and a fixed seed, both invocations must return identical NES/FDR columns, letting the author verify that pathway calls are not an artifact of sampling noise before the results were exported and plotted. Preserve the seed if you re-run; changing it shifts FDR q-values near the significance boundary.

Sources: [19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb](notebooks/19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb#L124-L155), [19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb](notebooks/19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb#L200-L233), [19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb](notebooks/19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb#L712-L850)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Raw RSEM counts<br/>9 samples] --> B[int64 cast +<br/>gene sum > 10 filter]
    B --> C[DeseqDataSet<br/>design_factors=Condition]
    C --> D[dds.deseq2<br/>NB fit]
    D --> E1[DeseqStats MUT vs WT] --> F[Wald-stat ranking<br/>dedup Symbol + stat]
    D --> E2[DeseqStats WT vs C] --> G1[Volcano + MAPK overlay]
    D --> E3[DeseqStats MUT vs C] --> G2[Volcano + neurodegeneration overlay]
    D --> E4[DeseqStats WT vs MUT] --> G3[Volcano WT_vs_MUT_vp.svg]
    F --> H[gp.prerank KEGG_2021_Human<br/>seed=4, 1000 permutations]
    H --> I[res2d + abs_NES]
    I --> J1[FDR < 0.15 → GESA_significant.csv]
    I --> J2[Jaccard clustermaps<br/>heat_dowm.svg / heat_up.svg]
    I --> J3[Custom ES figure<br/>GESA_TEMP.svg]
```

## Pathway-Level Results and Their Visual Grammar

The enrichment table is filtered at three nested stringency levels: `FDR q-val < 0.15` rows are exported to `GSEA_significant.csv` as the canonical result set (cell 18); an inspection band of `FDR < 0.2 & abs_NES > 1.5` (cell 14) and subsequent `abs_NES > 1.6/1.7` cuts (cells 37, 59) are used for display. NES sign follows the ranking direction: because the ranking is MUT-vs-WT, negative NES marks pathways suppressed in the V451P mutant. The two signature suppressed pathways — `MAPK signaling pathway` and `Pathways of neurodegeneration` — anchor the downstream graphics ([19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb](notebooks/19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb#L213-L223)).

The visualization layer has three distinct grammar rules. First, redundancy among enriched pathways is quantified by **Jaccard similarity of lead genes**: for all pairs of pathways with NES < −1.7 (down) and NES > 1.7 (up), cell 21 defines the similarity function and cells 24–25 render `sns.clustermap` matrices with a shared SymLogNorm (linthresh 0.15) and the teal–gray–magenta diverging colormap, exporting `figures/heat_dowm.svg` and `figures/heat_up.svg`. Second, the enrichment-score curve is hand-built rather than delegated to `gseaplot`: cell 36 extracts the running enrichment score (`RES`) and hit positions from `pre_res.results`, and cell 39 composes a 12×12 `GridSpec` figure layering the ES curves for both signature pathways, a twinned axis with the ranked-metric bar spectrum, and two thin hit-index strips — annotated with NES values read from `out_df.loc[18]` and `out_df.loc[12]` — exporting `GESA_TEMP.svg`. Third, contrast volcanoes are annotated by *pathway membership* rather than by raw significance: cells 47, 50, and 52 label only genes that pass a −log10(FDR) cutoff and appear in a pathway's `matched_genes` list, visually tying single-gene statistics to the enrichment result.

Sources: [19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb](notebooks/19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb#L268-L310), [19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb](notebooks/19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb#L352-L419), [19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb](notebooks/19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb#L562-L650), [19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb](notebooks/19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb#L758-L878)

A final cell worth noting is the mdSAM tie-in: cell 57 executes `AF2.loc[9137].AAseq.find('VSVWVLQS')`, locating the HTR7 mdSAM motif inside the receptor sequence from the shared AlphaFold table — the programmatic reminder that the V451P mutation under test is the proline substitution inside this motif, connecting the transcriptome data back to the motif-discovery layer described in [mdSAM Concept and Discovery Rationale](4-mdsam-concept-and-discovery-rationale).

Sources: [19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb](notebooks/19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb#L927-L931), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L5-L7)

## Reproducibility Contract

For an advanced developer re-running this layer, the parameters below constitute the full statistical contract. Run both notebooks with `notebooks/` as the working directory, since all relative paths assume `../files/` for shared tables and `GPCR_ThT/RNAseq/` for transcriptional data — a requirement stated for all notebooks in the repository manifest. The dependency set is larger than most notebooks in the repo because it spans two ecosystems: the DESeq2 re-implementation stack (`pydeseq2`, `scanpy`) and the enrichment stack (`gseapy`, plus `sanbomics` for plot utilities).

Sources: [19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb](notebooks/19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb#L33-L36), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L3-L4)

| Parameter | Value | Location (notebook 19) | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| Design formula | `design_factors="Condition"` | cell 6 | Single-factor 3-level design |
| Gene filter (pre-fit) | row sum > 10 | cell 3 | Removes ultra-low-count genes |
| Gene filter (post-stats) | `baseMean >= 10` | cells 8, 44, 49, 51 | Independent-filtering analogue |
| GSEA gene sets | `KEGG_2021_Human` | cells 12, 15 | Pathway library |
| Permutations | `permutation_num=1000` | cells 12, 15 | Gene-set permutation null |
| Random seed | `seed=4` | cells 12, 15 | Deterministic FDR |
| Ranking metric | Wald `stat`, descending | cell 8 | GSEA pre-ranked input |
| FDR export cutoff | `FDR q-val < 0.15` | cell 18 | Canonical result set |
| Clustermap NES bands | \|NES\| > 1.7 (down/up) | cells 24, 25 | Redundancy display set |
| Volcano FDR highlight | −log10(FDR) > 1.3 (vs C); > 0 (WT vs MUT) | cells 47, 52 | Pathway-member labeling |

Sources: [19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb](notebooks/19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb#L124-L155), [19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb](notebooks/19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb#L200-L268), [19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb](notebooks/19_htr7_rnaseq_gsea.ipynb#L352-L419)

| `GESA_TEMP.svg` | nb 19, cell 39 | Custom dual-pathway ES figure |
| `GPCR_ThT/RNAseq/WT_vs_MUT_vp.svg` | nb 19, cell 52 | WT vs MUT volcano with MAPK overlay |

Within the catalog, this page is best read as the third act of the HTR7 story: start with [HTR7 End-to-End Case Study](21-htr7-end-to-end-case-study) for the biological framing, then [cAMP Dose-Response Mixed Models](20-camp-dose-response-mixed-models) for the signaling-level measurement whose transcriptional consequences are quantified here. # BioGRID Interaction Enrichment



This page documents `notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb`, the interactomics integration notebook of the mdSAM repository. The notebook asks a single architectural question in three ways: **do membrane proteins that carry mdSAMs (membrane-disordered Self-Assembly Motifs) participate in protein–protein interactions in a way that distinguishes them from mdSAM-negative membrane proteins?** It answers this by analyzing the BioGRID physical interaction database through three complementary network constructions — compartment-stratified bipartite graphs, a plasma-membrane TM↔TM network, and a genome-wide TM network for self-interactions — each probed with hypergeometric and Fisher exact statistics. The paper-facing outputs are panels **S6B** (self-interaction enrichment) and **S6C** (plasma-membrane PPI partner enrichment) of Supplementary Figure S6. The notebook also contains substantial exploratory work that never reached the figures, which this page flags explicitly.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L68), [README.md](README.md#L223-L228)

## Why the Interactome Is the Right Test Bed

The mdSAM hypothesis (see [mdSAM Concept and Discovery Rationale](4-mdsam-concept-and-discovery-rationale)) predicts that amyloid-like motifs in disordered regions drive **self-association and clustering** of membrane proteins. If true, two interactomic signatures should exist: (1) mdSAM-containing proteins should self-interact in curated databases more often than expected, and (2) the *soluble partners* of mdSAM-positive plasma-membrane proteins should be a biased population — for example, enriched in signaling regulators — compared to partners of mdSAM-negative proteins. The notebook operationalizes both predictions against BioGRID release **4.4.215** (tab3 format), intersected with the shared mdSAM and topology tables from `files/`.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L68), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L7-L9)

## Pipeline Architecture

The notebook follows a strict funnel: one cleaned interaction table feeds three independently constructed networks, each with its own statistical machinery. Understanding this branching is essential before reading the cells, because all three branches share the same cleaned edge list.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["BioGRID-ALL-4.4.215.tab3.txt"] --> B["Filter: human only<br/>Organism ID 9606"]
    B --> C["Canonicalize unordered pairs<br/>via frozenset groupby"]
    C --> D["Drop '-' and multi-isoform '|' accessions"]
    D --> E1["Compartment bipartite graphs<br/>G_PM, G_ER, G_Golgi,<br/>G_Endo_Lyso, G_Other"]
    D --> E2["PM↔PM network GG<br/>GO:0005886 nodes"]
    D --> E3["All-TM network GGG"]
    F["dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl<br/>(mdSAM calls)"] --> E1
    F --> E2
    F --> E3
    G["hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl<br/>(human TM set)"] --> E1
    G --> E3
    H["HPA_frac_df.pkl<br/>(gmm_new compartments)"] --> E1
    E1 --> I["Per-partner hypergeometric<br/>+ Benjamini-Hochberg FDR"]
    E2 --> J["Edge-type counts<br/>(yes-yes / no-no / yes-no)<br/>hypergeom + Fisher"]
    E3 --> K["Self-interaction 2×2<br/>Fisher exact"]
    I --> L["Volcano plots → S6C"]
    J --> M["Edge-type odds / PMF plots"]
    K --> N["Obs vs Exp bar → S6B"]
```

Sources: [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L17-L64), [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L126-L176)

## Input Data and Preprocessing

The preprocessing cell (notebook cell 1) is the foundation everything else inherits, so its four cleaning steps deserve precise attention.

**Human-only filter and identifier hygiene.** The raw tab3 table is filtered to `Organism ID Interactor A == 9606`, SWISS-PROT accession columns are renamed to `acc1`/`acc2`, and rows where either side is `-` (no curated accession) are dropped. Because BioGRID stores directional records, the same physical pair can appear multiple times; the notebook groups rows by `frozenset` of the two accessions and keeps one representative per unordered pair while counting duplicates — a canonicalization that converts a directional database into an undirected graph edge list. Finally, accessions containing `|` (multiple isoforms collapsed into one field) are removed entirely to keep node identity unambiguous.

> [!TIP]
> The `groupby`-on-`frozenset` idiom at lines 43–50 is the load-bearing trick of the whole notebook: it deduplicates A→B and B→A records in one pass *and* preserves the interaction count in a `Duplicates` column, so downstream degree statistics operate on true physical interactions rather than database re-annotations.

Sources: [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L39-L55), [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L36-L37)

**Shared analysis tables.** The mdSAM calls come from `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl`, the transmembrane reference set from `hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl`, and the AlphaFold residue table from `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl`. From `hTMs` the notebook derives `sub_TMs` (all human TM proteins) and `non_TMs` (BioGRID accessions that are not TM proteins) — the two node classes that drive every graph construction. Note the naming convention: older notebooks, including this one, use the variable name `dSAMs` where the paper says *mdSAM*.

Sources: [files/README.md](files/README.md#L7-L9), [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L57-L63), [README.md](README.md#L21)

**Compartment labels.** Subcellular assignment reuses the hyperLOPIT Gaussian-mixture clustering from notebook 07: `HPA_frac_df.gmm_new` cluster 0 maps to plasma membrane (PM), 1 to ER, 2 to endosomes/lysosomes, 3 to Golgi, 4 to other. These five sets are materialized as Python sets and parameterize the compartment graphs.

Sources: [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L110-L116), [hyperLOPIT Organelle Enrichment](14-hyperlopit-organelle-enrichment)

## Three Interaction Networks from One Edge List

| Network | Variable(s) | Nodes | Edges retained | Statistical role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Compartment bipartite (×5) | `G_PM`, `G_ER`, `G_Golgi`, `G_Endo_Lyso`, `G_Other` | Compartment TM proteins + their soluble partners | Edges with **exactly one** endpoint in the compartment TM set | Per-partner enrichment of mdSAM+ TM neighbors |
| Plasma-membrane TM↔TM | `GG` | Plasma-membrane TMs (UniProt GO:0005886), labeled `mdSAM` yes/no | TM–TM interactions between *distinct* proteins | Edge-type assortativity (yes-yes / no-no / yes-no) |
| All-TM network | `GGG` | All human TM proteins | TM–TM interactions including self-loops | Self-interaction contingency (S6B) |

Sources: [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L126-L176), [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L1288-L1307)

**Compartment bipartite graphs.** `Graph_organelle()` is parameterized by one compartment set. It adds every node with an `mdSAM` yes/no attribute, then iterates the cleaned edge list and keeps an edge only when exactly one endpoint is a TM of the compartment — TM↔TM and soluble↔soluble pairs are both skipped, yielding a strictly bipartite graph. Hub control is applied by pruning nodes with degree ≤ `min_egde` (1) or ≥ `max_edge` (90), removing both singletons and extreme hubs that would dominate the hypergeometric denominators.

Sources: [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L126-L162), [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L172-L176)

**The PM↔PM and all-TM networks.** The plasma-membrane membrane-protein-only network `GG` is built later in the notebook from `PM_TMs` (GO:0005886 ∩ TM set), keeping only edges between distinct proteins (`acc1 != acc2`) and then removing degree-0 nodes. The all-TM network `GGG`, used for the self-interaction test, is the same construction generalized to every human TM protein. This three-graph design separates two confounded questions: *whom* mdSAM proteins talk to (bipartite analysis) versus *whether like talks to like* (TM↔TM analysis).

Sources: [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L1288-L1307)

## Statistical Machinery

Every test in the notebook answers the same primitive question with a different sampling frame, summarized below.

| Test | Scope | Null hypothesis | Implementation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per-partner hypergeometric | each soluble node in a compartment graph | The node's TM partners are a random draw from the graph's TM population | `stats.hypergeom.cdf` with direction flip |
| Benjamini–Hochberg FDR | all partner rows per compartment | — | `rankdata`-based `fdr()` helper |
| GTPase-domain enrichment | IPR005225 members among enriched PM partners | Enriched set is random w.r.t. domain membership | `stats.hypergeom.cdf` |
| Endocytosis GO enrichment | GO:0006897 genes among enriched PM partners | Same | `stats.hypergeom.cdf` |
| Edge-type tests (yes-yes / no-no / yes-no) | `GG` | Edge labels independent of mdSAM status | `stats.hypergeom.sf` + `fisher_exact` |
| Self-interaction test | `GGG` | Self-interaction independent of mdSAM status | `scipy.stats.fisher_exact`, 2×2 |

Sources: [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L200-L211), [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L262-L269)

**The per-partner test** (`G_hypergeom`) frames each soluble protein as drawing `number_winners` (= its degree among TM nodes) proteins from a population of `total_runners` TM nodes of which `number_team_A` carry mdSAMs. The p-value is computed via `hypergeom.cdf` and flipped with `p = 1 - p` when the observed mdSAM-neighbor count exceeds expectation — the manual equivalent of a survival function, giving a one-sided enrichment p-value. `G2df()` then assembles a per-compartment results table with observed edges, expected edges, `obs_exp` (observed minus expected), fold change, −log₁₀ p, and the BH-FDR columns `fdr`/`log_fdr`, retaining only partners with at least one TM edge and a resolvable gene name.

> [!TIP]
> The `obs_exp` column is a *difference*, not a ratio — volcano x-axes in this notebook plot `deg(Obs) − deg(Exp)` in raw edge counts, with significance gates at |obs_exp| ≥ 8–10 combined with FDR < 0.25 (i.e. `log_fdr > 0.602`). Reading the x-axis as fold change is the most common misinterpretation of these plots.

Sources: [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L200-L212), [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L232-L252), [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L280-L286)

**Edge-type tests in the PM network.** For `GG`, the notebook tallies edges into three classes — mdSAM+↔mdSAM+ (`yes-yes`), mdSAM−↔mdSAM− (`no-no`), and mixed — with an assertion that counts sum to the total edge count. Each class is then tested two ways: a hypergeometric test against the count of possible same-type edges in the complete graph (`n_nodes·(n_nodes−1)` frame), and one-sided Fisher exact tests on 2×2 contingency tables. A binomial-test variant (`stats.binomtest`) exists in the notebook but is commented out; the active final implementation is hypergeometric + Fisher. Odds ratios for the three classes are visualized in `Membrane_graph_BioGrid_v6.svg`.

Sources: [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L1515-L1592), [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L1395-L1433), [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L1618-L1642)

## Paper Outputs: Panels S6B and S6C

**S6B — self-interaction enrichment.** The final consolidated contingency table hardcodes the interaction counts and tests them with a two-sided Fisher exact test:

| | Self-interactor | Not self-interactor | Row totals |
|---|---|---|---|
| mdSAM+ | 111 | 658 − 111 = 547 | 658 |
| mdSAM− | 348 | 2,642 − 348 = 2,294 | 2,642 |

The observed self-interaction proportions are 111/658 ≈ 16.9% versus 348/2,642 ≈ 13.2%. The companion figure cell renders observed versus *expected* self-interaction counts (from `scipy.stats.contingency.expected_freq`) as a paired bar plot with the expected bar hatched, saved as `self_association_BioGrid_v3.svg`.
