Per the repository's figure map, this panel is drawn at notebook cells 171–172 (0-based), with the mdSAM+ (n=658) and mdSAM− (n=2,642) node counts printed in the panel description. Exact p-values are not recoverable from the repository because notebook outputs are cleared by design.

Sources: [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L2975-L2984), [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L2837-L2904), [README.md](README.md#L223-L224)

**S6C — plasma-membrane partner enrichment.** The primary S6C visualization is a volcano plot over the `G_plot_PM` table: x = `obs_exp` (excess mdSAM+ partners), y = −log₁₀(p) or −log₁₀(FDR), points colored by total TM-edge count via a gray→blue→red colormap. Two annotated reference populations are overlaid: proteins carrying the InterPro **small GTP-binding domain (IPR005225)** as white-outlined circles, and **endocytosis genes (GO:0006897)** in amber — hence the `Rho_enrich_PM_*.svg` script names. The enrichment of each population among significant partners is quantified with dedicated hypergeometric tests (the GTPase-domain test runs against partners with `obs_exp > 0`; the endocytosis test against `obs_exp > 2` and `log_fdr > 0.6`). Panel cells 78, 81, 84, and 86 correspond to the successive plot iterations (`Rho_enrich_PM_v6.svg` through `v9.svg` and the mosaic layout in `v8`). The same volcano machinery is re-run for the PM↔TM network's membrane-protein nodes (`GG_plot`, highlighting UniProt keywords KW-0813 *Transport* and KW-0418 *tyrosine-protein kinase*) and analogously computed for ER, Golgi, endo-lysosomal, and "other" compartments, though those are not mapped to paper panels.

Sources: [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L415-L450), [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L358-L386), [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L1252-L1259), [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L2131-L2215), [README.md](README.md#L225-L228)

## Beyond the Panels: Exploratory Analyses

The README explicitly notes that this notebook "contains further interaction analyses that are not part of the paper figures." When reading or reusing the notebook, the following cells belong to that exploratory layer and should not be mistaken for figure sources:

- **Degree comparisons** — mdSAM+ vs mdSAM− node degree in `GG`/`G_PM_All`, tested with Welch's t-test and a two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, visualized as box+swarm and ECDF plots (`Dgree_Sol-MP.svg`).
- **Keyword sweep** — a loop running Fisher exact per UniProt keyword over the enriched/non-enriched partition of PM partners, producing an enrichment-vs-FDR scatter (mirroring the approach of [UniProt Keyword Enrichment](13-uniprot-keyword-enrichment)).
- **External endocytosis dataset** — loads a Nature supplementary Excel (4,609 scored genes, `41586_2010_BFnature08779`), maps gene IDs to accessions, and re-tests overlap among high-confidence partners.
- **InterPro domain scan** — reads locally cached InterPro JSON results to flag domain-bearing partners (the source of the `IPR005225` annotation set).
- **Per-node hypergeometric on `GGG`** (`GGG_hypergeom`) — an mdSAM-partner enrichment score for every TM protein in the all-TM network, tabulated in `GGG_plot`.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L68), [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L1134-L1172), [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L700-L714), [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L1215-L1231)

## Practical Reproducibility Notes

Running this notebook requires more staging than the average notebook in the repository, for three verifiable reasons. First, several inputs are read from **hardcoded absolute macOS paths** that are not in the repository: the BioGRID tab3 download, two UniProt id-mapping TSVs (accession→gene names and keyword/GO annotations), a directory of cached InterPro JSON files, and the endocytosis supplementary Excel; only the three `files/` tables are repo-relative (`../files/...`). Second, `HPA_frac_df.pkl` — the hyperLOPIT compartment table consumed at line 37 — is an intermediate from notebook 07 and is likewise not distributed in `files/`, so reproducing the compartment graphs requires running [hyperLOPIT Organelle Enrichment](14-hyperlopit-organelle-enrichment) first. Third, as with all notebooks here, run from `notebooks/` as the working directory and observe the pickle-compatibility caution in `files/README.md`.

Sources: [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L36-L37), [15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb](notebooks/15_biogrid_interactions_by_mdsam.ipynb#L61-L95), [README.md](README.md#L244-L248), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L13-L14)

## Where This Fits in the Catalog

Within the *Omics and Interactomics Integration* group, this page pairs with [RNA-seq Differential Expression and GSEA](22-rna-seq-differential-expression-and-gsea): both ask whether mdSAM-bearing proteins occupy systematically distinct molecular contexts, one in cis (transcriptional programs) and one in trans (interaction partners). The S6C finding that soluble signaling regulators — GTPase-domain and endocytosis proteins — are enriched partners of mdSAM+ plasma-membrane proteins connects directly to the cell-based clustering evidence in [Thioflavin-T and Amytracker Screens](16-thioflavin-t-and-amytracker-screens) and [TIRF Puncta Poisson GLM](17-tirf-puncta-poisson-glm), and to the HTR7 case study that validates the mechanism end-to-end in [HTR7 End-to-End Case Study](21-htr7-end-to-end-case-study). For the provenance of the underlying mdSAM calls and compartment assignments, consult [Shared Data Tables Reference](8-shared-data-tables-reference) and [hyperLOPIT Organelle Enrichment](14-hyperlopit-organelle-enrichment); for locating every figure cell mechanically, see [Figure-to-Notebook Reproducibility Map](9-figure-to-notebook-reproducibility-map), and for extracting reusable patterns from this notebook's statistics and plotting style, see [Reusing the Analysis Toolkit](27-reusing-the-analysis-toolkit).


# Alignment-Based Conservation Metrics



This page documents `notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb`, the residue- and motif-level evolutionary conservation module of the mdSAM pipeline. The notebook asks a single mechanistic question in two complementary ways: **are membrane-domain aggregation motifs (mdSAMs) evolutionarily conserved like functional elements, or like random disordered sequence?** It answers this at the *residue level* by scoring every position of PANTHER multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) with three independent conservation estimators, and at the *motif level* by measuring how often the dSAM state itself recurs in orthologous sequences across taxa. It is the classical-alignment counterpart to the protein-language-model approach in [ESM Embedding Conservation](25-esm-embedding-conservation).

## Architectural Overview: Two Scales, One MSA Substrate

The notebook is organized as two stacked analyses sharing a common substrate — per-protein PANTHER ortholog MSAs plus AlphaFold-derived residue annotations. Understanding this layering is the key to navigating the 1,600-line notebook, which mixes exploratory plotting with reusable primitives.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Inputs["Data substrate"]
        A[dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl<br/>mdSAM motif table]
        B[AF2_with_ENSG.pkl<br/>full-length AF2 sequences]
        C[PANTHER MSAs<br/>acc_msa.fa per protein]
        D[Per-residue AF2 pkls<br/>pLDDT / helix / accessibility]
    end
    subgraph ResidueLevel["Residue-level analysis"]
        E[msa2cons_scores<br/>pycanal Canal → KL, Shannon, Lockless]
        F[Environment labeling<br/>IDR / Structured / mdSAM]
        G[conservation_df<br/>long-format per-protein means]
        H[Boxplots, KDEs, t-tests]
    end
    subgraph MotifLevel["Motif-level analysis"]
        I[msa3aln<br/>gap-aware column mapping + SAM flag]
        J[±20-column window scan<br/>% orthologs with mdSAM]
        K[MSA-depth confound control<br/>sampled non-mdSAM IDR windows]
    end
    A --> E --> F --> G --> H
    B --> A
    C --> E
    D --> F
    C --> I --> J --> K
    D --> I
```

The residue-level branch produces the "Conservation" and "Divergence" figures; the motif-level branch produces the "across orthologs" recurrence figures. Both persist their outputs as pickles for downstream notebooks.

Sources: [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L9-L19), [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L36-L41), [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L131-L160), [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L891-L925)

## Data Substrate and Motif Coordinate Anchoring

The notebook loads four pickles: the mdSAM motif table `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl` (from `files/`), the full-length `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` human proteome sequences, the ortholog registry `hTM_ortologs.pkl`, and `hMP_AF_orthologdb.pkl`. Because the motif table stores motifs as bare peptide strings rather than genomic coordinates, the first computation anchors each motif to its parent sequence: for every dSAM row, `str.find` locates the motif inside the full-length AF2 amino acid sequence, writing `start` and `end` columns used by all downstream window logic. An MSA-depth census then counts orthologs per human accession, which later serves as the covariate for detecting depth-dependent bias.

Sources: [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L36-L41), [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L51-L55), [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L66-L69)

## Residue-Environment Taxonomy: The Four-Way Comparison Frame

Before any conservation score is interpreted, the notebook partitions every residue of every protein into one of four structural environments derived from the AlphaFold residue-level pickles. This taxonomy is the experimental design: mdSAMs are compared against a *negative* disordered background and two *structured* baselines of varying solvent exposure, so that any conservation signal can be attributed to aggregation propensity rather than to order or burial per se. The labeling rules evaluated per residue in `msa2cons_scores` are:

| Environment tag | Criteria (per-residue AF2 pickle) | Role in comparison |
|---|---|---|
| `IDR` | `AF2_SS_helix_count == 0` **and** `AF2_pLDDT_max < 70` **and** accessibility `***********` (exposed) | Disordered negative control |
| `Structred_exposed` | `AF2_pLDDT_max > 70` **and** accessibility `***********` | Structured, solvent-exposed baseline |
| `Structred_burid` | `AF2_pLDDT_max > 70` **and** accessibility `...........` (buried) | Structured, buried ceiling baseline |
| `dSAM` | Position within a motif's `start`–`end` range from the anchored motif table | Class under test |

The environment classification reuses the same low-pLDDT/no-secondary-structure/exposed heuristics documented in [AlphaFold-Based Disorder Filtering](7-alphafold-based-disorder-filtering), so conservation results are directly comparable with the disorder-filtered motif set. After annotation, the per-residue frame is tagged with the parent accession and accumulated across all proteins into `concervation_msa.pkl`; two accessions (`Q6UXD1`, `A8MZ97`) are explicitly skipped because their PANTHER MSA files are absent.

Sources: [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L131-L160), [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L181-L198)

## Three Complementary Conservation Estimators via pycanal

The scoring engine is the `pycanal` library: `Canal(fastafile=<msa>, ref=0, startcount=1)` treats the first MSA row (the human reference) as the coordinate frame, and `canal.analysis(include=None, method='all')` returns per-column scores for every estimator the library supports. The notebook deliberately exploits **three orthogonal definitions of conservation**, which is the strongest methodological feature of this analysis — a conclusion that holds under all three metrics is robust to the known pitfalls of any single one:

| Metric (pycanal column) | Plotted as | What it captures | Caveat addressed |
|---|---|---|---|
| `relative` | KL divergence (`Divergence`) | Divergence of the observed column distribution from a background model | Sensitive to MSA composition |
| `shannon` | `1/H` (`\\\\frac{1}{H}`) | Inverse Shannon entropy — column purity | Ignores amino-acid similarity classes |
| `lockless` | `Conservation` | Statistical coupling / Lockless score | Computationally heavier, context-aware |

These are unified into a tidy long-format frame `conservation_df` with columns `acc`, `ele` (environment), `conservation` (mean per protein–environment cell) and `Conservation_type`, persisted as `conservation_df.pkl` for reuse. Per-protein means (rather than per-residue pooling) are the unit of statistical replication, avoiding pseudo-replication from correlated residues within a motif.

Sources: [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L131-L160), [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L364-L372), [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L654-L656)

## Statistical Testing Strategy and Publication Figures

The inferential design pairs an initial *paired* test with follow-up *independent* tests. Because each protein contributes a mean value to all four environments, the first pass pivots the per-protein means into a protein × environment matrix and applies `stats.ttest_rel` between the IDR and dSAM columns — a within-protein comparison that cancels protein-specific MSA depth and phylogenetic breadth. Subsequent `stats.ttest_ind` calls compare KL-divergence means of IDR vs. dSAM, buried vs. dSAM, and Lockless IDR vs. dSAM across proteins. The final figure (`Divergence.svg`) renders three-environment notched boxplots (Disordered / mdSAM / Structured*) with p-values formatted as scientific-notation annotations via a small lead-digit/exponent extraction routine, and annotates the sample size `n=929` proteins.

Sources: [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L261-L273), [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L456-L464), [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L581-L614)

> [!TIP]
> Environment tags `Structred_exposed` / `Structred_burid` contain typos (single "r", "burid"). These strings are load-bearing keys across joins, pivots, and plot `order` lists — if you refactor, rename them everywhere at once or every comparison silently degrades to empty selections.

## Gap-Aware Coordinate Remapping: `msa3aln`

Alignments introduce gaps, so ungapped motif coordinates cannot be compared across orthologs without remapping. The notebook first prototypes the idea with a regex: gaps in the reference are replaced by `.`, the query motif becomes a regex pattern, and `re.match` locates it against the gapped reference; an index array converts alignment columns to ungapped positions. The production function `msa3aln(acc, msa_seq)` generalizes this to *every* MSA row: it builds a column→ungapped-position map from gap positions, then emits one record per alignment column carrying `msa_pos` (column index), `original_pos` (ungapped position in that ortholog), and a discrete **SAM flag** marking which residues satisfy the mdSAM criteria *in that specific organism* — HUMAN rows require the full IDR signature plus `WT_Windows_above_thershold > 0`, while non-human rows use the lighter `pLDDT < 70` + window-threshold rule, reflecting the absence of the full human annotation stack for orthologs.

| Record field | HUMAN row | Non-HUMAN row |
|---|---|---|
| `SAM = 2` (mdSAM-state) | IDR criteria **and** `WT_Windows_above_thershold > 0` | `AF2_pLDDT_max < 70` **and** `WT_Windows_above_thershold > 0` |
| `SAM = 1` (baseline) | all other residues | all other residues |
| `msa_pos` | alignment column (gap-aware) | alignment column (gap-aware) |
| `original_pos` | ungapped index into `AF2_with_ENSG` sequence | ungapped index into ortholog sequence |

This SAM-flag matrix per protein is the substrate for the motif-level recurrence analysis: the human row tells you *where* the mdSAM is in alignment space, and the ortholog rows tell you *whether the same alignment window is also mdSAM-like*.

Sources: [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L664-L697), [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L891-L925)

## Motif-Level Recurrence: % Orthologs with mdSAM in the Alignment Window

The recurrence scan is direct: for each mdSAM of each protein, `msa3aln` records are concatenated across all MSA rows, a ±20-alignment-column window is centered on the human SAM=2 columns overlapping the motif, and `pre` is computed as the percentage of non-HUMAN taxa whose SAM=2 columns fall inside that window, alongside `number_of_tax` (MSA depth). The result — persisted as `number_of_tax_vs_pre.pkl` — is visualized as a histogram of `%Orthologs with dSAM` with an inset showing taxon counts, a joint scatter of prevalence vs. log MSA depth, and a motif-level boxplot binned by MSA depth. A crucial positive-control cell re-runs the identical window statistic on ~1,000 randomly sampled transmembrane proteins *without* mdSAMs, anchoring the window at a random disordered residue instead, so the mdSAM prevalence distribution can be interpreted against the null expectation for ordinary disordered sequence.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    M[mdSAM start/end] --> W["±20 msa-column window<br/>(HUMAN SAM=2 columns)"]
    MSA[All MSA rows] --> A2[msa3aln SAM-flag records] --> W
    W --> P["pre = % non-HUMAN taxa<br/>with SAM=2 in window"]
    CTRL["Control: 1000 sampled TMs<br/>random IDR anchor"] --> P2["null prevalence distribution"]
    P --> F[Recurrence figures +<br/>depth-stratified boxplots]
    P2 --> F
```

An additional derived quantity, `with_sam = pre × number_of_tax / 100`, converts prevalence into an absolute count of orthologs carrying the mdSAM state, and the diagnostic scatter against reference lines at `x`, `x/2`, `x/4`, and `x/10` exposes how recurrence decays with evolutionary distance.

Sources: [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L941-L961), [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L981-L1000), [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L1167-L1220)

## MSA-Depth Confound and Sparse-Alignment Sanity Check

A recurring threat to alignment-based conservation claims is that deep MSAs are available only for well-studied, slowly evolving proteins — so apparent conservation could be a study-bias artifact. The notebook confronts this explicitly: the joint scatter and depth-binned boxplots stratify prevalence by `number_of_tax`, a custom colormap scatter colors each MSA-depth point by how many proteins share that depth (with a gray band flagging MSAs of fewer than 20 sequences), and a fraction computation quantifies how much of the motif cohort sits in the sparsest MSA-depth bins. If mdSAM recurrence were merely a depth artifact, it would co-vary with taxon count; the stratified views make that testable rather than assumed.

Sources: [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L1042-L1063), [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L1262-L1294)

## Phylogenetic Utilities: Identity Distance and Neighbor-Joining Trees

Two auxiliary functions extend the MSA handling toolkit. `para2dist` (evolved variant) computes a BioPython identity `DistanceCalculator` matrix over the MSA, extracts each sequence's distance to the first (reference) row, and filters orthologs by `tree_cutoff=0.7` — a simple phylogenetic pruning step restricting comparisons to near-reference orthologs. `para2dist_tree` returns both the filtered distance table and a **neighbor-joining tree** built with `DistanceTreeConstructor().nj(dm)`, which the notebook exports in Newick format (e.g., `tree-Q96RJ3.nwk`) for external tree viewers. These utilities are exercised interactively on test accessions (`P08138`, `Q96RJ3`) and are the natural building blocks if you need distance-restricted conservation estimates in your own reanalyses.

Sources: [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L769-L803), [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L812-L849), [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L859-L872)

## Reproducibility Notes and Known Quirks

Repurposing this notebook requires awareness of several verifiable quirks. All heavy inputs live on an external volume (`/Volumes/aelazar/...`) — PANTHER MSA FASTAs, per-protein residue pickles, and the ortholog databases — and only the mdSAM table and AF2 sequences ship in `files/`, so a full re-run requires reconstructing that substrate first (see [Shared Data Tables Reference](8-shared-data-tables-reference)). In `msa2cons_scores`, the dSAM-annotation loop filters `dSAMs.acc=='Q9NQW8'` rather than the loop variable `acc`, so only that one protein receives correct `dSAM` environment tags on a fresh execution — the persisted `concervation_msa.pkl` in the authors' environment was produced from a corrected run. The output artifacts to look for when validating an execution are `concervation_msa.pkl`, `conservation_df.pkl`, `number_of_tax_vs_pre.pkl`, and the SVG figure exports (`Conservation_new_version*.svg`, `Divergence.svg`, `across_orthologs_v2*.svg`, `msa_v2.svg`).

Sources: [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L131-L160), [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L157), [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L196-L198), [20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb](/notebooks/20_conservation_alignment_based.ipynb#L1062-L1063)

> [!TIP]
> When porting `msa2cons_scores` to a batch setting, replace the hard-coded `Q9NQW8` filter with the loop's `acc` and pre-load per-residue pickles outside the MSA loop — the current implementation re-reads each protein's residue pickle once per call, which dominates runtime on large cohorts.

## Position in the Conservation Trilogy and Reading Path

This page is the first of three evolutionary-conservation analyses. Notebook 20 establishes the *alignment-based ground truth*: mdSAM residues show divergence/conservation profiles distinct from both disordered and structured backgrounds, and the mdSAM state itself recurs in orthologous alignment windows above the disordered-sequence null. The natural next steps are [ESM Embedding Conservation](25-esm-embedding-conservation), which asks whether a protein language model's representations encode the same signal without any MSA, and [Ortholog Peptides and Motif Overlaps](26-ortholog-peptides-and-motif-overlaps), which turns recurrence into experimentally testable orthologous peptide constructs. For the upstream definitions that feed every threshold on this page, see [mdSAM Concept and Discovery Rationale](4-mdsam-concept-and-discovery-rationale) and [AlphaFold-Based Disorder Filtering](7-alphafold-based-disorder-filtering); for turning these primitives into your own pipeline, see [Reusing the Analysis Toolkit](27-reusing-the-analysis-toolkit).

# ESM Embedding Conservation



This page documents `21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb`, the embedding-based half of the repository's evolutionary-conservation analysis. The notebook asks whether mdSAM windows — self-assembly motifs predicted inside intrinsically disordered regions — carry an evolutionary signature detectable by a protein language model, rather than by classical alignment statistics. It does this by ingesting per-residue ESM2-derived conservation scores produced by an external pipeline, and benchmarking mdSAM windows against three controls: known short linear motifs from the ELM database, length-matched random windows inside IDRs, and length-matched random windows inside structured regions. All inference operates on precomputed score tables; no language-model inference happens inside this notebook.

Sources: [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L9-L28), [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L37-L38), [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L48-L61)

## Why an Embedding-Based Track

The conservation question is interrogated through two independent instruments in this repository. The alignment-based track ([Alignment-Based Conservation Metrics](24-alignment-based-conservation-metrics)) derives per-column statistics from ortholog multiple sequence alignments. Notebook 21 instead consumes per-residue conservation scores produced from ESM2 embeddings — the output pickle is explicitly named `ESM2_conservation.pkl`, and the notebook pins its methodological anchor to a Briefings in Bioinformatics article on embedding-based conservation (URL preserved as a comment in the second cell). The design logic: sequence-level alignment metrics can miss functional constraint that manifests as *semantic* conservation (different residues, similar encoded context), which embedding divergence is designed to capture. Running both tracks over the same mdSAM set makes the two instruments mutually corroborating rather than redundant.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph A["Alignment-based track — notebook 20"]
        MSA["Ortholog multiple sequence alignment"] --> ENT["Per-column substitution statistics"]
    end
    subgraph B["Embedding-based track — notebook 21"]
        PLM["Pretrained ESM2 model (external pipeline)"] --> RES["One per-residue conservation CSV per UniProt accession"]
    end
    ENT --> HYP{"Are mdSAM windows more<br/>evolutionarily constrained than<br/>matched backgrounds?"}
    RES --> HYP
    HYP --> C1["Positive control: ELM motifs (known SLiMs)"]
    HYP --> C2["Background: length-matched random IDR windows"]
    HYP --> C3["Background: length-matched random structured windows"]
```

Sources: [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L37-L38), [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L189-L210)

## Pipeline Architecture

The notebook is a linear extraction-and-test pipeline with one external ingestion boundary. Per-residue CSVs are discovered by globbing a local `kibby/sample_data/csvs/` directory — one file per UniProt accession, read as two unnamed columns (`AA`, `conservation`). Accessions are recovered from filenames, forming the `accs` index that gates every downstream comparison: a protein participates only if an embedding-conservation file exists for it.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph EXT["External inputs — not shipped in repo"]
        KIB["kibby/sample_data/csvs/*.csv<br/>'AA','conservation' per residue"]
        ELMDB["elm_all.tsv<br/>ELM database: Primary_Acc, Start, End"]
    end
    subgraph SH["Shared tables — files/"]
        AF2["AF2_with_ENSG.pkl: acc, AAseq, pLDDT array"]
        MDS["dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl: start_new, end_new, AA_length"]
    end
    ING["glob ingestion → accs index"]
    DEDUP["mdSAMs.drop_duplicates(subset='AAseq')"]
    SAMP["Length-matched window sampling<br/>random_idr_start / random_structre_start"]
    CON["kibby_con: slice residue vector s:e"]
    TIDY["Tidy records {value, ele, acc, ind}"]
    DF["df → ESM2_conservation.pkl"]
    MED["groupby(['acc','ind']).median() → zz"]
    STATS["KS-2sample · ANOVA · pairwise t-test"]
    FIG["mean_embedding_con.svg · venn_snp_hTM_all.svg"]
    KIB --> ING --> SAMP
    AF2 --> SAMP
    MDS --> DEDUP --> SAMP
    ELMDB --> SAMP
    SAMP --> CON --> TIDY --> DF --> MED --> STATS --> FIG
```

The deduplication step matters for statistical hygiene: motif records are collapsed on unique `AAseq` before sampling, so repeated identical sequences cannot vote multiple times. The final tidy frame is pickled to the working directory, making the residue-level raw data the checkpoint artifact for re-analysis without re-ingestion.

Sources: [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L48-L61), [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L120-L121), [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L189-L210), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L7-L9)

## Data Dependencies and Contracts

| Artifact | Contract (columns consumed) | Role | Producer |
|---|---|---|---|
| `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl` | `acc`, `AAseq`, `start_new`, `end_new`, `AA_length` | Case windows | mdSAM identification pipeline |
| `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` | `acc`, `AAseq` (length validation), `pLDDT` (per-residue array) | Structural masks | `02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb` |
| `hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl` | loaded, not referenced in retained cells | Vestigial in this notebook | `03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb` |
| `elm_all.tsv` | `Primary_Acc`, `Start`, `End` | Positive controls | External ELM download (absolute local path) |
| `kibby/sample_data/csvs/*.csv` | `AA`, `conservation` per residue | Scoring source | External embedding-conservation pipeline |
| `conservation_df.pkl` | `Conservation_type`, `ele`, `conservation` | Secondary KL track | Upstream precomputation (not in `files/`) |

Note that `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` is documented in `files/README.md` as read by notebook 21, but the current `files/` tree ships only the mdSAM and hTMs pickles — reproducing this notebook requires regenerating the AlphaFold table via notebook 02.

Sources: [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L23-L26), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L7-L13)

## The Structural Null Model

The core methodological move is **context-matched, length-matched background sampling**. A helper `ranges()` compresses a sorted index list into contiguous `[start, end]` intervals, and two samplers draw a random start inside a region only if the region is long enough: `random_idr_start` scans intervals where `pLDDT < 70` (the repository-wide disorder proxy, defined by the AlphaFold filtering convention in [AlphaFold-Based Disorder Filtering](7-alphafold-based-disorder-filtering)), while `random_structre_start` scans `pLDDT >= 70` intervals. Both enforce a `motif_length + 2` minimum region length, and `randrange(r[0], r[1]-motif_length)` leaves a two-residue margin so the window fits strictly inside the region.

> [!TIP]
> Every `randrange` call is unseeded — the background sets are non-deterministic across runs. Any figure-level reproduction must either fix a seed before the main loop or persist `ESM2_conservation.pkl` and work from the checkpoint downstream.

The loop over mdSAMs draws three windows per motif — the real mdSAM window, a random IDR window, and a random structured window — all of identical length `AA_length`. The structured draw is explicitly guarded with `if ss_r is not None`, because proteins can lack any structured interval long enough for the motif; the IDR draw is used unguarded, which is safe in practice only because mdSAM-containing proteins are, by construction, IDR-bearing. A second loop walks ELM entries whose `Primary_Acc` appears in `accs`, extracting each annotated motif window, guarded by a check that the AF2 row's `pLDDT` entry is not the `'A'` placeholder used for proteins lacking predicted structures.

Sources: [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L71-L88), [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L136-L168)

## The Four Window Classes

| `ele` tag | Window origin | Coordinates as coded | Inferential role |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mdSAM` | mdSAM table | `start_new - 1` (1-based → 0-based) through window of `AA_length` | Case |
| `random` | `random_idr_start` | Length-matched, random position in `pLDDT < 70` intervals | IDR background |
| `random_struct` | `random_structre_start` | Length-matched, random position in `pLDDT ≥ 70` intervals | Structured background |
| `ELM` | ELM database | `Start` through `Start + (End - Start) + 1` (exclusive end) — *no* −1 offset applied, unlike the mdSAM branch | Positive control (known functional motifs) |

Two asymmetries deserve attention when reproducing. First, mdSAM start coordinates are decremented to 0-based indexing while ELM `Start` values are consumed as-is; if ELM annotations are 1-based inclusive (their standard convention), ELM windows sit one residue left of their annotated span — verify against your ELM release before extending. Second, the variable `strcutre` passed as the mask for the structured class is built with the `pLDDT < 70` filter (line 147), not `>= 70`; as shown below, this parameter is currently inert, but it becomes load-bearing the moment background normalization is re-enabled.

Sources: [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L136-L168)

## Scoring and Aggregation Mechanics

`kibby_con(acc, s, e, idrs)` is the single scoring gateway. It reads the per-accession CSV, validates that the CSV row count equals the AlphaFold `AAseq` length (returning `[]` on mismatch — a silent length-based exclusion), slices rows `s:e`, and returns the raw per-residue conservation values. The function also computes a same-amino-acid IDR background mean for normalization, but the division is commented out and the `idrs` argument is a bare no-op expression inside the function body: **scores are consumed raw**.

> [!TIP]
> The commented normalization (`WT_con / background`) is the notebook's one acknowledged extension point. If you re-enable it, first fix the mask bug at line 147 (`strcutre` must use `>= 70`), otherwise structured-class scores would be normalized against the IDR background — a subtle inversion of the null model.

Aggregation is deliberately two-tiered to defeat residue-level pseudoreplication. The tidy frame `df` holds one row per residue, then `groupby(['acc','ind']).median()` collapses each window to its median, producing motif-level distributions (`zz`) for `random`, `mdSAM`, `ELM`, and `strctre`. All primary statistics in the notebook operate on these motif medians, not raw residues — the correct unit of independence, since residues within a motif share a protein and a window.

Sources: [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L97-L110), [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L234-L256)

## Statistical Framework

| Test | Function | Comparisons | Analysis unit | Output anchor |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kolmogorov–Smirnov 2-sample | `stats.ks_2samp(...)[-1]` | random vs mdSAM; ELM vs mdSAM; ELM vs random | Motif medians | p-value annotations on main figure, `mean_embedding_con.svg` |
| One-way ANOVA | `scipy.stats.f_oneway` | ELM, mdSAM, random, strctre (4 groups) | Motif medians | `F, p` printout |
| Pairwise Welch t-tests | `scipy.stats.ttest_ind` | All 6 pairs of the 4 classes | Motif medians | Console table |
| Pairwise t-tests + Bonferroni alpha | `scipy.stats.ttest_ind` | IDR, Structred_burid, Structred_exposed, dSAM | Residue values (KL table) | Console table |
| Tukey HSD | `scipy.stats.tukey_hsd` | Same 4 KL-track groups | Residue values | Full HSD result printout |

Two precision notes on the primary figure cell. The box order is `['random','mdSAM','strctre','ELM']` but the tick labels are `['$IDR_{random}$','$mdSAM$','$ELM$','$Structured$']` — as written, the third positional label `$ELM$` lands on the `random_struct` boxes and `$Structured$` lands on the `ELM` boxes. The palette (`teal, red, amber, gray`) follows the box order, so color-to-class mapping is unambiguous even where the strings are not; reconcile this mapping if you regenerate the SVG. Second, the pairwise t-test cell computes a Bonferroni-corrected alpha (`0.05 / C(4,2)`) but prints raw unadjusted p-values; apply the correction yourself when consuming that output. A complementary ECDF plot over raw residue values and an unguarded-ylim box plot provide distribution-shape checks beyond the median summaries.

Sources: [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L267-L302), [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L314-L326), [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L338-L348), [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L427-L453)

## Secondary Track: KL-Divergence Conservation

The final block pivots to a different precomputed artifact, `conservation_df.pkl`, filtered to `Conservation_type == 'Kullback-Leibler'`. Here the comparison classes are residue-level environment categories rather than motif classes: `IDR`, `Structred_burid` (structured, buried), `Structred_exposed` (structured, solvent-exposed), and `dSAM` residues. This reframes the question from *are mdSAM windows constrained* to *is the burial-specific conservation gradient consistent with dSAM residues behaving like functional surface sites*. The track applies pairwise t-tests with a computed Bonferroni alpha and `scipy.stats.tukey_hsd` across the four groups, the latter requiring a SciPy release that provides `tukey_hsd`. Unlike the primary track, no sampling happens here — the table arrives fully classified, so this block is pure inference over upstream output.

Sources: [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L481-L494), [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L509-L530), [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L540-L574)

## Reproducibility Notes

Repointing this notebook requires three path edits: the absolute ELM path (`/Users/aelazar/notebooks_for_paper/elm/elm_all.tsv`), the absolute Kibby CSV glob, and regeneration of `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` via notebook 02 since it is absent from the shipped `files/` tree. Both shared pickles carry the repository's standard pickle-safety caveat: load only from this repository with a compatible pandas version. The retained cells carry more imports than they use (`TSNE`, `cmasher`, `fisher_exact`, `expected_freq` are unreferenced), so a minimal dependency set is: pandas, numpy, scipy, seaborn, matplotlib, tqdm. Note also that `hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl` is loaded but never queried — the filename `venn_snp_hTM_all.svg` on the raw-residue figure is inherited naming, not evidence of a transmembrane filter in this analysis.

Sources: [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L9-L28), [21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb](notebooks/21_conservation_esm_embedding.ipynb#L348-L348), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L13-L14)

## Related Pages

The embedding track presupposes the AlphaFold disorder convention — start with [AlphaFold-Based Disorder Filtering](7-alphafold-based-disorder-filtering) for the pLDDT threshold rationale, and [Shared Data Tables Reference](8-shared-data-tables-reference) for the table schemas consumed here. Compare the orthogonal methodology in [Alignment-Based Conservation Metrics](24-alignment-based-conservation-metrics), then continue to [Ortholog Peptides and Motif Overlaps](26-ortholog-peptides-and-motif-overlaps), which moves from conservation scores to experimentally screened ortholog-derived peptides.

# Ortholog Peptides and Motif Overlaps



This page documents the final two notebooks of the Evolution branch — `22_ortholog_peptide_tht.ipynb` and `23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb` — which close the loop on mdSAM conservation from two complementary directions. Notebook 22 asks an *experimental* question: if mdSAMs are evolutionarily constrained, do the orthologous motifs from other vertebrate species still self-assemble, and does a proline mutant abolish that signal? Notebook 23 asks a *comparative* question: how does the mdSAM-containing protein set overlap with three independent motif-family catalogs (LARKS, WIRS, FINCHES-predicted fuzzy interactions) once everything is projected onto the human transmembrane proteome? Together they produce Figure 7D, Supplementary Figure S7C, and Supplementary Figure S7D of the manuscript.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L79-L86), [README.md](README.md#L172-L173), [README.md](README.md#L238-L240)

## Position in the Pipeline

Both notebooks sit at the end of the Evolution (Fig 7 / S7) section, consuming the outputs of the computational conservation analyses. Notebooks 20 and 21 establish that mdSAMs are conserved *computationally* (alignment-based metrics and ESM embeddings). Notebook 22 converts conservation into a *functional* claim by synthesizing ortholog peptides and measuring Thioflavin-T (ThT) amyloid reactivity; notebook 23 then maps the mdSAM family onto the broader landscape of known/prone-to-assembly motif families to establish that it is related to — but distinct from — LARKS, WIRS, and FINCHES fuzzy interactions.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    N20["20: Alignment-based<br/>conservation metrics"] --> N21["21: ESM embedding<br/>conservation"]
    N21 --> N22["22: Ortholog peptide ThT<br/>Fig 7D + S7C"]
    N22 --> N23["23: Overlap with LARKS,<br/>WIRS, FINCHES<br/>S7D"]
```

The mapping from figures to notebook cells is explicit: Fig 7D comes from cells 6 and 16 of notebook 22; S7C from cells 20–21 of the same notebook; S7D from cell 16 of notebook 23 (cell indices are 0-based, matching `FIGURE_MAP.csv` conventions used throughout the repository).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L79-L86), [README.md](README.md#L165-L173), [README.md](README.md#L230-L240)

## Notebook 22 — Thioflavin-T of Ortholog Peptides

**Design rationale.** The mdSAMs of two human proteins — **NGFR** and **TNFRSF13C** — were traced to orthologous sequence windows in other vertebrates. Each ortholog peptide was synthesized twice: as the wild-type ortholog sequence and as a proline mutant (`_MUT`), the same β-strand-breaking negative-control design used across all peptide ThT screens in this repository. If an mdSAM is functionally conserved, ortholog WT peptides should retain amyloid-like ThT signal while their proline mutants collapse toward blank. The notebook is entirely plot-centric: it ingests raw plate-reader workbooks, normalizes against blanks, melts spectra into long form, and renders the point plots and spectra that became Fig 7D and S7C.

Sources: [22_ortholog_peptide_tht.ipynb](notebooks/22_ortholog_peptide_tht.ipynb#L51-L74), [22_ortholog_peptide_tht.ipynb](notebooks/22_ortholog_peptide_tht.ipynb#L113-L131), [README.md](README.md#L58-L60)

### Assay Design and Plate Layout

Two physical plates underlie the analysis. The first workbook (`2025_05_03_NGFR_Orthologs.xlsx`, sheet `Day3`) holds the NGFR ortholog endpoint plate. The second workbook (`20250512_Ortholog_ThT_2.xlsx`, sheet `Table End point`, read with `header=10`) holds a combined NGFR + TNFRSF13C plate with full emission spectra. The plate map is constructed programmatically in cell 7 from an ordered name list: wells 01–12 alternate WT and mutant for six peptide pairs, and the `ele` column is derived purely from list parity (even index → `WT`, odd → `mut`).

| Protein | Ortholog species (UniProt code → common name) | Mutant control |
|---|---|---|
| NGFR | CHICK (chicken), LEPOC (spotted gar), BOVIN (cattle) | Proline mutant per species |
| TNFRSF13C | CHICK (chicken), FELCA (domestic cat), MACMU (rhesus macaque) | Proline mutant per species |
| Human reference | Both proteins | WT endpoints from the 96-well screen table |

Sources: [22_ortholog_peptide_tht.ipynb](notebooks/22_ortholog_peptide_tht.ipynb#L51-L56), [22_ortholog_peptide_tht.ipynb](notebooks/22_ortholog_peptide_tht.ipynb#L113-L131)

### Data Flow and Figure Cells

**Blank normalization is asymmetric between the two plates.** The NGFR endpoint plate uses a single hardcoded blank constant (`blank = 9848.166667`) drawn as a dashed reference line, while the combined spectra plate computes a per-wavelength blank by averaging all rows whose well ID contains `H` (H-column wells), then drops both the `H` and `G` rows from the data. The combined plate is melted into a long-form table with one row per (well, wavelength) across 465–555 nm in 5-nm steps, then annotated with `human_ortholog`, `spe`, and `ele` columns via a well→name dictionary. Crucially, the human WT reference points are not on the ortholog plate at all — they are appended from `ThT_96.pkl` (the human peptide ThT table keyed by `gene_name`, an intermediate of the 96-well screen workflow that is not distributed in the repository) at the 490 nm endpoint.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    T96["ThT_96.pkl<br/>human WT endpoints (gene_name-keyed)"] -->|"appended @ 490 nm"| LP["df_plot<br/>long-form table"]
    E1["NGFR ortholog plate Excel<br/>sheet 'Day3'"] --> P4["column parser:<br/>spe + WT vs 'P'"] --> PP["endpoint records"] --> C6["cell 6: point plot NGFR<br/>→ ThT_orthologs_NGFR.svg (Fig 7D)"]
    E2["Combined ortholog plate Excel<br/>endpoint + spectra 465–555 nm"] --> BL["blank wells (H) → per-λ mean;<br/>H and G rows dropped"] --> LP
    LP --> C16["cell 16: point plot TNFRSF13C<br/>→ ThT_orthologs_TNFRSF13C.svg (Fig 7D)"]
    LP --> C21["cells 20–21: per-species spectra<br/>WT vs mutant + blank overlay (S7C)"]
```

The final figure cells follow this structure: the NGFR Fig 7D panel (cell 6, re-rendered at cell 17 with BOVIN excluded and the species order fixed to CHICK/LEPOC/human) is a point plot of WT vs mutant per species on a log y-axis; the TNFRSF13C Fig 7D panel (cell 16) is the equivalent for CHICK/FELCA/human with a hardcoded blank reference at 166.5; and the S7C spectra panels (cells 20–21) overlay each species' WT-vs-mutant emission band against the grey blank curve.

Sources: [22_ortholog_peptide_tht.ipynb](notebooks/22_ortholog_peptide_tht.ipynb#L33-L35), [22_ortholog_peptide_tht.ipynb](notebooks/22_ortholog_peptide_tht.ipynb#L151-L170), [22_ortholog_peptide_tht.ipynb](notebooks/22_ortholog_peptide_tht.ipynb#L251-L257), [22_ortholog_peptide_tht.ipynb](notebooks/22_ortholog_peptide_tht.ipynb#L305-L330), [README.md](README.md#L172-L173), [README.md](README.md#L238-L239)

## Notebook 23 — Overlap with LARKS, WIRS and FINCHES

**Core question.** Is the mdSAM family the same phenomenon as previously characterized assembly-prone motif families, or does it occupy distinct sequence space? The notebook answers this with set algebra: three external motif catalogs, each intersected with the human transmembrane proteome (`hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl`), are compared against `dSAM_MP` — the set of mdSAM-containing transmembrane proteins. Note the naming convention: `dSAM` in file and variable names is the legacy term for mdSAM (the structured-region counterpart being mSAM/sSAM).

Sources: [23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb](notebooks/23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb#L39-L52), [README.md](README.md#L21), [README.md](README.md#L86)

### Building the Four Sets

All set definitions are computed in one dense cell (cell 2) plus one for the fourth family. **LARKs_MP** and **WAVE_MP** are direct intersections of UniProt accessions: `TMs.acc ∩ LARKS.csv['UniProt ID']` and `TMs.acc ∩ WAVE_cell_2014.txt['Uniprot ID']` (the WIRS catalog, despite the WAVE filename). **dSAM_MP** is assembled through the AlphaFold bridge: the mdSAM table is deduplicated by `AAseq`, filtered to rows whose `ENST` appears in `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` entries whose accession is a transmembrane protein, and reduced to the unique `acc` set. The fourth family, **Fuzzy** (`alex_set`), comes from the FINCHES supplement (`science.adq8381_table_s1.xlsx`): UniProt IDs in the transmembrane set whose ` epsilon` score falls below the 5th percentile of the distribution — i.e., the strongest fuzzy-interaction predictions.

| Set | Source file (as read by the notebook) | Selection rule | Variable |
|---|---|---|---|
| LARKs | `LARKS.csv` (tab-delimited despite extension) | Any catalog hit that is a human TM protein | `LARKs_MP` |
| WIRS | `WAVE_cell_2014.txt` (tab-delimited) | Any catalog hit that is a human TM protein | `WAVE_MP` |
| mdSAMs | `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl` + `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` | Proteins with ≥1 mdSAM, ENST-joined to the TM set, dedup by `AAseq` | `dSAM_MP` |
| Fuzzy | `science.adq8381_table_s1.xlsx` | TM proteins with `epsilon` < 5th percentile | `alex_set` |

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    LARKS["LARKS.csv"] --> IA["intersect with<br/>TMs.acc"]
    WIRS["WAVE_cell_2014.txt (WIRS)"] --> IA
    TMs["hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl<br/>human TM proteome"] --> IA
    IA --> MP["LARKs_MP · WAVE_MP"]
    DS["dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl"] --> DSET["ENST-join via AF2_with_ENSG.pkl<br/>dedup by AAseq → dSAM_MP"]
    FZ["science.adq8381 Table S1"] --> FSEL["epsilon &lt; 5th percentile"] --> FUZZY["alex_set (Fuzzy)"]
    MP --> V["weighted + unweighted venn3<br/>+ hypergeometric p-values (cells 2, 8)"]
    DSET --> V
    MP --> F["2×2 contingency + Fisher exact<br/>(cells 6–7)"]
    DSET --> F
    MP --> UP["UpSet membership logic<br/>cell 16 → S7D"]
    DSET --> UP
    FUZZY --> UP
```

Sources: [23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb](notebooks/23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb#L39-L52), [23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb](notebooks/23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb#L87-L97), [23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb](notebooks/23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb#L204-L207), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L5-L9)

### Statistics: Hypergeometric and Fisher Exact

Two layers of statistical support are computed. First, **hypergeometric tail probabilities** (cell 2) test whether the observed mdSAM overlaps exceed chance given the size of the transmembrane proteome: the WIRS overlap (35 proteins) yields p = 8×10⁻⁷ and the LARKS overlap (22 proteins) yields p = 1×10⁻⁵, both printed and annotated as text on the Venn figures. Second, **Fisher exact tests** (cells 6–7) build explicit 2×2 contingency tables (overlap / one-sided-only / neither) and compare observed cell counts against `expected_freq`, reporting enrichment and a two-sided p-value per family. Both weighted (`venn3`) and unweighted (`venn3_unweighted`) Venn renderings are produced, the latter normalizing circle sizes for legibility.

Sources: [23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb](notebooks/23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb#L53-L76), [23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb](notebooks/23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb#L125-L164), [23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb](notebooks/23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb#L173-L195)

### The UpSet Rendering (S7D)

Because a four-set comparison cannot be drawn honestly as a Venn diagram, the final figure switches to **UpSet**. Cell 14 prototypes the plot with the region counts baked in as membership data — [WIRS]=41, [LARKs]=22, [mdSAMs]=887, [LARKs,WIRS]=0, [mdSAMs,WIRS]=35, [mdSAMs,LARKs]=22, [mdSAMs,LARKs,WIRS]=1 — which tells you the headline numbers at a glance: the mdSAM-only region dominates (~887 TM proteins), while the overlaps with WIRS and LARKS are significant but thin slices. Cell 16 (the README-designated S7D source) then derives all non-empty regions *programmatically* for all four sets via a `combinations` walk: each region is computed as `intersection(included) − union(excluded)`, guaranteeing disjoint, summing-correct bars, and renders `upsetplot_setlogic.svg`.

Sources: [23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb](notebooks/23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb#L253-L271), [23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb](notebooks/23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb#L290-L326), [README.md](README.md#L240)

## Reproducibility Caveats

Like several late-stage notebooks in this repository, notebooks 22 and 23 were written as interactive session transcripts and retain **absolute local paths** (OneDrive and `~/Downloads`) for the plate-reader workbooks, the UniProt GO idmapping table, and the FINCHES supplement. The three shared pickle tables required by notebook 23 ship in `files/` and must be referenced as `../files/...` with `notebooks/` as the working directory; notebook 22 additionally depends on the undistributed `ThT_96.pkl` intermediate. Notebooks ship with outputs cleared, so all plots must be regenerated by execution.

> [!TIP]
> Blank handling in notebook 22 is deliberately asymmetric: the NGFR endpoint plate subtracts one hardcoded constant (9848.166667), while the combined spectra plate averages H-column wells per wavelength. Reproduce both rules exactly, or the Fig 7D/S7C baselines will not match.

> [!TIP]
> In notebook 23 cell 3, the variable `PM` is assigned `set(hTMs.acc)` — the GO:0005886 (plasma membrane) intersection is computed into `PM_TMs` but then commented out on the assignment line. As the code stands, the Fisher-exact cells 6–7 therefore test overlap across the *full* transmembrane proteome, not strictly PM-annotated proteins.

Sources: [22_ortholog_peptide_tht.ipynb](notebooks/22_ortholog_peptide_tht.ipynb#L52-L56), [23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb](notebooks/23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb#L87-L97), [23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb](notebooks/23_overlap_with_larks_wirs_finches.ipynb#L205-L207), [README.md](README.md#L244-L248), [files/README.md](files/README.md#L3-L13)

## Reading Progression

This page is the practical payoff of the Evolution section. Read it after the two computational conservation notebooks — [Alignment-Based Conservation Metrics](24-alignment-based-conservation-metrics) and [ESM Embedding Conservation](25-esm-embedding-conservation) — which motivate why the ortholog peptides in notebook 22 were chosen at all. The ThT assay methodology and the proline-mutant control design are introduced in [Thioflavin-T and Amytracker Screens](16-thioflavin-t-and-amytracker-screens); the shared pickle tables that notebook 23 consumes are documented in [Shared Data Tables Reference](8-shared-data-tables-reference). For the complete panel-to-cell mapping of Fig 7D/S7C/S7D, consult the [Figure-to-Notebook Reproducibility Map](9-figure-to-notebook-reproducibility-map), and to adapt this overlap-statistics pattern (hypergeometric + Fisher exact + UpSet) to your own set comparisons, continue to [Reusing the Analysis Toolkit](27-reusing-the-analysis-toolkit).

# Reusing the Analysis Toolkit



This page explains how to lift the mdSAM analysis machinery out of this notebook-only repository and apply it to new questions. There is no installable Python package here — the "toolkit" is the set of 23 numbered notebooks, three shared pickled tables in `files/`, the persisted random-forest model from `01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb`, and a handful of conventions (working directory, relative paths, column names) that every notebook obeys. Everything below is documented strictly from what the repository contains, so you can replicate the reuse patterns with zero speculation.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L23-L29), [files/README.md](/files/README.md#L1-L14)

## What "the Toolkit" Actually Is

The repository is organized as a producer/consumer graph rather than a library. Three artifacts *produce* shared state, and twenty notebooks *consume* it. Notebook `01` trains and saves the random-forest classifier; notebook `02` builds the AlphaFold-derived per-residue table `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl`; notebook `03` builds the human transmembrane-protein table `hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl` (plus `AF_IDR_v3.pkl`); and the external mdSAM identification pipeline contributes the motif table `dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl`, which is shipped pre-built in `files/`. A new analysis plugs into this graph by loading the same assets with the same conventions.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Producers
        N01["01_train_waltzdb_classifier"] -->|"joblib.dump"| M[("models/rf_4.sav<br/>RF model + feature DataFrame")]
        N02["02_alphafold_residue_table"] -->|"AF2.to_pickle"| AF[("files/<br/>AF2_with_ENSG.pkl")]
        N03["03_mdsam_sequence_logos"] -->|"TMs.to_pickle"| TM[("files/<br/>hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl")]
        PIPE["mdSAM identification pipeline<br/>(STAR Methods)"] -->|"to_pickle"| DS[("files/<br/>dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl")]
    end
    subgraph Consumers
        C["Notebooks 04-23<br/>and your new analysis"]
    end
    M --> C
    AF --> C
    TM --> C
    DS --> C
```

This is why reusing the toolkit means copying *cells and conventions*, not importing modules: each notebook re-declares its imports and helpers at the top (for example, the identical `MUNV940103` amino-acid index dictionary appears in both notebook 01 and notebook 02), so a new notebook should do the same rather than expecting an importable package.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L24-L29), [files/README.md](/files/README.md#L5-L9), [notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](/notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L22-L25), [notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](/notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L22-L24)

## Core Reusable Assets

Three pickled DataFrames and one model checkpoint form the complete reusable state. The `files/README.md` documents exactly which notebooks read which file, and the motif sequence always lives in the `AAseq` column — a naming convention reinforced inside the notebooks themselves (notebook 03 renames an unnamed first column to `AAseq` with `df_enumerate.rename(columns={0: "AAseq"})`).

| Asset | Contents | Producer | Consumed by (notebook numbers) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `files/dSAM_MPs_v_paper_v2_new_locs.pkl` | The mdSAM motif table; motif sequence in `AAseq` | External mdSAM identification pipeline (STAR Methods) | 05, 06, 07, 08, 09, 15, 18, 20, 21, 23 |
| `files/hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl` | Human transmembrane proteins with UniProt topology annotation | `03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb` (`TMs.to_pickle`) | 03, 05, 06, 07, 08, 09, 15, 18, 20, 21, 23 |
| `files/AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` | AlphaFold-derived per-protein annotations with Ensembl gene IDs (ENSG) | `02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb` (`AF2.to_pickle`, cell 205) | 02, 03, 05, 06, 07, 08, 11, 15, 18, 19, 20, 21, 23 |
| `models/rf_4.sav` + `RandomForestClassifier_DataFrame.sav` | Trained random-forest classifier and its training feature DataFrame | `01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb` (`joblib.dump`) | Cross-notebook scoring runs |

> [!TIP]
> Two naming traps when reusing: (1) older notebooks and file names say **dSAM** where the paper says **mdSAM** — they are the same object, per the README's naming note; (2) cell references in all documentation are **0-based** indices into the notebook's `cells` list, so "cell 205" means the 206th cell.

Sources: [files/README.md](/files/README.md#L5-L13), [README.md](/README.md#L21), [README.md](/README.md#L33), [notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](/notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L48-L53)

## Pattern 1 — Scoring New Peptides with the Saved Classifier

The single most reusable component is the hexapeptide classifier workflow: build a feature vector (summed beta-strand free energy from AAindex entry `MUNV940103` plus one-hot-encoded residues), load the persisted model with `joblib`, and call `predict`. The final production classifier uses `RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=700, min_samples_split=2, min_samples_leaf=1, max_features=3, max_depth=None, bootstrap=False)`, evaluated with `StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5)`; one fitted model per fold is written to `models/rf_%d.sav`, and notebook 01 reloads fold 4 for its test-set analysis. Reuse follows exactly the same sequence:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Input peptide sequence"] --> B["Sum MUNV940103 beta-strand<br/>free energy over residues"]
    B --> C["One-hot encode residues<br/>pd.get_dummies(pd.Series(list(seq)))"]
    C --> D["Assemble feature vector in the exact<br/>training column order"]
    D --> E["joblib.load('models/rf_4.sav')"]
    E --> F["rf.predict(features.reshape(1, -1))"]
    F --> G{"Prediction"}
    G -->|"1 (amyloid)"| H["SAM candidate"]
    G -->|"0"| I["Non-amyloid window"]
    H --> J["Apply disorder gates:<br/>pLDDT < 70, solvent-exposed,<br/>non-TM, non-signal-peptide"]
    J --> K["mdSAM call requires<br/>consecutive positive windows ≥ threshold"]
```

The table below contrasts each step's original notebook cell with the minimal adaptation for a standalone script:

| Step | Notebook 01 original | Minimal standalone adaptation |
|---|---|---|
| Beta energy | `dff.append({'beta': np.sum([MUNV940103[i] for i in waltzdb.loc[k,'Sequence']])})` | `beta = sum(MUNV940103[a] for a in seq)` |
| One-hot encoding | `pd.get_dummies(waltzdb['Sequence'].apply(lambda x: pd.Series(list(x))))` (batch) | `pd.get_dummies(pd.Series(list(seq)))` (single peptide) |
| Model load | `rf = joblib.load('models/rf_4.sav')` | identical, after re-running notebook 01 to regenerate `models/` |
| Prediction | `rf.predict(np.array(df.drop(['classification','type'], axis=1).loc[i,:]).reshape(1, -1))[0]` | `rf.predict(X.reshape(1, -1))[0]` where `X` follows the saved column order |
| Persistence | `joblib.dump(rf, '.../RandomForestClassifier_model.sav')` + `joblib.dump(df.drop(['type'],axis=1), '.../RandomForestClassifier_DataFrame.sav')` | keep both saves — the DataFrame *is* the column-order contract |

> [!TIP]
> The saved `RandomForestClassifier_DataFrame.sav` is the true interface, not just a byproduct: one-hot encoding via `pd.get_dummies` only emits columns for residues actually present, so single-peptide inference can silently produce a different column layout than training. Always reindex your inference matrix against that saved DataFrame's columns (minus `type`) before calling `predict`.

For hyperparameter exploration, notebook 01 also contains the full `RandomizedSearchCV` grid (200–2000 estimators, `max_features` in `['auto','sqrt']`, depth 10–110 or `None`, `min_samples_split` 2/5/10, `min_samples_leaf` 1/2/4, bootstrap on/off), which you can lift directly if you retrain on a updated WALTZ-DB export.

Sources: [notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](/notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L22-L25), [notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](/notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L148-L161), [notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](/notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L303-L340), [notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](/notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L402-L429), [notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](/notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L528-L529), [notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](/notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L613-L633)

## Pattern 2 — Reusing the Shared Tables in a New Notebook

Every consumer notebook follows one loading convention, and your new notebook should copy it verbatim: launch Jupyter with `notebooks/` as the working directory, then load shared assets with the relative prefix `../files/`. Notebook 03 demonstrates the canonical form: `AF2 = pd.read_pickle('../files/AF2_with_ENSG.pkl')`. Because the shipped tables are pickled DataFrames, they load with full column structure intact — the motif table's `AAseq` column, the topology table's UniProt annotations, and the AlphaFold table's ENSG keys are immediately queryable without any parsing code.

| Convention | Rule | Why it matters for reuse |
|---|---|---|
| Working directory | Run with `notebooks/` as CWD | All relative paths (`../files/...`, `models/...`) resolve only from there |
| Shared asset path | `pd.read_pickle('../files/<name>.pkl')` | Matches every consumer notebook; breaking this breaks the cross-notebook cache |
| Motif sequence column | Always `AAseq` | All filtering/joining logic across 10+ notebooks keys on it |
| Identifier columns | `acc` (UniProt) and `ENSG` (Ensembl gene) | The join keys linking motifs ↔ AlphaFold residues ↔ topology |
| New outputs | Persist with `df.to_pickle(...)` / `joblib.dump(...)` | Same mechanism that produced `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` and `hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl` |

The pickles carry a documented safety caveat: they can execute code on load and depend on the pandas version that wrote them, so load them only from this repository and keep a compatible pandas version. When your new analysis produces a derived table other notebooks might use, mirror the producers: write it to pickle and document it in a `files/`-style README.

Sources: [files/README.md](/files/README.md#L3), [files/README.md](/files/README.md#L13-L14), [notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](/notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L38-L40), [files/README.md](/files/README.md#L7-L9)

## Pattern 3 — Rebuilding the Annotation Tables Instead of Trusting the Pickles

If you need the pipeline to run end-to-end (for example, after a WALTZ-DB update), the two shipped tables are regenerable from the notebooks themselves. Notebook 02 writes `AF2_with_ENSG.pkl` at cell 205 (`AF2.to_pickle`), and notebook 03 writes `hTMs_uniprot_v1.pkl` via `TMs.to_pickle` plus `AF_IDR_v3.pkl`. The disorder logic that turns raw AlphaFold predictions into mdSAM calls is visible in notebook 02's gating function, `f(x, y) = (1/(1+exp(-2*(x-2)))) * (1/(1+exp(.5*(y-70))))` — a logistic decay over the number of consecutive amyloid-classified windows and the pLDDT score, encoding the "pLDDT < 70" and "consecutive positive windows" thresholds from the discovery protocol. Lifting this function gives you the exact scoring surface without re-deriving the statistics.

Notebook 03 also shows what regeneration *doesn't* cover: it reads side intermediates (`enumerate/enumerate.pkl`, `topology_df`, and an `AF2_background.pkl` on an external volume) that are not shipped in the repository, and the README explicitly notes some notebooks still read unshipped intermediates. Budget for reconstructing those from the STAR Methods if you need the full logo/topology stage.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L40-L41), [files/README.md](/files/README.md#L8-L9), [notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb](/notebooks/02_alphafold_residue_table_and_early_plots.ipynb#L82-L84), [notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](/notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L48-L53), [README.md](/README.md#L248)

## Locating Reusable Code: FIGURE_MAP.csv and the Cell-Level Index

Because the toolkit is cell-granular, the fastest way to find a reusable snippet is by *figure panel*. The repository ships `FIGURE_MAP.csv` — a machine-readable map from paper panel → notebook → cell — and the README expands the same mapping as human-readable tables (e.g., panel 1D → notebook 01 cell 26; panel 2D membrane-leaflet distance → notebook 08 cell 45). Cell numbers are 0-based indices into the `.ipynb` `cells` list. Notebooks are distributed with outputs cleared, so locate the cell, run the notebook, and the plotting/statistics code materializes in place — this locate-then-run loop is the intended reuse path for every panel in the paper.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L28), [README.md](/README.md#L33), [README.md](/README.md#L90), [README.md](/README.md#L96-L99), [README.md](/README.md#L112-L113)

## Practical Constraints and Troubleshooting

Reusing cells outside their original environment hits a small, well-defined set of obstacles. All of them are visible in the code itself:

| Symptom | Cause in the code | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `ImportError: iupred2a_lib` | `sys.path.append('/Users/aelazar/Downloads/iupred2a/')` — a local, author-machine path | Install/clone IUPred2A and point `sys.path` at your own copy |
| `FileNotFoundError` on `enumerate/enumerate.pkl`, `topology_df`, `/Volumes/aelazar/...` | Unshipped intermediates read by some notebooks (03 and others) | Rebuild those intermediates or skip those cells; README flags this explicitly |
| `AttributeError: 'DataFrame' object has no attribute 'append'` | Notebooks use the removed `df.append(...)` (pandas ≥ 2.0) | Replace with `pd.concat` |
| `ValueError` on `max_features='auto'` | Removed in scikit-learn ≥ 1.3 (appears in notebook 01's exploration cells) | Use `max_features=3` as the final production classifier does |
| Model files missing | `models/rf_4.sav` was saved at runtime; notebooks ship with cleared outputs | Re-run `01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb` to regenerate `models/` |
| Pickle load warnings or failures | Pickles execute code and bind to the writing pandas version | Load only from this repo with a compatible pandas version |

Notebooks were written for interactive sessions and import a wide stack (`Bio`, `Levenshtein`, `fcsparser`, `geopandas`, `gseapy`, `holoviews`, `localcider`, `logomaker`, `joblib`, `iupred2a_lib`, among others — pip names may differ from import names), so provision the environment before running any notebook rather than cell-by-cell.

Sources: [notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](/notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L16-L19), [notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb](/notebooks/03_mdsam_sequence_logos.ipynb#L48-L53), [notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](/notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L159), [notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](/notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L314), [notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb](/notebooks/01_train_waltzdb_classifier.ipynb#L340), [files/README.md](/files/README.md#L13-L14), [README.md](/README.md#L244-L250)
